content: This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Jensen Huang, the 24-year-old software engineer and founder of the AI startup Lycana. He is based in Singapore. This essay has been edited for length and clarity. Since grade school, I've known that Nvidia's Jensen Huang exists. I've followed his news forever. When I was young, I really looked up to him. I've been really interested in computing and building stuff for a very, very long time. I remember asking my mom for a GPU when I was 16. It was a GTX 1080. I used it for a lot of gaming, and I did some app-building and programming of my own. I remember being a kid and knowing this technology would blow up. It's come full circle, since I'm now an AI founder. The first time someone in passing talked about my name was when the AI boom was starting. Most of it is: "Oh! Your name is exactly like that guy." Or: "Hey, give me Nvidia stock." The name makes me particularly memorable. When I go to a networking event, if I see someone I've seen one time before, they'll remember me. They'll be like: "It's you! The Nvidia CEO!" Most of the job interviews I've had in the last four years have said, "Oh yeah, you're the Nvidia CEO." I think that has given me a particular edge when it comes to employment. I believe that if people can remember your name, that's a huge leg up. When I interviewed for AI companies, some of them would say, "Got any extra GPUs?" My first thought was: Holy crap, my name's going to be dragged through the mud.                                    Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                  To me, he's always been the guy announcing GPUs. It's fairly clean. I don't know if it's a result of my Asian upbringing, but I never thought he'd be capable of doing that. The first reported affair was like, "Holy crap, that's crazy." The second one was like, "I don't even know how to react to that." My opinion of him has definitely diminished. I still think his accomplishments are his and that they're visionary, but that doesn't give him a free pass to do this kind of thing. It doesn't excuse the behavior. My friends come up to me like, "Yo, what are you doing to my stock?" Or, "How many girls is it this time?" It's not that funny, but I don't take it personally. There's no such thing as bad publicity. On a whim, I was like: "Let's say something and be funny." I didn't expect my LinkedIn posts to go so viral. Some commenters are just joking, but others are serious. Some of them think it's actually him and ask: Why did you cheat? I'm not sure that's the best for my image. A future employer may look at that. The problem comes when people think I'm him. I've had friends send me stuff on Reddit and the Chinese social media platform RedNote. Someone took a screenshot of my LinkedIn post and used it to discuss Nvidia on Chinese social media. That was the big one: people who don't know me are putting me in the discussion. My Nvidia shares are in the dumps. It was my most profitable stock for a while, until now. Personally, I don't think it will be that bad. Most interviewers take me at the merit of my character or my skills. Let's pray none of that gets hit by virtue of my name. There are more eyes on what I'm building. I saw a 5,000-viewer spike from visitors who came to the site because of it. A few people bought subscriptions. I applied to Y Combinator and other accelerators from venture capital firms. The personal thesis I have is that some of these venture capitalists choose based on the ability of founders to market themselves. If this is what it takes for them to notice me, then hey, I'm all for it. Jump to

If you thought the foldable craze got crazy when only Android OEMs were involved, it got even crazier with the Apple iPhone Duo. A recent analytics report for Q3 2026 spells out how crazy things got and what 2027 could have in store. A report by Smart Analytics Global (SAG) on global foldable shipment performance in Q3 2026 highlights one Android OEM's staggering lead. The report states that global foldable shipments declined 2% YoY, which translates to "over 7.5 million units shipped." However, Samsung saw a 13% YoY increase this past quarter, thanks to the Galaxy Z Fold 8, accounting for 69% of the foldable market share. This is important—the form factor, specifically. The Fold 8 is the company's first wide-foldable. Many other OEMs, such as Chinese companies, have also adopted this wider, often shorter foldable design. SAG's report states Samsung experienced "double-digit shipment growth in both South Korea and Europe," as well. A notable competitor, Huawei, accounts for 14% of the foldable share in Q3. The Pura X View was a significant contributor, despite the report noting a small YoY decline in shipments. SAG then flips the script. While the market has struggled, it forecasts "a new growth cycle" next year. Shipments might grow 55% YoY in 2027. Wide foldables might account for most phone shipments next year, driven by Samsung's device, the Apple iPhone Duo, and others from Chinese makers.      Some of this data is a little interesting. This was a while ago, but in 2024, Huawei topped Samsung in foldable shipments. The Chinese OEM became the world's leader in foldable shipments. This was a "turning point," one could say, for Samsung. It came at a time when many believed Samsung had become complacent with its Galaxy Z series: the Flip and Fold. Samsung's shipments fell 42% year-over-year in Q1 2024, while Huawei increased by a massive 257% YoY. Currently, you have Huawei's Pura X View, the industry's first wide foldable, which didn't perform as well for the company as the Fold 8 did for Samsung. SAG's 2027 outlook is certainly intriguing, but it will take consumers buying new phones to make it happen. The market dropped 20% YoY. Still, Samsung claimed the top spot because of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra. Everything is in flux right now. Some analysts foresee a turnaround, while others firmly believe we're in for more trying times in 2027. The main thing is pricing. If phones are priced well and buyers can afford them, things will change. But we've seen how prices have gone. Moto's Signature 27 is $1,599, and that's not even a foldable—it's a standard slab phone. Other foldables are $2,000; I know we were all paying attention to Apple's iPhone Duo launch. Wide foldables are cool (I almost got one), but plenty of variables are getting in the way of a turnaround. Nickolas is always excited about tech and getting his hands on it. Writing for him can vary from delivering the latest tech story to scribbling in his journal. When Nickolas isn't hitting a story, he's often grinding away at a game or chilling with a book in his hand. It was July of 2024, and Jensen Huang was punchy. I had agreed to travel to Denver, Colorado, to interview the Nvidia CEO at SIGGRAPH, the annual confab of computer graphics PhDs and practitioners. Early that year I’d conducted a lengthy sit-down interview with Huang for a WIRED magazine feature, which apparently went well enough—both for WIRED and for Nvidia’s executive communications team—that I had been asked to interview Huang again at this conference. Another opportunity to grill the CEO of the modern world’s most consequential company? Yes, of course. I began preparing. What ensued was, in a word, bizarre. During the first prep call for the conference, the type of call-in which PR handlers typically try to coax specific questions out of journalists to prevent an ambush, a youngish, vaguely familiar woman took the lead. This was Madison Huang, Jensen’s daughter. She was clearly intelligent, commanding respect. She told me about the slides Jensen would be presenting on stage at SIGGRAPH and offered suggestions for key moments when I might tee him up to talk about the slides. Slides? Tee up Jensen? What kind of “interview” was this? I raised my concerns with both my editors and Nvidia. We agreed that I would ask the questions I intended to ask him, which included questions about the environmental impact of data centers, and that Huang would also be referring to slides. Let’s just say the interview didn’t go smoothly. (It’s on YouTube.) To this day, former and current Nvidia workers sometimes tell me that I “handled” the whole thing well. Huang was domineering, evaded some of my questions, and, immediately after our session concluded, did an impromptu Q&A session with a much more adoring crowd than me. Then I was guided offstage, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg hopped on, where he and Huang had a lovey-dovey fireside chat. As a longtime journalist I’m used to occasional adversarial interactions; I really don’t lose sleep over them. This was just a CEO being a CEO. Huang later agreed to meet with me again, in December 2024. But that interview in Denver had underscored for me how much Jensen Huang wanted to control the narrative. Not just wanted to; he assumed he would. And to a large extent he did. Until this week. Narrative has always been a critical part of Huang’s success. He was not just your average electrical engineering nerd who toiled away on something that would eventually find a product-market fit. By Huang’s own telling, he was an immigrant founder, an underdog, a wife guy who chased (and eventually married) his college sweetheart, a scrappy startup guy who dined at Denny’s in the early days. A visionary who worked Sundays and who didn’t sleep well because he always heard the hoof steps of competitors. A parent who brought his kids into the corporate fold. A man who loved Nvidia so much he tattooed an abstract version of the company logo on his arm. Huang built the highest-valued publicly traded company in history. That part’s not just fairy tale. It’s true. Now, it’s starting to read more like a Greek tragedy. Back in January 2024, when I sat down with him for our first-ever in-person meeting, Huang right off the bat talked about the importance of storytelling. Here’s an excerpt: Jensen Huang: Somebody who I really admire, as a leader and a person, is Shantanu Narayen, the CEO of Adobe. He said he always wanted to be a journalist because he loved telling stories. WIRED: It seems like an important part of building a business, being able to tell its story effectively. Yes. Strategy setting is storytelling. Culture building is storytelling. You’ve said many times you didn’t sell the idea of Nvidia based on a pitch deck. That’s right. It was really about telling the story. Of course, even then, Huang was caught up in the crosshairs of the US–China AI war and at the mercy of regulators, as I wrote at the time. After Donald Trump’s reelection that year, Huang once again deployed his storytelling skills and lobbied the Trump administration to loosen export controls, so he could sell some of his company’s chips to China. Another crucial part of the Huang lore is that he ran a “flat” organization, with a few dozen top executives reporting to him. (This is sometimes reported as being “60” people; insiders have told me at times it’s closer to 35.) Huang once said the structure allowed Nvidia “to adapt a lot more quickly, which we need because our technology is moving so quickly.” Huang was also known to be controlling of all aspects of the business—participating in every significant meeting, seemingly aware of every moving part, and staying in the loop on sourcing, supply chains, and the company’s allocation of chips. This is where Huang’s cult of leadership, and his Nvidia storytelling, may have come to a stupidly disappointing final chapter. As one former employee put it, Huang can’t simultaneously have had knowledge of every element of Nvidia’s business and then potentially feign ignorance about where the chips may have fallen, both figuratively and literally. His apparent lapses in judgment have now led him to resign from the very company he coaxed into existence and have shattered the mythos of its ever-prescient founder. It’s certainly not the narrative ending Huang would have chosen, were he still in control. This is an edition of Steven Levy’s and Lauren Goode's Backchannel newsletter. GameStopX25Xbox Series X  Microsoft just made its 25th Anniversary Xbox Series X console available, and it was on sale for approximately 0.3 seconds. Scalpers swooped in and bought the lot in the most tediously predictable way, with presumably one or two legitimate customers squeaking in alongside them. And in the midst of all this, GameStop managed to list the $900 machine for $4,950. In fact, even the direct link from Microsoft’s own site will take you to a page offering it for that price. The special edition Series X is made in a translucent green to match the design of the original Xbox from 2001, and is intended to sell for an already incredibly steep $900. (Bear in mind this is just the 1TB model.) It comes with a modern controller in matching see-through green, with both machine and controller engraved with “XBOX 25,” and you get a copy of Halo: Campaign Evolved thrown in too. However, none of this justifies a $5000 price. It’s deeply peculiar that in these times, when pretty much any special edition of anything gaming-related sells out instantaneously, Microsoft wouldn’t have instituted some sort of limitations on how the console could be bought. Instead, the green machines were in stock for a matter of seconds before being listed as “sold out” or “coming soon.” Or in the case of Walmart, just entirely delisted from the store like it never existed. GameStop still seems to have stock, however! At the time of this writing, I was able to add the $4,950 X25 edition to my basket, where it then added $7.99 in shipping and handling, and another $353.26 in tax. A mere $5,311.25! Gamestop increases preorder prices of the Xbox 25th Console by $500 overnight. byu/plagueislandcc inxbox  Last night Reddit users noticed that GameStop had bumped the pre-order price for the X25 up to $1,500, ahead of it actually going on sale. Now another $3,450 as been tacked on. Why? Our best guess is that this is GameStop attempting to price-match what it’s finding elsewhere for “used” versions, i.e. the scalping prices people are aiming for on secondhand markets. eBay is currently flooded with offers for the machine at around $1,700, and the highest I’ve found is $2,395.95,Â so somehow GameStop is even doubling this. This very much matches GameStop’s current model for selling PokÃ©mon cards, with the outlet appearing to have become a store-based scalping company for the TCG. Nvidia's drama adds a new twist to Anthropic's upcoming IPO, a longtime partner of the chip giant. Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on Thursday after an extramarital affair and possible foreign influence scandal rocked the company — and the wider AI industry. Here are three ways Nvidia's woes could affect Anthropic and its $1.4 trillion IPO. Mandeep Singh, an analyst for Bloomberg Intelligence covering Anthropic, said in a note published before Huang's ouster that Nvidia's $10 billion share of a planned IPO-day investment "could face heightened scrutiny" if Huang were removed. Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, now leads in the interim. "A leadership transition could prompt Nvidia's board to reassess the size, timing or strategic rationale of the commitment to Anthropic," Singh wrote. "Any delay or reduction could weaken an important signal of support for Anthropic's IPO pricing at around $1.4 trillion, though commitments from Google and other strategic investors might limit the financing impact." Harrison Rolfes, an analyst for PitchBook, expects the deal to go through as planned. "It has nothing to do with Jensen's overall control," he told Business Insider. "It's just: 'We made the investment, and we're good to go.'" The bigger question mark, in Rolfes' mind, concerns Anthropic's rush to secure access to as many computing chips as possible as it scales. That relies in part on deals with Nvidia-backed "neoclouds," or AI data center developers. The IPO prospectus listed a $45 billion agreement with Nscale and a $41 billion agreement with Lambda — both are for Nvidia chips, and both companies rely on Nvidia's support for financing. Rolfes expects current deals to stay, and later ones to come in more slowly. "Instead of, let's say, Dario or Elon Musk just calling Jensen to say, 'Hey, I need this by whenever,' it's now going to have to go through the bureaucracy of Nvidia," Rolfes said. Kunjan Sobhani, a Bloomberg Intelligence analyst who covers Nvidia, likewise said he expects the company's commitments to remain in place, though future rounds might slow down since Huang was so instrumental in dealmaking. Amodei and Huang's fortunes and successes were often tied at the hip. Nvidia's chip breakthroughs have enabled Anthropic to deliver more AI tokens and boost its revenues. At the same time, the two had a stark and long-lasting disagreement over US chip export policy. In 2025, Amodei wrote a Wall Street Journal op-ed calling export controls a "valuable tool in slowing China's AI development," adding that President Donald Trump's actions would "help determine whether democracies or autocracies lead the next technological era." Huang, meanwhile, lobbied in the other direction and secured the Trump administration's approval for the sale of his H200 chips in China, with individual Commerce Department approvals. At the Davos conference last February, Amodei likened the US administration's choice to allow certain Nvidia chips to be sold to China to "selling nuclear weapons to North Korea." Huang rejected the comparison as "lunacy" in a podcast shortly after. While Huang cozied up to Trump during his second term, his exit from Nvidia could weaken his influence. And the House Committee on Foreign Affairs is probing his relationship with Chinese executive Alice Huang, whose Singapore-based firm bought many Nvidia chips. Politico reported Thursday that the former Nvidia CEO has agreed to testify. Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are now coming out in support of stronger chip export restrictions — a win for Amodei. Huang also supported open models, which compete with Anthropic's and OpenAI's closed models. The promotion of open models aligns with Nvidia's business strategy, Sobhani said, so he doesn't expect the company to withdraw its support, though "the investment in that area could slow down." One pillar of Anthropic's IPO pitch looks particularly strong amid Nvidia's turmoil: it doesn't rely too heavily on Nvidia's hardware. In addition to Nvidia's chips, Anthropic uses chips from Amazon Web Services, Google, Broadcom, and AMD. AMD and Broadcom both compete with Nvidia, and each saw its stock jump on Thursday's news. More of Nvidia's top-end chips wouldn't hurt, though. If the government does impose tighter export restrictions, it would likely mean more of its chips end up in American data centers, expanding the pool of compute that Anthropic buys as it scales. Sobhani said he doesn't expect Huang's exit to affect Nvidia chips' performance, competitiveness, or the overall supply the company can make available, at least in the short- to medium-term. That said, Nvidia's first earnings report without Huang at the helm takes place Tuesday, with Anthropic's IPO expected in the days after that. "We'll get more color next week about what really we should expect," Sobhani said. Have a tip? Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger are having a viral moment following Jensen Huang's departure as Nvidia CEO. The AI chipmaker's founder stepped down Thursday following a scandal-filled week surrounding his personal life and relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. The dayslong saga prompted many online commentators to share famous warnings from the former chairman and late vice-chairman of Berkshire Hathaway. "My partner Charlie says: there's only 3 ways that a smart person can go broke -- he says 'liquor, ladies and leverage'" - Warren Buffet                                  https://t.co/r9DOOfcnEZ "My partner Charlie says that there's only three ways that a smart person can go broke: liquor, ladies, and leverage," Buffett said in a 2018 interview. Charlie Munger seeing his “Liquor, Ladies, Leverage” quote being used more times in a 72 hours timeframe than any other time in human history https://t.co/NA5yNOOKdL "Now, the truth is the first two he just added because they start with 'l' — it's leverage," Buffett added. Charlie Munger once said liquor, leverage, and ladies are the downfall of men.                                  Everyone thought AI would blow up over leverage, but no one was prepared for it to be women. Huang admitted to being "unfaithful" to his wife following reports that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. He resigned as CEO after fresh claims that he had an affair with a subordinate. Charlie Munger once said smart people go broke in three ways. Liquor, ladies, and leverage. https://t.co/6Ip17Gs9XH Munger's caution about the risks of romantic entanglements has even been translated into other languages in recent days: «Solo hay tres formas en las que una persona inteligente puede arruinarse: el alcohol, las mujeres y el apalancamiento».                                  Charlie Munger https://t.co/rYsqGdBRM0 X users have also been relaying a classic piece of Buffett wisdom about how reputations are hard-won and easily lost. “It takes 20 years to build a reputation  and 5 minutes to ruin it.”                                  Buffett tried to tell them all and no one listened Buffett has been issuing similar refrains for decades. He famously warned Salomon Brothers employees as their interim chairman in 1991: "Lose money for the firm, and I will be understanding. Lose a shred of reputation for the firm, and I will be ruthless." But we can't afford to lose reputation—even a shred of reputation." “It takes 20 years to build a reputation and five minutes to ruin it.”                                  — Warren Buffett https://t.co/wZcic1lkQx The legendary investor has also famously advised people to never do anything they wouldn't want printed on the front page of their hometown newspaper for all their friends and family to see. Munger, Buffett's right-hand man for over 45 years, died at age 99 in November 2023. Buffett, now 96, stepped down as Berkshire's CEO at the end of last year, and as its chairman in September. Berkshire stock has rallied strongly in recent days as investors have soured on AI stocks like Nvidia amid concerns about overinvestment and fears of a regulatory crackdown. An unspecified problem forced Elon Musk's SpaceX on Friday to abort the recovery of the booster for the world's biggest and most powerful rocket, the Starship, but the company hoped it could yet pull off a first-ever "catch" of the spaceship. The 124-meter (407-foot) Starship roared into the sky from Starbase in southern Texas for its 15th test flight, but minutes later, the landmark nature of the mission went awry. After lift-off and the mid-air separation of the two stages, an issue with the Super Heavy booster forced SpaceX to divert it to an "offshore splashdown" -- scuttling what would have been a groundbreaking twin capture of both components of the rocket. A fireball erupted as the booster fell into the Gulf of Mexico near the launch site, with a section sticking out vertically afterward. "Not sure right now why we weren't able to bring it back," SpaceX's Dan Huot said. Meanwhile, the Starship spacecraft that gives the rocket system its name entered Earth's orbit, where it was expected to circle the globe 14 times before returning Saturday. Successful recoveries of both Starship and its booster would have marked a milestone in the space industry's decades-long pursuit of fully reusable rocket systems that can drastically reduce mission costs and make frequent launches possible. Clayton Swope, an aerospace expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, called the mission a "mixed bag so far" after the failure to catch the Super Heavy, something SpaceX has done three times previously. "At least the Starship made it to orbit, like on the last test flight," he said. Some versions of the Starship spacecraft are designed to launch internet satellites and data centers into orbit, while other iterations will be made to ferry people to the Moon and Mars. US space agency NASA is counting on Starship to serve as a lunar lander on its Artemis mission, and administrator Jared Isaacman congratulated SpaceX Friday for "another spectacular launch" -- without mentioning the booster disappointment. - System checks - SpaceX plans to return Starship to Earth after more than 22 hours of flight and recover it at around 3:20 pm (2120 GMT) Saturday at the launch site. The "catch" is extraordinarily complex because the spaceship will be falling much faster and from a much higher altitude than the booster, with the vessel forced to withstand the extreme heat of reentering Earth's atmosphere. Like the three previous Super Heavy recoveries, Starship is meant to carry out a controlled descent and nestle between two mechanical "chopstick arms" at the launch site. "We'll only go for it if the ship passes all of these system checks and decision gates along the way, and there are lots of them," SpaceX's Kate Tice said. Due to the risks of losing control of Starship, SpaceX has planned for various scenarios where it will shorten the test flight and plunge the spaceship into the Pacific Ocean if necessary. While in space, the Starship launched 26 satellites to join others in Musk's Starlink satellite internet constellation. - Refueling challenge - Musk, the world's richest person, has already revolutionized the space sector with the partially reusable Falcon rockets, which are regularly employed to launch satellites and carry astronauts to the International Space Station. But the Starship project has been plagued by years-long delays as SpaceX grapples with novel engineering challenges, including how to transfer fuel to the spaceship while in orbit -- a requirement for any journey to the Moon or Mars. Following SpaceX's high-profile stock market debut in June that raised about $85.7 billion, the company is investing heavily in stepping up production and launch capabilities. Tech > Services & Software > AI Tech insiders and commentators say Nvidia will survive Huang's departure, but it's time for more accountability among CEOs. Principal Writer Principal Writer  				Edited by Jon Skillings  November 12, 2026, 8:30 pm ET What now for Nvidia? This was the question on everyone’s lips at the illustrious Web Summit technology conference in Lisbon on Thursday in the hours after CEO Jensen Huang announced his resignation. Huang’s departure followed a series of allegations that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an Nvidia employee and one with a woman who has been identified as a possible Chinese spy. The company, whose computer chips are at the core of generative AI’s disruptive powers, is valued at around $4 trillion, making it one of the most valuable in the world. A co-founder, Huang has been with Nvidia since its earliest days three decades ago, making it hard to imagine the company without him at the helm. There’s nothing quite like a salacious, market-moving scandal to create a buzz at a tech event. The Web Summit organizers leaned into the news, quickly assembling a panel of tech experts to discuss whether Nvidia was bigger than its CEO. More from CNET Nothing in the allegations changes the fact that Huang is probably the godfather of the AI revolution, said investor and financial writer Adam Kobeissi. “He was the central figure,” Kobeissi said, even if he wasn’t the only person responsible for Nvidia’s success. “This company is going to survive and thrive with or without him,” he added. “I don’t think this is some sort of bubble-popping moment where everything comes crumbling down.” Sweeping financial investments and expectations across the AI industry have driven stock prices and company valuations to dizzying heights, with many critics warning of a bubble just waiting to burst with destabilizing effects. As powerful as Nvidia has become, it could be caught in the center of such a maelstrom.  While such a concentration of power is not the way to create resilient companies, said Ryan LaSalle, CEO of cybersecurity company Nisos, like Kobeissi he thinks Nvidia will weather the storm.  Interim Nvidia CEO Collette Kress, who has been with the company since 2013, is known for having a ton of loyalty within Nvidia, he said. “In a company of that much brainpower, there will be some natural leaders who can help shepherd them to the next chapter.” One big question put to panel participants was whether Nvidia’s board made a mistake allowing one person to have so much power.  It wasn’t just a mistake of corporate culture, said Carissa Veliz, associate professor of philosophy at the Oxford Institute for Ethics in AI. It was also a mistake in terms of democracy. For one person to wield so much power over decisions affecting the economy and national security means something has gone wrong and has revealed how vulnerable we are, Veliz said. If we look at the history of corporations, she said, there used to be a tradition of proving to the government that you were doing good for your country to earn your right to exist and get certain tax breaks. “At the moment, we have shifted from that kind of framework to a framework in which a corporation is allowed to be essentially a kind of psychopath that only cares about its own profits, that only has duties to shareholders and which can be structured in any way, including a very powerful CEO with very little oversight,” she said. Gil Duran, author of The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy, said that he thought Nvidia’s errors in the lead-up to this moment would be studied in business and public relations crisis management classes. “The board was completely missing out on most of the truth and the facts,” he said, referencing news reports that said Huang a year ago hired a law firm known for covering up sex scandals and President Donald Trump in May had been told about the CEO’s affair with the alleged Chinese spy. “I don’t think there’s any other way to look at it but a catastrophe,” he said.  Duran and Veliz agreed that it was time to ensure tech CEOs face real oversight. “These guys face no accountability and no supervision, and that’s part of the problem,” said Veliz. “These kind of small kings have their own small kingdoms… and they get away with almost anything.” CEOs like Elon Musk at SpaceX and Sam Altman at OpenAI have enormous influence not only in their own companies but also across the national economy. What we’re seeing in Huang’s downfall is the shattering of a myth about genius founders, said Duran. He questioned whether it would spark actual change, however, given that the market’s addiction to the narrative of great, powerful founders. “The fact that they can just tumble markets with their personal lives that become geopolitical crises – this is an insane amount of power to outsource,” he said.  If we can tone down the myth, this moment provides a chance to look at where we’ve gone wrong and do better, Veliz said. There’s opportunity here, she added – to raise up companies that can build the kinds of technology we need, support democracies rather than erode them, aren’t based on surveillance and prediction, and can behave transparently. For every other tech behemoth out there, there is plenty to be learned from Huang’s downfall. The concentration of power in one individual is not, as LaSalle pointed out, a safe long-term strategy. What’s needed is more oversight and accountability from a company’s board of directors. In announcing Huang’s resignation, Nvidia also said it was appointing its first chairman for its board. Huang’s entanglement with a potential honeypot is also an opportunity for tech companies to think about security, said LaSalle. No matter how sophisticated cybersecurity threats are becoming in the age of AI, he added, “people are still the simplest way in.” Duran warned about the potential damage ahead if we fail to seize this as a moment to change. “If you look at the AI CEO vision of the future, it’s massive economic destruction so that a handful of people can become trillionaires,” he said. “No one voted for that. Nobody wants that, and we have a short window of time to collapse it before they collapse us.” Disclosure: Katie Collins traveled to Lisbon as a guest of Web Summit to serve as a panel moderator. Her reporting from the event was independent of that role.  		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. All rights reserved.

Home > Kitchen & Household If you're skipping this step when making pasta, you're leaving behind liquid gold. Contributor Contributor  				Edited by David Watsky  November 13, 2026, 10:06 am ET Among the suggestions home cooks often hear about unforgivable pasta sins, two top the list: overcooking and underseasoning. But you’ve already got this! You know to ignore the recommended cooking time by a minute or two, understanding that crossover cooking and/or added sauce will keep moving the needle toward perfect al dente, and you’re absolutely in the habit of salting your pasta cooking water to a degree that’s “like the sea.” Those two steps are crucial to get the best outcome for your pasta, no matter the shape, and they deserve top billing. But the world’s most practiced pasta cooks also follow a third maxim: Save your pasta water. I spoke to three chefs about why hanging onto this liquid gold is a habit you should always practice, no matter what kind of sauce you have — or even if there’s no sauce — simmering nearby. More from CNET  When pasta meets boiling water, it absorbs the seasoned liquid and releases starch. After its cooking time of roughly 5 to 10 minutes (shape and size dependent), what’s left over is almost akin to a stock and should be treated accordingly. While 10-minute pasta water may not have the texture and flavor of a long-simmered stock, it still delivers broth. Why toss it? “Pasta water is starchy, and when added to a sauce, it helps to bind the sauce to the pasta when the pasta and sauce are tossed together,” said chef Melissa Mastrianni-Oleary, founder of Keeping It Simple Italian. “It also helps prevent the sauce from drying out during tossing.” “If you ever hear your pasta sizzling in the pan as it cooks with your sauce, it’s your cue to add more pasta water to the pan,” said Jessica Mode, culinary instructor of Homebody Eats. “This sound means all of your liquid has cooked off, and you’ll need the water to keep the pasta hydrated and the sauce creamy.” When creaminess is the goal, the starchiness of the pasta water also acts as a natural thickener or emulsifier when it meets one or more other ingredients likely in your sauce. “The pasta water especially helps when doing buttery sauces,” said Ciro Fodera, culinary director of Capri Italian Steakhouse. “The starchy water allows the butter to emulsify into the sauce, giving that rich and creamy gloss of a properly made cacio e pepe.” While we’re on the subject of cacio, a ladle of pasta water also keeps shredded cheese from clumping in your pan. The starchy water also helps emulsify non-dairy ingredients, such as olive oil, into something that looks and feels creamy. Taking your pasta pot to the sink and draining all that goodness away is both unforgivable and unnecessary. Depending on the shape and how much pasta you are cooking, I personally subscribe to a method where a strainer or colander isn’t even necessary: A good pair of tongs or a slotted spoon can easily move the pasta from the boiling water directly into the saucepan. Some residual water on the pasta during the transfer will already start the magic. If that seems risky, messy, or time-consuming — admittedly, it takes practice — use a glass measuring cup to scoop out a generous amount of cooking liquid right before draining or set a pot or bowl in your sink to catch the drained water. Pasta pots with built-in colanders are also made for this. The more pasta water you save, the more you have to work with, both for the dish in progress and for the future. More on that below. Combining your cooked pasta with your sauce and adding a bit of pasta water to marry it all relies on intuition, but you can set yourself up for success with some practiced guidance. Start by undercooking your pasta. Yes, perhaps even more so than you already are. “You only want to slightly cook the pasta in boiling water,” said Mode. “After that, you’ll transfer the pasta to the pan with your sauce in it. During this process, you’ll ladle the pasta water along the side of the pan,” she said, while cautioning not to dump it directly on top of the pasta so that it emulsifies the sauce rather than gets further absorbed by the noodles. “Next, turn your heat to high and vigorously stir the pasta around,” Mode said. “The high heat, plus movement, in combination with pasta water is what gives you restaurant-quality pasta that’s perfectly cooked, with a creamy, jammy emulsion.” “I like to toss the pasta for a good 2 to 3 minutes so the pasta picks up the sauce and pasta water,” said Mastrianni-Oleary. “Sauce should not sit on top of pasta. The sauce should be absorbed by the pasta and flavor it a little from the inside.” Since it’s contributing flavor, Mastrianni-Oleary also notes another important consideration: “Not all pasta water is created equal,” she said. “Really good pasta water starts with really good pasta. Cheaper pasta does not produce great pasta water, so I prefer slightly more expensive pastas like Rummo.” Also, because you’ve generously seasoned your pasta water, keep that in mind when you first season your sauce. “I definitely have underestimated how salty my sauces can be when adding pasta water,” said Fodera. “Generally, the rule is to make sure you start your sauce with only a little salt. When you add the pasta water, it should increase the amount of salt to the perfect amount,” he said. “You can always add [salt], but you can’t take it away.” Saving pasta water for sauce cooking alongside the pasta is arguably mandatory, but as a present to future you, consider setting some aside for other projects where pasta isn’t actively cooking. “You can definitely freeze the pasta water,” said Fodera. Let it cool, then portion it into small containers or even an ice cube tray. “I’d use it for soups,” said Mastrianni-Oleary. “It will add a little starchiness to the soup along with salt.” A natural thickener and seasoning agent, reserved pasta water can also be used when cooking other grains. Plus, freezing your pasta water is a failsafe. “I’ve definitely been at home and not paying attention, so I dump all of my pasta water out in the sink,” Fodera said. “I’ll just pop an ice cube of the pasta water to finish my sauce with, so I don’t lose any of that flavor.”  		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. When shooting both photos and videos on my iPhone, I make regular use of a few different third-party apps, mostly because I like to take manual control. But a combination of the new Pro controls on the iPhone 18 Pro and a new feature introduced with iOS 27 means there are more times when I can stick to Apple’s stock Camera app. If you aren’t already using customizable controls, I highly recommend doing so … Developers know that a big reason for using third-party camera apps is being able to use them in much the same way you would a standalone camera. A key part of this is having easy access to manual control over things like aperture (on the iPhone 18 Pro), shutter speed, white balance, and choosing between manual and auto focus. Those settings are right there on the main screen of almost all third-party apps. With the iPhone 18 Pro, the same set of controls are also available in Apple’s stock camera app. By default, these are tucked inside a menu, requiring an initial tap to open it. As we noted back in September, however, iOS 27 brings customizable controls to the camera app. Simply open the menu and tap the Edit button (top-left when holding the phone vertically) and you can add any of the controls to the main screen. This makes them available in a single tap. For still photography, I have these: Aperture, shutter speed, and white balance as these are the three main manual controls I use. Exposure compensation, because sometimes the only reason I want to take manual control is to increase or decrease the exposure, and that provides a faster way of doing so (quicker than the alternative drag up/down within the photo, in my experience). Finally, I have one-tap access to the histogram to help in setting exposure. It’s a similar story in video mode. I again have aperture and white balance along with exposure compensation and the histogram. But here I add instant access to frame-rate and focus modes (as I’m more likely to switch focus mode when shooting video). Of course, third-party apps still have an important role, but this one change has made a big difference to me when using the stock camera app for both photos and video. Do you make use of this feature yourself? If so, please share the details in the comments. FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More. TOPICS                      columnists                           In the aftermath of Jensen Huang's resignation, not only may the AI bubble pop, but the world economy is in some peril      It's a story as old as time. Billionaire nerd boy meets girl. Girl is later suspected of being a spy. News at 11. Oh, and it's also been reported that he was having an affair with one of his direct-report employees. When Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang makes a "romantic" blunder, he doesn't do it halfway. The boss of the world's most valuable company – well, it was until recently, anyway – publicly resigned yesterday, November 12, as CEO, president, and board member, effective immediately. We don't know if he jumped or if he was pushed.  He left after admitting to having an affair. Although he never named an affair partner, one of the affairs was reported to be with Alice Huang, AKA Huang Le. She's head of the Chinese company Megaspeed, which was an Nvidia partner. Megaspeed is accused of being a front for China's government that was used to transfer Nvidia chips to China, although this hasn't been proven. Some US officials also suspect [PDF] she's working for Chinese intelligence, although the DoJ said it hasn't yet reached a conclusion about this. The final nail in Jensen's coffin came when The New York Times reported he had also allegedly had an affair with Nvidia's VP of health care, Kimberly Powell. Jeeze, guy!   In the aftermath, Nvidia's  CFO, Colette Kress, was appointed interim CEO. She won't, I suspect, be in the job for long. CFOs are not CEOs. The jobs aren't remotely the same.  In most companies, Huang would be replaced by the COO. That can't happen here. Nvidia doesn't have a COO. Both inside and outside of Nvidia, Huang is seen as Nvidia, and Nvidia as Huang. These days, billionaire CEOs are perceived as God-kings who know all and rule all. Much more often than not, that's BS.  That isn't the case with Nvidia. Huang co-founded Nvidia on April 5, 1993. He was appointed CEO on day one, and he never left the job. At first, the company staggered forward. When it released the GeForce 256 in 1999, which it marketed as the first GPU, it started on its path to becoming the chip manufacturer of choice for PC gamers. It still is today. That's a great niche, but it doesn't make a company a trillion-dollar business. No, the path to that dizzying height came when, in 2006, Nvidia unveiled CUDA. This programming architecture opened its GPUs' parallel-processing capabilities to scientific and other non-graphics workloads. From there, CUDA would become the foundation for most high-performance and AI computing.  Huang was at the center of it all. He still was until now. At KubeCon North America, the trade show for Kubernetes, used in well over half of all AI projects, I spoke to many Nvidia employees. There were two things they all mentioned. First, they were in a state of shock. Maybe the top brass and government officials both in China and the US knew Huang was fooling with fire; the developer rank-and-file folks I spoke to hadn't had a clue. The second was that every month, Huang held an all-hands meeting where, instead of a per-forma corporate pep rally, he answered questions from everyone and gave them real answers. He knew his technology well and actually led his company instead of just impressing gullible stock buyers.  Nvidia can't replace him. It really can't. I'm reminded of when John Sculley forced Steve Jobs out at Apple in 1985. If you're not old enough to remember, Apple did fine for a while, but then by the mid-90s, it lost its way. Apple got its mojo back, and started its rise to being one of the world's top companies only after Jobs came back in 1996.  The big difference, of course, is that Huang's not coming back. I heard many people say that Huang was "too big to fail." True, morality no longer matters much in the US – see Trump's kleptocracy – but this is different. Huang betrayed not just his wife, but his board, employees, and stockholders. If, as some suspect, the board knew full well what was going on, they should be tossed out too, but that's a story for another day. Oh, and as for Trump's suggestions that Apple's former CEO Tim Cook should become Nvidia's CEO? Give me a break.  Now the question of the day is: how can Nvidia recover from this blow? I don't think it can. I used to say that I didn't know where the AI companies were going, but I was sure that so long as capital kept flowing into Big AI, Nvidia was the one company you could count on that would make money. I think I was wrong.  What does that mean? In the short term, Nvidia stock, after dropping 14 percent in early trading on Thursday, is down "only" five percent. Despite all the Sturm und Drang over Huang's departure, the NASDAQ is actually, when I wrote this, up. Even Nvidia's bonds are holding steady.  Amazon and Google, which have their own horses in the AI TPU races, are hoping, of course, that Nvidia's misfortune will help them lever open the AI hardware market. In these early hours, I don't see that happening. Frankly, I'm amazed at how stockowners are shaking off Huang's resignation. The AI fever dream, for now, is continuing unabated.  That said, can this go on? This irrational exuberance rests on the belief that, no matter what happens, AI will continue to rule the stock market. Eventually, though, the bubble may pop, and that could put some strain on the global economy. For now, people are ignoring how bad this blow is, or perhaps they're not aware of it.  In a few years, I expect Huang's affair will be seen as the first needle in the AI bubble. ®      Safety reasons and unspecified communications issue cited       Forensic report finds Blackwell's fingerprint in DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group models       PARTNER CONTENT: Real-time endpoint data keeps AI-driven IT operations accurate, fast and under control       ‘We don’t have a security problem anymore. Employers are facing down a potential rush of PTO requests amid a packed run of blockbuster video game releases — and Logitech has an unconventional answer. The tech company is giving its more than 7,000 employees an extra day off to play a game of their choice, a new perk it calls "Logi Game Day." Workers can use the day when they choose — but the initiative, announced on Tuesday, comes amid a surprisingly packed month of nostalgic AAA video game releases. Last week, Blizzard Entertainment, owned by Microsoft, launched "World of Warcraft: Forever," a day before Nintendo published "The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time." That's all ahead of the release of "Grand Theft Auto 6," the most anticipated video game in years, debuting on November 19, roughly 13 years after the franchise's runaway hit, "GTA 5." Logitech isn't the only company that's turning major game releases into an extra holiday: UK-based Raptor PR recently told Business Insider that they've given their nine-person team an extra day off for gaming, and the US Army's 9th brigade engineer battalion in Georgia went viral for offering a four-day pass for reenlistees to boot up their consoles. A post shared by U.S Army WTF! Moments (@usawtfm) Logitech, which builds some gaming hardware, is among the largest corporate employers to offer time off tied to video game releases. The company says it benefits when its workers disappear into Vice City, Kalimdor, or Hyrule for a day: it cites company-commissioned surveys where gamers said playing builds real-world confidence. "We believe that the time employees spend playing will enhance the time they spend working," Robin Piispanen, the general manager of the tech company's gaming brand, told Business Insider. "We know excellence doesn't come from constant grinding. It comes from having space to recharge and have fun." Piispanen, himself a former competitive gamer, is set to host a community streaming event at the company's San Jose headquarters on the day of "GTA 6's" release. "There's definitely a steep learning curve, but with some extra time on my hands, I'm ready to dive in and hone my skills." Nina Cabuil Shariff, Logitech's European go-to-market and operations manager, said she and her husband plan to settle "household disputes" in "Call of Duty," while Steven Kuo, an electrical engineer, is eyeing a date with "Elden Ring." For years, Jensen Huang embraced a flat leadership model as he molded Nvidia into one of the world's most powerful companies. His sudden exit Wednesday amid scandal puts that arrangement to the test like never before. After cofounding the chip giant at a Denny's restaurant in the early 1990s, Huang went on to lead Nvidia with as many as 60 direct reports. That deliberately flat structure at the top was something he credited with helping the company keep information "fluid" and employees empowered. Yet the halo surrounding a successful tech founder, combined with an org chart light on top layers, can leave a company with a thin succession bench, C-suite observers told Business Insider. "It's hard to imagine any of those direct reports are able to get the scale, scope, and experience to even be qualified to be the CEO," said David Astorino, a senior partner at leadership consulting firm RHR International. Nvidia hadn't publicly disclosed a succession plan. The company's appointment of an internal interim CEO to replace Huang while launching a search for a permanent replacement, including internal and external candidates, suggests it also didn't have an obvious candidate in mind behind the scenes, said Astorino. Nvidia didn't respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Astorino said Huang's outsize status created "key-person risk," in which too much control rests with a single executive. He said the problem is particularly acute for Nvidia because of its central position in the AI ecosystem. Dan Kaplan, managing partner and head of the HR practice at the consulting firm ZRG, said founders can be conditioned to brush off doubts after years of being told their ideas would fail, making it especially hard to persuade them to plan for a future without them.                                    Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                  "They're not great at hearing no," he said. "They develop the thickest skin possible" after years of hearing from skeptics while building their companies. "When you have a flat organization like this, it's great for speed. It's not great for developing leaders," Kaplan said. Nvidia's succession crunch reflects a broader corporate dilemma: Boards too often begin planning only after the window to prepare has narrowed.  In a 2025 Nasdaq survey of about 700 board members, CEOs, executives, and governance professionals, 21% said their boards had no CEO succession plan, while another 16% said they had only an emergency plan. Huang resigned as CEO, president, and board member amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs and a board investigation into concerns that he may have been the subject of a foreign intelligence effort. Nvidia named Colette Kress, its CFO, interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement. The abrupt transition underscores a common vulnerability for founder-led companies, said Bradley Akubuiro, a partner at Bully Pulpit International and former Fortune 50 chief spokesperson. The reason, he said, is that founders' identities often become tied to an organization's success or failure. Boards in general can mitigate that risk by adding an independent director, lead director, or chair who can bring more governance to a founder-led company and keep succession planning on the agenda, Akubuiro said. They should ensure that someone can provide continuity if a CEO leaves unexpectedly. "It isn't always going to be misconduct," he said. "Any number of things could happen." A viable succession plan requires more than putting a name on an org chart, Akubuiro added. Potential successors need substantial operational experience, exposure to the board, and sufficient visibility with investors, customers, and other stakeholders to inspire confidence that they have what it takes to step in, he said. Even when companies do that planning work, however, they often keep it quiet, said Umesh Ramakrishnan, cofounder and chief strategy officer at the executive search firm Kingsley Gate. That's because publicly naming a successor can turn the sitting CEO into a lame duck, prompt passed-over contenders to resign, and invite internal jockeying for influence around the heir apparent, he said. "The organization starts gravitating toward the successor because they know that's where the power center is going to be," Ramakrishnan said. Still, he said that boards should begin succession planning well before a crisis, cultivating two or three serious internal candidates, giving them substantial operating responsibility, and creating incentives for them to stay through the transition. Lior Prosor, cofounder and managing partner at the venture fund Deep33, said Nvidia has been a "super sticky organization" for years, in part because employees could take part in the company's extraordinary stock run-up. With the company's shares taking a hit, the leadership upheaval could give rivals a fresh opening to recruit some of its most valuable talent. "For the first time ever," employees may be asking, "How much will my equity be worth? How quickly does it come back?" Prosor said. Nvidia's troubles could serve as a learning opportunity for companies that have flattened management structures, said Alexander Kirss, a director analyst in Gartner's HR practice. "No employee is irreplaceable," he said. "That includes the CEO." The latest on Jensen Huang's ouster from Nvidia and what it means for the company's future Jump to

Jensen-Gate isn't just Nvidia's problem anymore. Data center operators across Southeast Asia might be getting caught in the fallout. In case you missed it, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has had a rough week. On Sunday, The New York Times published an exposé that the executive had an affair with Singapore-based Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, believed to be passing sensitive Nvidia information to Beijing. Alice Huang worked at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company that is the largest Nvidia customer in Southeast Asia, per Bloomberg. US authorities have investigated the company on suspicion that it helped Chinese customers obtain advanced Nvidia AI chips in violation of US export restrictions. Huang resigned from his role on Thursday. Industry sources in data center financing and operations told Business Insider that Jensen-Gate could increase scrutiny on Southeast Asia's AI infrastructure companies. Chris Miller, the author of "Chip War" and a professor at Tufts University, said to Yahoo Finance on Monday that it was widely known that Megaspeed was "primarily building data centers in Southeast Asia to serve Chinese customers, especially Alibaba in their case." He added that Megaspeed isn't alone, and that there are many data centers in Malaysia, Thailand, and Singapore that buy advanced American chips and sell them to customers in China. He expects these relationships to face more oversight from Washington after Huang's scandal. More scrutiny means slower and more expensive processes. Lior Prosor, the managing partner of Deep33, an NYC-headquartered venture fund that invests in AI infrastructure, told Business Insider that the Huang affair would intensify scrutiny of American tech deployments in Southeast Asia, especially which customers' hands they end up in. "That could increase financing costs and create additional hurdles for some operators," Prosor said. He said this could temporarily create a broader risk premium for Southeast Asian operators, even those with no connection to Megaspeed. Chinmoy Baruah, the CEO of Dublin-based semiconductor company ChipX, said he expects approvals for AI infrastructure projects in the region to take longer, as investors and partners will ask more detailed questions on compliance. ChipX has committed to building wafer fabrication plants in Malaysia. "That may slow some projects at the margin, particularly those with less transparent structures," Baruah told Business Insider. Michael Heinrich, the CEO of Singapore-based decentralized AI compute company 0G, said he could see fundraising for AI infrastructure get more selective over the next year. "The next round of capital will go to the operators who can prove where their chips are, who uses them, and who owns the business," Heinrich said. The Huang scandal won't have a lasting impact on demand for Southeast Asian AI infrastructure, but rather on the standards for it, said Baruah. He said the region's fundamentals — growing digital economies, supportive governments, improving connectivity, and rising AI adoption — remain strong. This incident, however, will make rules clearer and increase diligence among operators, chip suppliers, and regulators. "That is a positive outcome for Southeast Asia, because it strengthens the region's position as a reliable, long-term destination for global digital infrastructure investment, not a shortcut around the rules," Baruah said. Prosor from Deep33 added that AI compute is in "extraordinarily short supply, and capital will flow to wherever companies can reliably build up compute. "Southeast Asia remains an important part of that equation," he said. The Huang scandal comes as the data center industry in Southeast Asia is booming. Ember Energy, a London-headquartered energy think tank, wrote in a 2025 report that ASEAN — a bloc of 11 member states in Southeast Asia — was emerging as a "global data center hot spot" due to lower construction costs and electricity levies. Malaysia, for instance, had live data center operations totaling about 1.3 gigawatts in June, which was a tenfold increase from 2022, per a report by BloombergNEF, a think tank under Bloomberg. It has another 4.7 gigawatts planned or under construction, the report added. Indonesia had about 450 megawatts of live data-center capacity as of June, with more than four times that amount currently under construction or committed, per the BloombergNEF report. Huang's resignation comes after a tumultuous few days for Nvidia. Its stock took a hit after the US midterm elections on November 3, which flipped control of Congress to the Democrats, many of whom had made anti-data-center messaging a major part of their campaigns. A few days after reports on Huang's affair, on Wednesday, the Times published another report that said Huang had had a second extramarital relationship, this time with Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, Kimberly Powell. The Wall Street Journal wrote on Wednesday that Nvidia's board was preparing to oust Huang. Early Thursday morning, Nvidia announced that Huang had resigned from the role, and CFO Colette Kress would take over as interim CEO. CEOs need this eight-step, modern reputation audit to figure out what customers are seeing.   		Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.	 Your customers can now investigate your company without visiting your website or clicking a traditional search result. They can ask an AI platform to compare your company with competitors, summarize customer complaints, research your leadership and identify potential reasons not to do business with you. The resulting answer can shape an opinion before the customer reaches your website. That changes what CEOs need to monitor. Google results, news coverage, reviews and social media still matter, but an online reputation audit in 2026 should also examine what AI platforms say about your business, which sources support those answers and whether inaccurate or outdated information keeps appearing. Google reported this year that AI Overviews had more than 2.5 billion monthly active users and AI Mode had surpassed 1 billion monthly users. CEOs should account for this behavior in the same way they learned to pay attention to Google results and online reviews. I work in online reputation management, and at my company Reputation Pros, we recommend treating a reputation audit as a recurring business process. You do not need sophisticated software to start. You just need the right questions and a system for recording what you find. Here is an audit I recommend. Typing your company name into an AI platform will not tell you enough. Instead, put yourself in the position of a prospective customer conducting due diligence. Ask questions that require the platform to explain what it knows about your company. Start by copying and customizing this prompt: “I’m considering doing business with [COMPANY NAME]. Research its online reputation as a prospective customer would. Summarize what the company is known for, common positive themes, recurring complaints or criticisms, significant controversies and information that could reasonably affect a customer’s decision. Separate verified facts from allegations or opinions. Where possible, identify the sources supporting each important claim and flag information that may be outdated or uncertain.” Run the same prompt through several major AI platforms. Do not focus solely on whether the answers sound positive or negative. Look for patterns. Does the same complaint appear several times? Does one platform emphasize an old controversy? Does another describe your company incorrectly? Which publications, review sites or other sources appear repeatedly? Record the results. One response does not define your reputation. Differences between platforms can show you where additional investigation is necessary. CEOs naturally focus on branded searches, but customers do not always begin there. Someone looking for a financial adviser, attorney, software company or home services provider may start by asking for reputable companies in a particular market. The customer may then compare two or three businesses before searching any company individually. Test that part of the journey too. Use questions such as: Pay attention to how your company appears in those answers. Do not assume that an omission means something is wrong. Instead, investigate whether credible online sources clearly establish the expertise, history and services your company claims. This exercise can reveal a problem that a branded Google search will miss: The information people find about your company may look fine, while the broader information environment barely associates your company with the category you want to lead. Customers are not the only people conducting online research. Potential employees, investors, vendors and business partners can investigate company leadership before making decisions. A CEO’s online reputation deserves its own audit. Try this: “Research [CEO’S NAME] as if you were a potential business partner conducting due diligence. Summarize their professional background, current business affiliations, documented accomplishments, controversies, lawsuits or regulatory matters and recurring criticism. Distinguish verified facts from allegations and opinions. Identify the sources supporting significant claims and flag information that appears outdated, conflicting or uncertain.” Check the basic facts first. Is the current position correct? Are former positions described as current? Are business affiliations accurate? Does the answer confuse the CEO with someone who has a similar name? Do not ignore an error because it happens to make the CEO look good. An inaccurate award, inflated job title or incorrect company affiliation can create credibility problems just as easily as negative misinformation. Executives sometimes see an unfavorable result and immediately ask how to remove it. Ask whether it is accurate first. I use five simple classifications when examining reputation issues: Those categories force you to distinguish between information that damages your reputation and information that you simply dislike. A legitimate negative customer review requires a different response from a false claim about your company. An accurate article from six years ago requires a different approach from a biography that incorrectly lists an executive’s former employer. AI can help organize this part of the audit. Copy a concerning response and ask: “Extract every factual claim in the following response that can be independently verified. Organize the claims by Claim, Source Cited, Verification Needed and Potential Business Impact. Do not assume a claim is accurate because it appears in the response.” Then verify the important claims yourself using reliable sources. Do not use one AI system to declare another AI system correct. Use AI to identify what needs checking. Use primary and authoritative sources to determine what is true. An unfavorable AI answer is often the symptom rather than the underlying problem. Investigate the sources behind it. You may discover an outdated executive biography, an old news article, incorrect directory information, inconsistent company descriptions or customer complaints appearing across multiple sites. Ask the AI platform to show its work when the product supports citations. You can also use this prompt: “Based only on the sources available in your answer, identify the sources that support the major claims about [COMPANY]. For each source, list the claim it supports, its publication date if available and whether newer authoritative information appears to conflict with it. Do not infer a source if you cannot identify one.” Then open the sources. I consider this one of the most important steps in a modern reputation audit. Asking “How do we change this AI answer?” too early can send a company in the wrong direction. Ask a better question: “Why does this information exist?” A factual problem at the source gives you something concrete to investigate. AI has expanded reputation management, but it has not completely replaced traditional search yet. Search your company name, executive names and relevant combinations such as your company plus “reviews,” “complaints,” “lawsuit” and other terms a prospective customer might reasonably use. Look beyond position. A negative article does not become significant simply because it ranks highly. Determine its date, source, context and accuracy. Find out whether multiple independent sources support the underlying claim or whether dozens of pages repeat information originating from a single source. The same principle applies to positive coverage. Ten websites repeating the same press release do not provide the same independent validation as 10 separate authoritative sources. Your audit should measure the quality of the information surrounding your company, not simply count positive and negative links. Review management creates another risk CEOs should examine. The Federal Trade Commission’s Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule took effect in October 2024. It addresses practices including fake or false reviews and incentives conditioned on a review expressing a particular positive or negative sentiment. The FTC sent warning letters to 10 companies in December 2025 over potential violations of the rule and noted that violations can result in substantial civil penalties. Ask your marketing and customer service teams how they request reviews. Are incentives involved? Does anyone ask specifically for a five-star review? Do employees write reviews? Does an outside vendor manage the process? Does anyone discourage dissatisfied customers from leaving legitimate feedback? CEOs should understand the answers. I recommend one simple test: Could you comfortably explain your review-generation process to a regulator? If you hesitate, investigate it. Finish the audit by creating a basic spreadsheet. You only need seven columns: Run the same core questions every quarter and compare the findings. Label accurate information and isolated criticism as issues to monitor. Investigate recurring inconsistencies, outdated information and unsupported claims. Prioritize consequential factual errors, impersonation and rapidly spreading false information for action. Consistency matters more than complexity. The first audit tells you what your reputation looks like today. Repeating the process shows you where it is moving. A company preparing for an acquisition, leadership change, product launch or other major event may need to run the audit more frequently. Most CEOs can start with a quarterly review and adjust based on the risks they uncover. Your goal is not to make every search result positive or force every AI platform to praise your company. Neither goal is realistic. Your goal is to know what customers can discover about you, understand where that information comes from and correct factual problems where you legitimately can. In 2026, people increasingly ask machines to help them evaluate businesses and the people running them. CEOs should know what those machines are finding before an important customer, employee or business partner asks. Your customers can now investigate your company without visiting your website or clicking a traditional search result. They can ask an AI platform to compare your company with competitors, summarize customer complaints, research your leadership and identify potential reasons not to do business with you. The resulting answer can shape an opinion before the customer reaches your website. That changes what CEOs need to monitor. Google results, news coverage, reviews and social media still matter, but an online reputation audit in 2026 should also examine what AI platforms say about your business, which sources support those answers and whether inaccurate or outdated information keeps appearing. It's hard to believe that Spotify Wrapped is about to give us all a brutal reality check on how we soundtracked 2026. Though the idea of it sends shivers through me, it's still one of the most anticipated and exciting events on the tech calendar. If you thought it was too late to get in your final listening hours, fear not; Spotify hasn't stopped counting them yet. While we don't know when the exact cut-off is (Spotify's never disclosed it before, and the likelihood of it happening is slim), it's widely thought to be right up until the launch of Wrapped, which usually lands in late November or early December. The good news is that we still have between two and three weeks left before that day arrives, so if there was ever a good time to crack down on the final Wrapped preparations, it's now!      For years, your Spotify Taste Profile has been sitting behind the algorithm, using your listening behaviors to determine which new music it recommends to you. While you can exclude individual songs and playlists from infiltrating your Taste Profile, that's pretty much it as far as controlling how Spotify understands you. Thankfully, the platform brought Taste Profile to the forefront of the experience earlier this year, allowing you to see exactly how Spotify understands your listening habits and how it uses this to shape your recommendations, and to flag any mistakes it makes. Not only that, but you can also speak directly to it and actively shape what it feeds you. Using text prompts, you can ask your Taste Profile pretty much anything. If you want to explore a particular genre that's been on your list, you can prompt it to recommend more glam rock, experimental pop, or whatever you're feeling in the moment — and the same goes for artists. To find it, tap your profile image to open the sidebar where you'll find 'Taste Profile', and then the control is in your hands. You should also note that this tool is only available for Premium subscribers based in the US and New Zealand, so it's not available in every market. No matter how much you try to ignore them, they're bound to crop up in your Discover Weekly or whenever you're listening to a Spotify-curated playlist — it's better to rid them completely, I say. That's why I've gotten into the routine of blocking artists entirely from my feed. It's one of those features that, whenever I bring it up, others don't even know it exists. I'm here to tell you that it does, and it will change your life. All you need to do is head to an artist's page in the Spotify app, tap the three dots next to the 'Follow' button, and then select 'Don't play this artist'. Once that's enabled, their page will go gray, and their discography will disappear from playlists. Their music also won't show up in features like your Discover Weekly or Daylist, so your blocked artists won't get in the way of new music discovery.      If you're on Spotify's Family plan and your young kids can't keep out of your profile, then I feel for you. There's nothing worse than waiting all year for Wrapped to arrive only to find that your top songs and artists are from your kids' favorite TV shows — the Family plan has individual profiles for a reason! It's been difficult to avoid this in Wrapped's past, but rest assured Spotify has put its foot down on this infiltration this time around, and you can amend your settings to ensure this music stays far away from your Wrapped summary. In your settings, you'll find a toggle that, when enabled, excludes all kids and family music that's played on your profile. Not only does this help with steering your Wrapped in a more accurate direction, but it also ensures that your kids' favorite music doesn't affect your recommendations, Discover Weekly, and Daily Mix — so it's not just a benefit for Wrapped.
