What happens next at one of the world’s most valuable companies will have repercussions far beyond Silicon Valley. Save Share The departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the 63-year-old cofounder and face of the chipmaking company which has become the backbone of the modern AI industry, has shaken the US’s Silicon Valley. Nvidia, valued at nearly $4 trillion, is a critical pillar of the US economy where AI and tech companies make up some 40 percent of stock market valuations. The furore over Huang’s extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, has wiped hundreds of billions of dollars from the company’s market value, dragging down the S&P 500 and Nasdaq.     While CFO Colette Kress has temporarily stepped into the top job at Nvidia, the search for cofounder Huang’s successor continues. What happens next at one of the world’s most valuable companies will have repercussions far beyond Silicon Valley. So, what’s next for Nvidia? On October 29, The New York Times reported that US intelligence agencies suspected a Chinese businesswoman and executive associated with Singapore-based AI infrastructure company Megaspeed International, Alice Huang, had been tapped by China’s Ministry of State Security to gather information from Nvidia’s Huang. The newspaper reported that the two were involved in an intimate relationship, later confirmed by the cofounder of the company in an internal memo. Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang wrote in an internal memo to Nvidia staff. The business links go beyond just the affair, however, fuelling further concerns. Megaspeed purchased more than $4.8bn of Nvidia chips over roughly two years. Separately, The Information reported that Alice Huang facilitated at least $7.5bn in Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese firms, raising even more questions about skirting US export controls. Then, on Wednesday, the NYT reported a second alleged affair between Jensen Huang and Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, who reported directly to him. The next day, Huang was forced out of the company and off its board. Hours later, Reuters reported that Huang had allegedly been involved in a third affair with another Nvidia employee, citing two people familiar with the matter. In simple terms, if Nvidia sneezes, the AI industry and modern computing catch a cold. Nvidia controls nearly 90 percent of the market for advanced AI chips which are used to train frontier AI models, giving it an extraordinary degree of influence over the global AI industry and the infrastructure powering it. Observers say the company holds the keys to next-generation computing. Its customers include tech giants such as Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta, which rely on Nvidia hardware to build and operate their AI data centres. That’s also why Washington has restricted Nvidia from selling chips to China. Nvidia’s Huang has spent years lobbying in Washington against such restrictions, arguing that restricting sales would surrender a strategically important market to domestic Chinese competitors. That puts him at odds with US lawmakers who view access to Nvidia’s advanced chips as a national security risk, particularly given their potential military applications.      A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said Beijing has “always opposed the abuse of export control measures”, as pressure gains momentum yet again in Washington. Beijing has rejected allegations that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as “baseless”. In China, investors have been selling shares in Chinese AI-linked companies over worries that recent developments at Nvidia could deepen the technological divide between Beijing and Washington. On Friday, shares in Z.AI, one of China’s top AI model developers, tumbled more than 10 percent in Hong Kong while shares in rival MiniMax hit record lows. A Reuters review identified more than $3bn in Chinese computing projects built around Nvidia’s restricted processors – despite the American chipmaker claiming that US export controls effectively shut it out of the AI data-centre market in the world’s second-biggest economy. The examination shows projects stretching from China’s wealthy coastal technology hubs to remote western provinces, and underscores how deeply Nvidia’s technology remains embedded in China’s AI expansion. Nvidia shares rose 1.8 percent in premarket trading on Friday after losing around 11 percent of their value this week up to Thursday, when Huang exited the company he built. The company is on course for its longest streak of weekly losses since October 2012. US President Donald Trump is scheduled to meet his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, next week in Shenzhen at the APEC leaders’ summit. Similarly, shares in Nvidia’s customers, such as South Korea’s Naver, fell more than 5 percent. Nasdaq futures and S&P 500 futures fell 0.4 percent and 0.15 percent, respectively. “Jensen has obviously been a singular force in many ways so the impact will likely be felt far and wide,” UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri told Reuters. “The company has become a key source of funds for a host of AI industry participants including neo-clouds, LLM developers, ecosystem partners, and suppliers, and we have always seen Jensen as a key driving force for this effort,” Arcuri said. “Even if a new leader ultimately maintains a similar approach, there is likely to be some ‘pause’ in the company’s willingness and ability to continue pursuing these deals in the near term,” he added. From washing dishes at a Denny’s to building a $4 trillion technology giant, Huang has led Nvidia for nearly 33 years – and made one of Silicon Valley’s defining entrepreneurial stories. But the “cult-style” leaders at Silicon Valley – including Huang, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk – also reflect the concentration of market power that tech companies enjoy. Technology stocks now account for nearly 40 percent of the S&P 500’s total market value. That is likely to rise when AI companies Anthropic and OpenAI also go public. And in the absence of a clear succession plan, things could go awry, sending jitters among investors – a concern which Nvidia highlighted itself in its annual review for this year. Under the risk factors dealing with its dependence on key personnel, Nvidia’s report noted that the company is “highly dependent on the services of our longstanding executive team”. “Failure to ensure effective succession planning, transfer of knowledge, and smooth transitions involving executives and key employees could hinder our strategic planning, execution, and long-term success,” it said. Nvidia’s board has begun searching for a permanent successor to Huang, tapping CFO Kress as interim CEO. Meanwhile, President Trump, who has defended Huang as a “genius”, shared his two cents, too. He suggested former Apple chief executive Tim Cook could take over Nvidia. “A Legend replaces a Legend,” Trump wrote. Nvidia has said it will consider candidates from both within and outside the company.               Follow Al Jazeera English:

Home > Piracy >                          Popular game repacker DODI is retiring, citing his wedding and a move to France, noting that running a pirate site is not an option there. He says the domains, hosting and accounts were already handed to a new repack team. Meanwhile, the game industry wants the U.S. to list DODI's site as a notorious piracy market, citing crypto payments to exchanges including Binance.              Next to FitGirl, DODI Repacks is one of the best known names among game pirates. The site publishes ‘repacks’ of pirated games. These are compressed versions of cracked games, which are smaller to download and are shared through torrents and direct download links. However, yesterday the site’s operator announced that it’s time to say goodbye. In a farewell message, DODI explains that he is getting married later this month and will start a new life in a new country. “My marriage is on November 24, 2026. Retiring from creating game repacks is a must now. No way to own or operate a pirated content site in France,” DODI writes. Farewell     The site isn’t going offline though. “I already transferred Domains, Web hosting and all related accounts to the new repack team few days ago,” DODI adds. The retirement wasn’t entirely unexpected. In May, DODI informed his followers that 2026 would be a busy year. He had final exams coming up, followed by a pharmacy law exam in September, after which he would likely start a new job in France. In addition, he was getting married in November. “Don’t worry, I will not leave you but sure will not be as before,” DODI wrote at the time. Last month, DODI revealed that the handover had already started, noting that he only created four of the more than 65 repacks that were posted in the previous six weeks. The rest came from a new team, which would also handle all future releases. “I will only give instructions and watch,” he wrote. DODI’s exit also follows continued pressure from the game industry. In 2024, the Entertainment Software Association (ESA) added the site to its list of recommendations for the U.S. Trade Representative’s annual review of ‘notorious’ piracy markets. Last month, ESA flagged the site again, reporting 7.14 million visits in August and links to more than 2,000 games. According to ESA, the site removed only 22% of the links it reported over the past year. ESA on DODI     The game industry group also looked closely at the money trail, identifying crypto payments to exchanges that check the identity of users. “Cryptocurrency wallets associated with DODI have sent funds to know-your-customer exchanges, including Binance, which may create an attribution and enforcement path through appropriate legal process,” ESA writes. Previously, DODI’s site faced a security backlash too. In February, cybersecurity company Cyderes listed dodi-repacks.site among the indicators in its analysis of the ‘RenEngine’ malware, with a download link supposedly leading to an infected MediaFire file. The report didn’t say that DODI’s operator was involved. Malware concerns have also been mentioned in piracy circles. In 2025, the FMHY piracy index dropped the site and only linked to DODI’s 1337x page instead, with a warning. This year, r/Piracy’s moderators followed suit. “Because Dodi’s repacks themselves are still safe (even though his site is not), we have changed his listing on the megathread to send redditors to his user profile on 1337x,” the moderators wrote. Who is behind the new repack team is not known. For now, however, it appears that new releases continue to come out under the DODI name. The latest repack, posted on the same day as the farewell message, credits the “Dodi Repack Team.” It’s based on a Star Wars: Galactic Racer release from ‘voices38’, another familiar piracy name that ESA nominated as a notorious piracy threat. — A copy of ESA’s submission for the 2026 Notorious Markets review is available here (pdf). The most recent high-quality Volkswagen camper van we’ve seen is the one transformed in the workshops of Dutch converter Tonke. Called the Basecamp, it is a self-sufficient, luxurious campervan, designed to go where life takes you. A slightly more mellowed version of the Volkswagen adventure vehicle is the new Caddy Campervan, built by British converter Bodans. The new Cubert VW campervan is based on Volkswagen’s Caddy platform. The latter is the smallest ICE van, making the Cubert VW Caddy an ultra-compact campervan that blends comfort and convenience. It has a simple floorplan and a rear elevating roof that opens up to increase headroom and provide ventilation through the mesh windows. Designer: Bodans        The Cubert is based on Volkswagen’s 114-hp plug-in hybrid drivetrain and offers up to 116 km range. The floor plan features two seats in the cockpit and places the cabin behind them. A long convertible sofa sits on one side, while the kitchen occupies the space across the aisle. The basic essence inside the cabin is enhanced by gray flooring, furniture, and upholstery, while the integrated LED lights create a warm ambience. The kitchen is fully functional and comprises an electric induction hob for off-grid use. You also get the option to include a 2-burner gas hob. The kitchen space also includes a large sink, a drawer fridge, and cabinets for storage. The sofa on the opposite side converts into a double bed and includes under-bed storage space for camping equipment.        The most exciting aspect of the Cubert VW Caddy Campervan is the pop-up roof, which adds headroom to the standard interior height of the van. The roof doesn’t come with an additional bed, but the converter can offer a lift-away double bed to add to the basic two-person sleeping facility. Since the Caddy Campervan only has two seats and stock bedding for two, it is ideal for a couple, but with the additional bed, you can increase the sleeping space for two people. Given the floor space inside the cabin, I believe the campervan can feel cramped up for more than two people, it’s ideally modified for. Adventurers have the option to finish their campervan with a rooftop solar panel, a microwave, and a touchscreen for all onboard controls. The campervan Bodans informs can be made in a range of colors and interior finishes. The van converter says it can professionally customize the campervan to user requirements as well. Horus heresy Clicking a random link this morning, I was dazzled by the glare of a thousand laser batteries firing simultaneously. My ears trembled beneath the trundle of a million caterpillar tracks. Balls of ice, bolts of lightning, shipments of rare alloys, and cascades of drop pods went screaming down my nerves and detonated in my frontal cortex, painting starlanes across the inside of my skull. "Oh god, they've finally found us!" I yelled, hiding beneath my desk. "I for one welcome our new galactic overlords!" But then I realised that I wasn't looking at a live newsfeed, but merely the Steam page for Horu, a real-time 4X strategy game in which you can "command hundreds of thousands of units across land and space", in the summary of developer David "GlassBeaver" Nadaski. There's also a magic system, this being "the spice that makes your enemy's defeat bitter", which is a very genteel way to characterise glaciating a tank formation or conjuring a miniature blackhole. In development for years, and running on a custom C++ engine, Horu is inspired by 2006 hybrid RTS Star Wars: Empire at War - good, not great, in the words of turncoat jankonaut Graham, and the subject of many mods. Horu's way of bettering Empire at War is seemingly to add a shedload more of everything. You can engage in a fleet battle that looks like two migrating ant hives colliding, even as a frankly unnecessary quantity of cyborgs pour over the forgeworld beneath and get their shit kicked in by some tornado-summoning sorcerers. Offensives appear to work like this: any drop ships that push through the fleet battle add meat to the ground invasion, with the option of deploying wormholes to sneak your troops behind the defending armada. On the ground, you're basically out to capture control points. You're allegedly spared from "continuous babysitting" by semi-autonomous squadron commanders and an orders system that lets you queue up objectives, before units engage in battle. You can still give individual orders to units, but that seems like a recipe for acute wrist injury. There's also a boarding action mechanic whereby your hijackers move through vessels room by room. Again, I struggle to understand how you'll have time and dexterity to oversee such skulduggery when there are a bajillion particle cannons going off all at once. Outside of combat, there are planets to develop, shipyards to build, spy networks to groom, research trees to water, and stock markets to manipulate. It all looks like business as usual for an imperial 4X. Honestly, I can imagine the maximalist warfaring being a hot mess, and then there's the fact that the dev is running a Kickstarter "to fund the remaining assets needed for a playable build: more spaceships, more units, more animations, more sounds, more music, and everything in between." I've been burned by Kickstarter overpromising before. Still, I can only admire the vindictive intellect that would have me play a little game of FTL inside what looks like one of the larger PvP scraps from Eve Online. You can read more on Steam. Release date there is currently none. For an equally populous strategy experience that's closer in style to Supreme Commander, check out Sanctuary: Shattered Space. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including with an employee and a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence officials accuse of spying for Beijing. The company says Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO as the board searches for a permanent replacement. Nvidia’s computer chips are at the heart of the artificial intelligence boom, driving the company’s value above $4 trillion and making Huang one of the most influential business leaders in the world. His spectacular fall from the company he co-founded in 1993 comes as the U.S. stock market has become highly dependent on a handful of AI-related companies and amid intense competition between the United States and China over control of the technology, with access to Nvidia’s chips becoming a major point of contention between the two countries. Tech critic Paris Marx notes that the AI industry’s “circular financing,” in which companies are both clients and investors for one another, has created systemic risk. We also speak with Ramesh Srinivasan, director of the AI Futures Lab at UCLA, who says the “soap opera” of the Huang scandal has exposed “how precarious the governance of this AI truly is,” with only a handful of people and firms controlling “incredibly powerful technology that feeds off of all of us and the planet.” AMY GOODMAN: We begin today’s show looking at the fallout from Jensen Huang’s resignation as the CEO of Nvidia, one of the world’s most powerful companies. Nvidia’s advanced AI computer chips have powered much of the artificial intelligence boom. Huang cultivated close ties to President Trump and is credited with helping to shape U.S. policies around artificial intelligence and rules around the export of advanced AI chips. Huang’s resignation came days after reports emerged he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman named Alice Huang — no relation — whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of spying for Beijing and helping China obtain advanced Nvidia chips, which are banned by U.S. export controls. The Information news outlet reports Alice Huang helped route at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips to China via a Singapore-based cloud computing company called Megaspeed International. Jensen Huang confirmed he had an affair with the woman. Later, published reports revealed he also had affairs with two employees at Nvidia, including with a senior executive who reported to him. Nvidia has announced its longtime chief financial officer, Colette Kress, would serve as interim CEO as the board searches for a permanent replacement. On Thursday, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche took questions about Nvidia. REPORTER: When did the Justice Department learn, with regard to Nvidia, that Alice Huang might be a suspected Chinese asset? And there’s been concerns raised that the Commerce Department was giving favoritism to Nvidia and Megaspeed, which is Alice Huang’s company. Do you share the concerns that maybe the Commerce Department was impeding the ability to uncover the smuggling network that Alice Huang was involved in? ATTORNEY GENERAL TODD BLANCHE: Well, your first question assumes something that I have never said and that I don’t know to be true. So, you assume that DOJ learns that she is, in fact, a spy. I’m not — nobody said that. I certainly haven’t said that. And I don’t — all I said a minute ago, and all that I think I will say, is that, of course, DOJ is investigating or looking at it. So, there’s no — there’s no conclusions reached by the Department of Justice or by me or by Director Patel around who she is or is not. I don’t have concerns with the Commerce Department. I don’t. We have a good relationship with the Commerce Department. I’ve read some of the stories, which, you know, are sourced or not sourced, and so I don’t have any — but, no, I don’t have — the answer to your question is, no, I don’t have any — I don’t have any concerns. AMY GOODMAN: On Capitol Hill, Republican and Democratic lawmakers are calling for probes into Nvidia’s actions and the Trump administration’s policies regarding chip exports to China. Republican Senator Tim Scott, the chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has requested Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify. Democratic lawmakers Ron Wyden of Oregon and Richard Neal of Massachusetts are investigating the Trump administration’s decision to allow Nvidia to sell advanced chips to China. For more on Nvidia and questions about the concentration of power in the AI industry, we’re joined now by two guests. In Toronto, Canada, we’re joined by Paris Marx, a tech critic and host of the award-winning Tech Won’t Save Us podcast. He writes the Disconnect newsletter, author of the book Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires. And in Germany, we’re joined by Ramesh Srinivasan, professor of information studies, director of the AI Futures Lab at UCLA and host of the podcast Utopias. Paris Marx and Ramesh Srinivasan, welcome back to Democracy Now! Professor Srinivasan, let’s begin with you. What should we understand about what has just taken place? And talk about the centrality of Nvidia to the whole AI bubble, to the whole AI industry. RAMESH SRINIVASAN: Right. Thank you so much for having me, Amy. AI is not magic. It comes from the planet, and the technologies that produce it often return to the planet as electronic waste. It’s powered by water, energy sources, labor and our data, and those come from us, from the planet itself. Right? So, what has occurred is this astonishing technology that reduces life to data and numbers, and reduces intelligence to pattern recognition, has been — has now been governed and run by just a few people on the planet, mainly men, and men that you’ve discussed, you know, commonly on Democracy Now!, who were there at the inauguration and so on. So, now when we have soap opera sorts of moments, like Mr. Jensen Huang being connected to, you know, this Chinese — potential Chinese spy, various affairs and so on, you can see how precarious the governance of this AI truly is, because the administration has completely handed the keys to this incredibly powerful technology, that feeds off of all of us and the planet, to basically a few people, and they can do what they want — their vagaries, their mishaps, their corruption in certain cases, their gluttony. That is what is being accumulated more and more. So, the story of AI is a story that’s tied to data centers — right? — which you cover all the time, which are, you know, computing and so on, much like server farms in the past. They’re tied to chips, and that’s very key to this story, the Nvidia chips, or superchips, that were originally used in the context of gaming and now were applied to artificial intelligence and large language models. But it also comes from all of our data, and then the screens and systems that determine and shape our lives. So, this is a technology that is harvested, extracted from our planet and all of us to create potentially trillions of dollars of valuation, which might be a massive bubble — and we can talk about that — with returning almost next to nothing for the rest of us, other than anxiety, insecurity and deep concerns. The technology doesn’t have to go in that direction, but that’s the direction the Trump administration has taken it. And I think it’s incredibly notable that it’s the China — it’s the China scare yet again, just like we saw with Huawei, just like we saw with COVID. It’s the China scare that’s forcing all of this action and this spectacle and this controversy, rather than the real conditions of AI, which are disenfranchising and robbing people of many aspects of their futures. AMY GOODMAN: Paris Marx, if you could continue, talking about what is the role of Nvidia when it comes to, overall, fueling so much? And explain the issue of the ban on these — on these superchips, why they’re so significant, what kind of monopoly Nvidia has on this, and why you believe he is so close to President Trump, who didn’t want him to resign. PARIS MARX: Absolutely. Great to join you this morning, Amy. You know, Nvidia is key to this AI market. You know, it controls about 90% or so of the chips that go into, you know, all these data centers that are powering the AI boom that we have seen occurring now for the past few years, right? And as a result of that, Nvidia has become one of the most valued companies, and for a while has been, you know, the most valuable publicly traded company on the planet, which is just staggering to imagine, right? You know, it went from kind of just, you know, a regular old tech company, you know, not particularly notable — sure, it made some graphics cards for gamers — to being now one of the key companies that, as you say, you know, is so important for what so many other companies are doing. And it’s not just the fact that it creates these chips — right? — these chips that are just essential to, you know, the generative AI workloads behind ChatGPT and the image generators and those sorts of things, but because Nvidia has made so much money for the past number of years, it has also become a major investor, plowing more than $120 billion into other AI companies across the economy, across the United States, around the world, which has meant that now there are all these companies that not just depend on Nvidia’s chips, but also depend on Nvidia’s financing. You know, I’m sure you’ve been talking on the show about the upcoming Anthropic IPO, you know, Anthropic looking to go public. It is expecting about $10 billion from Nvidia as part of its public offering. And so, Nvidia has been really key here. And because of that, you know, because Nvidia was valued at something like more than $5 trillion until recently, it’s no surprise, then, that Jensen Huang has become very close with Donald Trump, right? It’s a very valuable company. It is a company that makes the technology that is very important to the broader AI boom that has been kind of lifting the U.S. economy and the U.S. stock market — right? — because of the investment, not just in all these AI products, but in all these data centers that, you know, have been being built across the country, as well. And so, Jensen Huang has become a major adviser to Donald Trump on AI policy and has certainly been pushing him to weaken the restrictions on, you know, basically, his ability to sell these chips to China. And I think now in light of these revelations, there are questions as to whether, you know, that is kind of a firmly held belief that Jensen Huang had because there was obviously, you know, as someone who runs a major company, a big market opportunity in selling those chips to China, or whether there was influence on his thoughts, you know, from Alice Huang. And I think those are questions that we don’t have answered yet, but certainly is probably, you know, what some of these lawmakers are hoping to try to get more insight into by having Jensen Huang come speak to congresspeople. AMY GOODMAN: Paris Marx, in your book, you quote one investor who describes Nvidia as “the central bank of AI.” And there are many descriptions of how Huang is really the conduit from the other tech billionaire bros to reaching President Trump and making the demands that they want. PARIS MARX: Absolutely. You know, as I was mentioning, when we look at Nvidia, it is not just a company that is selling all these chips. It is a company that has gone to a lot of these other AI and data center companies and made sure that they had investment, sure, so that they could, you know, grow, expand their businesses, what have you, but also that they — so that they could then buy more Nvidia chips from Nvidia, right? So, it’s kind of like a circular financing scheme, where Nvidia gives it the money to operate, and then they buy the chips from Nvidia, and Nvidia makes more money in that way, right? So the money comes back to Nvidia all the time. And then, of course, linked with that is it has also used that money to try to support companies that were in difficult situations. So, for example, a company called CoreWeave, that creates data centers to power AI and kind of sells that computing power to these AI companies, has been in trouble, on and off, for a number of years, and Nvidia has often been there to support that company when it has been in dire straits. And it’s not the only one like that. And so, of course, you know, linked to that, Jensen Huang has developed this really close relationship with Donald Trump. You know, we saw this just the other day, just yesterday, after Jensen Huang resigned, and, you know, Donald Trump came out and said that he was talking to Jensen and, you know, that things are difficult, and, you know, basically, had this really kind of personal relationship to him, seems to be someone who he really trusts. And as a result of that, I’m sure that Donald Trump has been open when Jensen Huang has been discussing AI and tech policy with him. And, of course, Jensen has been pushing to make sure that there is not regulation of AI products, in the way that your other guest has been talking about, you know, is really necessary, but then, on top of that, again, trying to weaken these restrictions on the ability to sell chips to China. And, of course, you know, the U.S. government’s concern and many lawmakers’ concern there is that by selling those chips, because they are some of the — because they are the most advanced chips that are out there, that if they get sold to China, you know, China will not just be able — Chinese companies will not just be able to use them to power their own AI products, but that there’s a concern that, you know, Chinese companies will be able to kind of reverse-engineer the technology and then have a big kind of leap in their — in their kind of chip-making capabilities, essentially. AMY GOODMAN: In October of last year, Jensen Huang spoke to the media about whether China should have access to Nvidia’s most advanced chips. JENSEN HUANG: The China market is large, and it’s a vibrant, vibrant market with a lot of developers. And those developers create AI technology that’s exported from China all over the world. And so, to the extent that American tech stack can run and operate those AI models, it’s good for the United States and around the world. REPORTER: So, would you want the Blackwell to be sold in China? JENSEN HUANG: I hope so. I hope so. But that’s a decision for President Trump to make. AMY GOODMAN: So, Professor Ramesh Srinivasan, if you can explain what he is saying there? And also, this whole issue of the so-called Chinese spy, what evidence do we have of this? Is it other competing companies saying this? Is there a big division within the U.S. government in the intelligence community who had informed Trump of this months and months ago? RAMESH SRINIVASAN: Right. It’s not clear what the evidence is as of this point. You could even see in the story, in the introduction to this story, that even the Attorney General Todd Blanche is, you know, very elusive and vague in his comments about, you know, what is — what exactly occurred here. But I do think it’s very important to note a couple things that were already mentioned here. First of all, the AI industry, there’s incredible amount of concern that this is an overspeculated bubble. That’s because many of the revenues are occurring in the circular way that your other guest just described. So the revenues seem to be inflated here. And talking about China, as we actually discussed before, Amy, back, you know, about almost two years ago, Chinese models around AI are performing nearly as well as the top American so-called frontier models. I mean, the question of what we’re building all these models for is a worthwhile question, I think a big elephant in the room. But they’re doing it at a fraction of the cost. So, we have to really consider what’s occurring here and what’s really occurring here, right? So, the president’s response around all these concerns is often to say that the economy is super healthy. And when he says that, what he’s talking about — Trump, I’m saying — is he’s talking about the S&P 500. But the vast majority of people in America and around the world do not have large amounts of investment capital. Investment capital is how people make money, but there’s a deep amount of concern that these — this is not going to actually produce the type of revenues that even legitimate it for investors. But what about the rest of us, as workers, as consumers? AI is being pushed out as a technology of replacement, not a technology to augment or expand or help us, you know, create together. It’s not a telescope. It’s not, you know, a microscope. It’s not what Steve Jobs once famously called a “bicycle for the mind.” It’s being — it’s using us. It’s surveilling us. It’s turning us into data. It’s turning life and intelligence into patterns to replace us, to read, write, speak for us. In fact, a CEO in Big Tech told me recently, because I’m from Silicon Valley and I have friends in that industry, “Hey, Ramesh, you don’t even have to do this interview with Democracy Now! Very soon, an AI can do that for you, and better than you.” What does that even mean? So, this is what’s at play here. And so, this has been cast, as I alluded to earlier, as some sort of flat, you know, geopolitical battle between the U.S. and China, when, in reality, what we need is cooperation between the two nations, and, most importantly, outside of the elites in those two nations, governance by stakeholders, not just in the Global South and around the planet, where I’m part of a Global South AI alliance, but also from workers, consumers and so on, to ensure that a technology that uses patterns to predict the present and construct the future is a technology that’s applied to the right domains. And no one, at the end of the day, has been paid for their data. None of us have equity in any of these companies, but these companies are feeding off us to potentially replace us. And that’s what I would call a parasitic technology. But it doesn’t have to go in that direction. AMY GOODMAN: Ramesh, can you show us your hands? AI models are notoriously bad at generating the correct number of fingers. I’m only kidding. OK, Paris Marx, Paris, this was from Bloomberg. You have Bloomberg in — let’s see, says, “Jefferies Financial Group Inc.’s Chris Wood said the most likely long-term outcome of the AI boom will be massive capital destruction in the U.S.” Do you see that coming now? PARIS MARX: It’s hard to say when exactly that would come. You know, I think that there are multiple moments over the past few years where it looked like, you know, maybe — maybe the bubble is going to start bursting, and then, you know, it has continued. I think that it is facing a serious threat in this moment, and not just because of the resignation of Jensen Huang from Nvidia. And to be clear, you know, Nvidia was a company that was really like Jensen Huang’s fiefdom. You know, it was not set up to have a lot of kind of people who could easily take over from him if he were to leave the company. You know, a number of his family members are also executives within the company. And so, you know, I think that there’s real concern about what this is going to mean for Nvidia’s future — right? — as such a key player in the AI market, you know, again, one of the most valuable companies in the world, supplying the key technology that these companies need, but also providing a lot of financing to other companies. But we’ve also been seeing, through this year, a lot of major companies kind of pulling back on their generative AI spending, because they’re finding they’re not getting the return on investment from what they’re doing there. There was just a report at the end of October from an analyst at Apollo called Torsten Slok, and he basically looked at the S&P 500 to see, you know, whether companies had really been benefiting from this rollout of generative AI, and found that with the big seven tech companies, you could clearly see an increase in profit margins and in revenue per employee, you know, from rolling out generative AI products, but for those other 493 companies within the S&P 500, he did not see, you know, kind of like a notable difference or that generative AI had really benefited them. So, there are growing questions there about the economic benefits of actually using this technology, not to mention, you know, kind of the many social harms that your other guest was talking about that need to be addressed and reined in. And so, you know, there are already — there’s already kind of skepticism and questions about all the money that has been put into these AI models, into these data centers in order to power them, whether they’re actually going to be as useful or whether the market for them is actually going to be as big as the companies are promising. And so, on top of those existing concerns, now these issues at Nvidia are kind of adding on top of that, which means that there is a potential kind of greater risk there, you know, of a collapse of some sort coming in the near future. But I certainly wouldn’t want to go as far as to call that this is the moment that it’s all going to happen. AMY GOODMAN: And, Paris Marx, as you look down on us in the United States from Toronto, and across, of course, at Alaska, I wanted to get your comment on the midterms. You’ve written extensively about the anti-data center movement in the United States. It certainly fueled a lot of people, might have driven a lot of people to the polls. If you can also talk about the possibility of Democrats investigating tech CEOs? And, of course, right now we have the demand of Democrats and Republicans to investigate Jensen Huang. PARIS MARX: Yeah, I would love to see it. Let’s bring on more investigations of the tech CEOs. Start with Jensen, and we can go from there. But I do think that the midterms were not just a repudiation of the Republican Party and Donald Trump, but also of these tech CEOs that have been wielding so much power over, you know, our societies collectively for such a long period of time. And especially it feels like they really took this to a new level with what they’ve been doing the past few years — right? — not just the rollout of this generative AI technology that, as I was saying, is not as beneficial as they promised, but also had a lot of negative social and environmental consequences that came along with it, but then, paired with that, trying to push these massive hyperscale data centers into so many communities across the United States and around the world. And so, what we saw is voters really push back against that. You know, so many races in the United States had a data center component to them. And if we look at key states like, say, Texas or Georgia or Ohio, we can see that data centers were really consequential in the battles that played out there, and that Democratic lawmakers recognized that, you know, going against data centers, promising moratoriums, was going to win the votes. I think now the question is where this goes from here, right? Are we actually going to see those Democrats follow through on those promises? Is the pressure going to keep up? Or is the tech industry, which I’m sure it is, you know, about to pivot at this moment, hiring a ton of lobbyists to try to find a way to shape some of what Democrats are going to try to do, try to shape that kind of tech regulation, data center regulation agenda to make sure it’s not going to be as biting as it might otherwise appear? And so, I think that’s what I’ll be watching, you know, going forward, how this is going to play out. AMY GOODMAN: Well, Paris Marks, I want to thank you for being with us, author of Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires, speaking to us from Toronto, and Ramesh Srinivasan, director of the AI Futures Lab at UCLA, today speaking to us from Germany. Thanks so much, both, for being with us. Coming up, an Israeli strike on Nasser Hospital in Gaza has killed at least six people, including a surgeon. We’ll speak to Dr. Feroze Sidhwa, who volunteered at Nasser and worked with Dr. Abu Shaira. Stay with us. [break] AMY GOODMAN: “Garden” by Nicolás Jaar. Governments, businesses, individuals disrupted as server failures stretch into second day. Save Share Microsoft has said its popular email and other services were improving but not fully restored more than 24 hours after a mass outage disrupted communications worldwide. The outage, which began around 16:00 GMT on Thursday and affected users in 74 countries, was caused by overloaded servers that became “unexpectedly available,” the company reported. There was no indication of a cyberattack or malicious activity, the tech giant said on Friday. “We’re seeing encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure,” the company said in a statement. Microsoft reported that “email queues [are] significantly reduced and approaching normal levels”. The outage affected Microsoft 365 services used by global businesses, institutions and individuals, including Outlook, Teams and Copilot, its artificial intelligence (AI) tool. It was one of the longest in Microsoft’s history and the second disruption to its services this year. While Microsoft has not said how many people were affected by the outage, the company announced in January that it had more than 450 million Microsoft 365 commercial subscribers. The United States-based tech giant is valued at more than $3.8 trillion. Microsoft reported midday GMT that email delivery and 365 services were improving across Europe, North America and the Asia Pacific but acknowledged that some services remained spotty. As the outage stretched into its second day, users scrambled to navigate the outages, which caused logistical headaches and forced some operations to stall or grind to a halt. The outage underscored how dependent institutions, businesses and people have become on a handful of tech companies providing services that power governments and global economies. “What we do know so far is that this is first and foremost a communication risk,” said Walter Pasquarelli, a strategy adviser to governments on AI and affiliated researcher at the University of Cambridge. “It’s not just workers across businesses who cannot get access to it, but there’s lots of government services and lots of government infrastructure that actually relies on that.” Foreign banks and financial institutions in Taiwan were hit especially hard, a ⁠trader told the news agency Reuters, as their data is emailed to overseas headquarters through Microsoft’s systems. Fax machines were used in Taipei while European exchange operator Euronext told companies to phone in their trades. Norway’s parliament and several ministries lost access to email, while 80 to 90 Danish municipalities were reportedly affected. Rail operators in Germany, the United Kingdom and Canada said the outage impacted timetables and emailed tickets, and the UK’s massive National Health Service pivoted to using paper records. In the United States, the House of Representatives and local governments were affected, Reuters reported. The US Department of Defense, which relies heavily on Microsoft’s services, did not comment on whether it was affected. The Pentagon was slated to upgrade its Microsoft infrastructure starting in June in a $9.7bn deal that included access to Microsoft 365. The server failures did not appear to shake Wall Street’s confidence in Microsoft, however, which said it would review the incident along with measures to prevent future disruptions. Microsoft’s stock was mostly flat in US market trading on Friday as the tech-heavy Nasdaq index fell slightly, led by the embattled AI company Nvidia.          Follow Al Jazeera English:

Apple published a new security research post this week detailing Secure Exclaves, a new architecture built to handle what the company calls “ambient sensing.” The latter isn’t anything new. “Hey, Siri” has been using a version of this always-on listening technology for years. The difference now (particularly on newer devices like Apple Watch Series 12 and HomeView) is new features need far more data from your surroundings, and Apple has changed where that data gets processed.  Today, on most Apple hardware, wake-word detections run locally on-device on a smaller, low-power chip. But once it thinks it heard you say “Hey, Siri,” the main operating system gets involved to confirm and wake up the smart assistant for use. There’s nothing necessarily wrong with this process. The split second of audio is all processed locally and not sent to Apple servers. The problem lies in Apple’s newer features that ask for a lot more from users than a wake word. Person recognition on HomeView identifies who’s in the room by face and voice, and Siri Recap and Live Rewind need to keep a running sense of what’s been happening around you. That adds up to a constant stream of sensitive camera and mic data, and it needs a more secure way of being processed than anything Apple had before. Much like the existing Secure Enclaves architecture for authentication, instead of passing operations to the main OS, Secure Exclaves (notice the x) run their own tiny, separate operating system. Raw data goes in and a simple “that’s Arin” or “that’s the wake word” is outputted back to the OS, everything else is thrown away. According to Apple, that data “cannot be accessed by the main operating system, apps, or Apple.” The changes don’t stop there. In recent SB column, I mentioned how on iPhone, the green dot that appears indicating that the camera or mic is live is all software connected, not like the hardwired LED that exists on the Mac. Now on iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone Duo, and MacBook Neo, the camera and mic indicators now live inside this new exclave, meaning even a compromised OS shouldn’t be able to hide them for malicious purposes. It’s apparent Apple is building toward this new level of ambient computing across every type of device when you read technical reports like this. Future AI-first products, like the heavily rumored AirPods Pro with inferred cameras, will most certainly built on this new Secure Exclave architecture. Overall, this new technical post reads like Apple laying the privacy groundwork for the always-listening, always-watching products that are here and coming in the near future. It’s the privacy-first approach we’ve come to love from Apple and further demonstrates its lead on this front. I highly recommend checking it out. Johnny Depp became a household name playing misunderstood monsters, eccentrics, and Disney-friendly scallywags, but in the last few years, Hollywood has turned him into a different sort of outcast. "Ebenezer," distributed by Paramount Pictures, is Depp's first major Hollywood feature since he sued his ex-wife, Amber Heard, in 2019 over domestic abuse allegations, which he denied, and the explosive defamation trial that followed. Jurors found both Depp and Heard liable for defamation, and they reached a settlement in 2022 — though not before testimonies and documents entered into evidence exposed disturbing details, from a photo of feces on the couple's shared bed (Depp blamed Heard, while Heard blamed their dog), to texts that Depp wrote about burning and drowning his ex-wife, and having sex with her "burnt corpse" (Depp said he's "not proud" of the messages, which he described as "dark humor"). Depp's professional reputation had suffered blows long before he took the stand. He lost a similar libel case in 2020 after the British newspaper The Sun called him a "wife-beater," and was subsequently ousted from lucrative franchise roles in the next installment of the "Harry Potter" spin-off film series, "Fantastic Beasts," and "Pirates of the Caribbean 6." Before that, Depp was mired in complex legal battles with his former business partners over his admittedly lavish spending. Rumors swirled about Depp's tardiness and unprofessionalism on set amid a series of box-office flops. But the years have passed, and Hollywood may be cautiously welcoming Depp back into the fold. Thousands of Depp supporters have stayed staunchly, outspokenly loyal to the star. Social media reactions to the defamation trial were overwhelmingly sympathetic to Depp amid reports of a targeted smear campaign to discredit Heard. By the time the actual jurors handed down their judgment, it looked like Depp had already been vindicated online. "Ebenezer" is positioned as Depp's big Hollywood comeback, complete with a splashy marketing campaign and top-line billing for its embattled star. "The Master of Misfits returns," one of the studio's taglines declares, with marketing materials drawing a connection between the film's title character and the man who "brought us Jack Sparrow, Edward Scissorhands, and The Mad Hatter." Yet "Ebenezer" isn't just another misfit role for Depp to add to his résumé. Scrooge's near-two-century life in the pop-culture canon is proof that audiences love a redemption story. Is Depp about to get his?                                    Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                  Paramount is certainly manifesting it. The first shot of Depp in character as Scrooge in the "Ebenezer" teaser trailer breaks the fourth wall, as Depp delivers his line to the camera with a knowing expression: "It's good to be back." Casting Depp in "Ebenezer" was a gamble for Paramount, but a cheaper gamble than one might imagine. Where Depp once fetched $25 million up front for 2017's "Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales," the total budget for "Ebenezer" was $38 million. The New York Times reported that Depp accepted a reduced salary of roughly $5 million in exchange for a larger share of the proceeds if the movie performs at the box office. In other words, for an established movie star, he was a steal. Representatives for Depp and Paramount did not respond to requests for comment from Business Insider. Paramount is certainly throwing its weight behind "Ebenezer," with the presumed expectation it will pay off in ticket sales. Depp has appeared in full Charles Dickens drag — top hat, overcoat, heavy prosthetics — for several promotional stunts, from New York's Bryant Park holiday market to San Diego's Comic-Con, where he drew an adoring crowd. According to The New York Times, one woman even called out to him, "Have my baby!" The movie's trailers and posters have relied heavily on name recognition for the actor and the character, betting on audiences to re-embrace both. As far as the promo is concerned, Depp and Scrooge are one and the same: a man with his feet to the fire, seeking salvation. "The studio is trying to test the public's willingness to embrace Johnny Depp again after all of the personal crises," said Tara Goodwin, founder of Goodwin Consulting and a crisis PR veteran. "This is allowing him, through the character Ebenezer, to be judged by his work rather than in a court of law or the court of public opinion." "One movie, one PR stunt, does not rebuild a reputation," she added. "But it does change the conversation from his personal narrative to his professional one." Will that be enough to get butts in seats? As PR professionals have told me over and over, the public is more forgiving than you think — especially if the celebrity in question has nostalgia to leverage. "Johnny Depp, his fans go back 40 years. They still remember him as the kid on '21 Jump Street.' In a lot of ways, he's a symbol of Generation X," said Ryan McCormick, cofounder and managing partner at Goldman McCormick PR. "Some of his iconic roles automatically pull people into a different era of time, like when they were younger and maybe when the world wasn't so crazy or intense." In that sense, Scrooge is the perfect character for Depp: a familiar face who learns to appreciate the generosity of others. He's the universal shorthand for second chances. Helmed by horror director Ti West, "Ebenezer" is a spookier-than-usual adaptation of Dickens' classic novella.  According to early reviews from critics — including this one — "Ebenezer" isn't a great movie; it currently holds a 53% critics score on Rotten Tomatoes at the time of publication. I found it to be insipid and tedious, caught somewhere between a trite Christmas parable and a Halloween fright fest. Your opinion of Depp's performance will depend on your tolerance for hammy commitment, as a prosthetic-laden Depp gesticulates and mugs his way through a series of ghostly encounters — clearly attempting to recapture the smarmy charm of Jack Sparrow, reincarnated as a 19th-century grump. But critics' assessments likely won't matter to Depp or any studios eyeing him for employment. Negative reviews are small potatoes if the theaters are crowded and the box office returns are strong. "It's the people that make the difference. It's not the critics," Goodwin said. If the people like it, Hollywood seems willing to hire Depp again. Sources told NBC News that a new "Pirates 6" script featuring the return of Depp as Sparrow has been kicked around at Disney. Studio executives are reportedly waiting to see how "Ebenezer" is received before giving "Pirates 6" the green light. In the meantime, Depp already has his next movie lined up: "Day Drinker," a thriller costarring Depp's old friend Penélope Cruz, will be released by Lionsgate in March. Mia Moody, a professor in the Department of Journalism, Public Relations, and New Media at Baylor University, agreed with Goodwin and McCormick that the future of Depp's comeback will depend heavily on the box office. The meta-narrative of "Ebenezer" as long-standing gospel — that no one, not even the bah-humbuggiest among us, is beyond redemption — is mostly a bonus. "Hollywood is different in general when you're looking at image repair, because it's not necessarily governed by moral consensus. It's more governed by commercial viability," Moody said. "So if Johnny Depp can have a hit and if his movie can make money, then that's the bottom line." Jump to

The long-awaited Motorola MA2 wireless Android Auto adapter is gone just days after it went on sale. Motorola MA2 is a wireless Android Auto adapter designed with Google. It was announced way back in March 2026 as the sequel to MA1, which itself launched back in 2022. Needless to say, it’s debut has been long-awaited, and that arrived earlier this week. By Max Goldbart  International TV Co-Editor  	Good afternoon friends, welcome back to another edition of the Deadline International Insider with Max Goldbart bringing you the latest. Scroll down. And sign up here.  AFM Heats Up  Kicking the tyres: The American Film Market (AFM) took place in Los Angeles this week with no shortage of packages announced in the days before and during. There’s been little reported in the way of major action on those packages so far but that’s not to say deals haven’t been done, they are just slower to be finalized these days, not helped by the Microsoft outage that has plagued emails for the past 24 hours or so. Among deals we revealed during the market were Lionsgate clinching Alma Har’el’s starry drama Wet and Venice Golden Lion winner An Unknown Woman getting a domestic deal with CMG. Meanwhile, Amazon continues to kick the tyres on some of the bigger projects in the market, one awash with horror projects as the industry continues to chase the next Obsession or Backrooms. Among the horror was NorthFiveSix’s Seeker with Cooper Tomlinson, Jessica Rothe and Mika Abdalla, and FilmNation’s Violet with Lili Reinhart, Danny Ramirez and Suki Waterhouse. Unusually, a number of leading sales companies didn’t announce a new title this market. A24, however, came with barrels loaded. The big-ticket project on sale was fantasy movie Elden Ring, which comes with a budget in the $180 million-$200 million range, making it the biggest budgeted stand-alone film ever at a market. We told you all about the project a couple weeks ago. There were new packages with Jeremy Renner, Idris Elba, Liam Neeson, Gillian Anderson and Renée Zellweger, while Jean-Claude Van Damme action pic Katana generated some serious interest on deadline.com. Very fitting for the genre-heavy AFM. We should hear more in the way of dealmaking in coming days. Here’s how it works.  We're experiencing always-on tech fatigue, which is in part why wearables like smart rings and now screenless fitness and health trackers are becoming popular. They can capture all the same data as a smartwatch or traditional fitness tracker, but do so passively, in the background, so you can go about your day without distractions. Screenless fitness trackers in particular are on the rise, graduating from a market once dominated only by Whoop to include huge brands like Google Fitbit and Garmin as well as smaller ones like Luna and Amazfit. Android Central has tested many of the latest screenless fitness bands extensively, often sporting more than one at a time to compare and contrast them and the data they collect. At their core, they all do the same thing. But there are also notable differences in design, battery life, app experience, and subscription options (or membership requirements). You'll want to pick the right one to use alongside your Android device based on your needs, preferences, and budget.     Best overall  Best overall The Google Fitbit Air is thin, comfortable, affordable, yet packs tons of power in a small band. Think Fitbit's history of accurate activity and sleep tracking combined with Google's knowledge in design, AI, and apps. With Google Health Premium, it's the best you can buy right now.  Read more below.     Best for fitness buffs  Best for fitness buffs The Garmin CIRQA is thicker and chunkier than others, but it's a solid choice if fitness is your main priority. That's thanks to accurate automatic tracking and a side button for quickly triggering an activity, cute shareable post-workout cards, and decent battery life that keeps it going for more than a week per charge. Read more below.     Best free AI app  Best free AI app The Luna Band combines some of the best aspects of apps like Google Health Premium in a subscription-free, AI-driven experience. I loved the LifeOS system with the Luna Ring 2, and with the consistent app updates, it continues to improve, making this a promising option. Read more below.     Best premium  Best premium You might need an executive-level salary to afford the Whoop MG's annual membership, but medical-grade ECG and blood pressure trends make it worthwhile for those with heart health concerns, especially. The app and system are among the most aggressive in terms of pushing you to get in shape, focus on your health, and slow the pace of aging. But for some, that's a good thing. Read more below.     Best for women  Best Whoop alternative You want something like Whoop, but those ones are too rich for your blood. Hume bands like this one are a more affordable option with no subscription (or a moderately priced step-up one if you decide to sign up for more) and a focus on lifespan health versus day-to-day tracking as well. Read more below.     Best budget  Best budget With features like live heart rate broadcasting to compatible devices like gym equipment and an optional arm sleeve, the Amazfit Helio Strap is meant for gym-goers and runners. It's a simple design with accurate data capture, and best of all, no subscription. Read more below.      Our expert review: The Fitbit Air is one of the most accurate screenless fitness trackers, combining Fitbit's long history in the business with top-notch vitals and sleep tracking, along with Google's powerful processing and AI integration. While you can use the Fitbit Air with the free version of the app and get basic details, you will get a lot more out of it with a Google Health Premium subscription. AI Coach is one of the best I have used, answering questions about the data, like why you might not have slept well and what you can do to improve, what exercise would be good to work around a shoulder injury, and even logging specific dumbbell weights and reps to gather more details about a workout. I love how easy it is to log meals by either dictating what you just ate or snapping a photo. You'll see a detailed breakdown of calories consumed (versus burned), protein, fat, carbs, and more. It's a solid food diary if you want to use it for that, too. The companion app is easy to navigate with all the essentials at a glance, like heart rate, a detailed breakdown of sleep, blood oxygen, readiness score, and more. Most notably, the app guides you through how to tackle the day with commentary, analysis, motivation, suggestions, and advice. It really is like a virtual coach. A couple of big omissions, our reviewer notes, are the lack of ECG and built-in GPS. But considering how affordable the band is, we can live with that. Along with what's captured from the band, the more information you provide with food logging, details about workouts, injuries, moments of stress, and more, the more intelligent it becomes in putting this all together. It's one of the few wearables where I'd say the subscription is worth the money. Given the affordable price of the band, use the three-month trial to get an idea of what Premium adds and decide from there. It's a no-brainer option to keep on top of fitness and vitals.      Our expert review: The Garmin CIRQA is thicker and wider than other bands, but it's still incredibly comfortable to wear. Most importantly, it tracks all the essentials for free. You can opt for the Garmin Connect+ subscription for add-ons like Garmin Coach, AI-powered insights, and nutrition tracking. But it's not robust enough to be worth it, and that's pretty much all that's behind a paywall. The band accurately tracks activity, vitals, and sleep; the data provided is typically in line with other wearables I rely on. What I love is that it's the only screenless band I have seen to date with a physical side button you can press to manually start and stop an activity. You can later clarify in the app what it was, like a cardio class or baseball game. But it does a pretty good job of automatically picking up activities with distinct movements, like walks, runs, boxing, and strength training. I love the ability to add a post-workout selfie to a cute card with workout stats you can share on social media or with friends. Features like Body Battery, similar to a readiness score, and Health Status are useful. The latter confirms if any baselines for heart rate, heart rate variability (HRV), respiration, pulse OX, and skin temperature are out of range. There's lots of additional data you can log in the app to enhance the experience. With LiveTrack, you can send your location to family members or friends, ideal if you're embarking on a hike or running in an unfamiliar town. If you're looking for a band mainly to track fitness, the Garmin CIRQA is a good option. You don't get all the bells and whistles that come with Google Health Premium and Fitbit Air. It's also a higher upfront cost for the band. But you can keep track of everything that matters, including a detailed diary of your workouts and stats.      Our expert review: One of the lesser-known brands in this space, Luna is best known for its smart rings. But the company launched its first screenless tracker at CES 2026 with the Luna Band, and it's a serious contender. It tracks all the same metrics as others and does so accurately, based on my month-plus of wearing it. This includes everything from activities to sleep, vitals like heart rate, HRV, stress, respiratory rate, and more. At the heart of the experience is the Life OS system, an AI-driven system that lets you ask questions, log things like stress and meals, get advice, dive deeper into data, and more. There's an "Ask Luna" hands-free voice option, though it's limited to iPhone support right now. Seemingly inspired by Ultrahuman smart rings and the company's PowerPlugs, the Luna app also includes downloadable micro apps you can add to customize the experience. These include, at the time of this writing, sleep alarm, cycle tracker, calorie tracker, and circadian rhythm. The app indicates that new features are coming soon, like a Luna Age (cardio fitness score), supplement planner, and hydration analyzer. The app has been updated and redesigned several times since I started wearing the band. So, if you are looking to get in with a brand that's experimenting and continuously developing, this is a good option. Most importantly, you can be confident that the data is accurate.      Our expert review: Around since 2015, Whoop isn't technically the originator of this category, but it has a similar reputation to Oura as the brand that put the category on the map. But before you get excited about a Whoop tracker, they're expensive with a capital "E." And the Whoop MG is the top-line model. It's a medical-grade tracker that, compared to its little sister, the Whoop 5.0, adds ECG and blood pressure insights. ECG is easy to measure any time by placing your thumb and index finger on the sensors on either side, and blood pressure requires an initial cuff measurement to then provide subsequent trend estimates. The app is packed (and I really mean packed) with data that you might initially feel like you need a medical degree to interpret. Thankfully, however, it's thoughtfully laid out and explained to help you make sense of it all. It tracks all the expected metrics and has a Healthspan and Pace of Aging feature. After the 31-day logging period, it will report a Whoop Age that you can compare to your biological age and determine your pace of aging. It's a moving target, so if there's ever a stat that prompts you to work out, go for that walk, eat better, and head to bed early, it's that one. There's an AI assistant, too, but it's more like a deadpan CEO barking orders instead of a motivational fitness instructor. The best thing about this tracker is the included Wireless Powerpack. It slides right onto the sensor while it's still on your wrist and recharges the unit on the go. You literally never have to remove it! For some, that alone might be worth the exorbitant price to sign up. If the Whoop MG is too rich for your blood and you are willing to forego ECG and blood pressure insights, consider the Whoop 5.0. Its membership options are slightly more affordable, but still more expensive than any other band over its lifetime.      Our expert review: If you love the concept behind the WHOOP MG but find the pricing too rich for your blood, even for the WHOOP 5.0, the Hume Band 2.0 is worth considering. While I haven't yet tested this model (stay tuned!), it is widely praised for offering some of the same benefits as WHOOP bands, including a focus on longevity and helping you reduce the speed of aging. While you get the core tracking features for free, including sleep, recovery, strain, HRV, skin temperature, and of course activity tracking as well as blood pressure trends, there is a Hume Premium subscription tier that unlocks more. But it's much cheaper at $8.99 per month, which works out to be almost half the price of the cheapest WHOOP One plan. The band and companion app capture useful data like metabolic capacity (similar to a readiness score), sleep apnea risk alerts, chronic illness detection (identifying early signs), and AI coaching with the subscription tier. You may have to take the data with a grain of salt. But the price of entry makes Hume Band 2.0 a good starting point if you're considering exploring the concept of a screenless tracker and value overall lifespan data more than daily metrics and workout stats.      Our expert review: Amazfit has a solid reputation in the smartwatch space, with many of its models ranking among the best affordable Android smartwatches. This reliability extends to the Amazfit Helio Strap, which is simple, affordable, and, based on customer feedback (we haven't reviewed this one yet), as reliable as its beloved smartwatches. One of the unique features is live heart rate broadcasting, which allows you to broadcast your heart rate to compatible devices, like a Garmin smartwatch, Apple Watch, or even gym equipment. The best part? There's no subscription required…for anything. There's a more premium option called the Amazfit Helio Strap Pro that boasts a dual-sensor system and is designed for hybrid athletes and HYROX training. But most people won't need that model. There are also useful accessories like an arm sleeve for wearing it around the bicep, something runners will appreciate so they can still wear a running watch on their wrist. This is a solid budget option for fitness enthusiasts who also want vital health tracking. Choosing the right screenless fitness band comes down to two core things: recognizing your needs and budget. What is your budget? If you want something you only need to pay a single price for and that doesn't require recurring fees, choose one of those options. If you are serious about health, want guidance and granular data, and can afford it, you may find value in some subscription-based bands. What are your goals? All these bands track both fitness and health, including vitals. But some focus more heavily on fitness, some on health, and some a mix of both. If you only want to monitor daily data, you can look for a simpler option. If you need guidance towards meeting goals, a more advanced one makes sense. For ECG readings, the Whoop MG is your only option in this category. If it's pricing doesn't meet your budget, however, you can consider a smartwatch with ECG instead.  Why you can trust Android Central     Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.       You'll be happy with any of these screenless fitness bands. For an AI-driven coaching experience, Fitbit Air can't be beat. But if you want to get something similar without a subscription, Luna Band is worth considering. If you exercise daily and want to track workouts as much as vitals, the Garmin CIRQA is a solid choice. The Whoop MG is a medical-grade device, ideal for serious athletes or someone who is especially concerned about heart health and/or blood pressure. But it comes in at executive-level pricing. It's worth noting that none of these trackers, even the Whoop MG, is a replacement for consultation from a medical professional, and they are not meant for diagnosis, only supplemental data. The best overall budget option is the Fitbit Air. It doesn't cost much upfront, and you can gauge how the subscription works through the three-month trial. Once the trial lapses, see the difference without it and decide from there if it's worth paying the nominal monthly fee. Even with Google Health Premium, the cost is one less takeout lunch a month when all is said and done. And even after a year, the overall cost is still less than the upfront cost of most of these other bands. Share Mary Shelley’s 1818 gothic novel Frankenstein follows a scientist who assembles a creature from various body parts in pursuit of his ideal creation.  Centuries later, a similar concept has entered the dating world through a troubling pattern known as “frankensteining.” The term refers to attempts to mold a romantic partner into someone who matches personal expectations rather than embracing their individuality. Although such efforts may initially stem from a desire to strengthen the relationship, they can gradually give way to frustration and unrealistic demands. Texas-based marriage and family therapist Sara Sloane recently explored how this behavior develops, why some people feel compelled to reshape their significant others, and what drives them to repair an unhappy relationship rather than move on.  fizkes/Adobe Stock (not the actual photo) Frankensteining can take many forms, from pressuring a partner to change their dressing style or appearance to insisting they adopt different hobbies and everyday habits. Sloane explained that the behavior can be difficult to recognize, particularly when someone believes they are simply helping their partner become a better version of themselves. “One easy to notice if you are frankensteining your partner is if you are thinking, ‘If they would (fill in the blank), it would be so much better,” the therapist said.  Universal Pictures She noted that people often engage in frankensteining because they become attached to their partner’s potential rather than accepting who they are in the present. “A lot of people Frankenstein their partner as part of wishful thinking, bringing to life their ideal partner,” she said. The therapist added that the pattern often emerges as the “new relationship energy wears off and you begin to notice things that feel less than optimal in your new partner.” “Rather than breaking up and risk having to start over completely,” in such cases, Sloane explained, “it can feel easier to Frankenstein your partner into something that fits your ideal.”  william87/Adobe Stock (not the actual photo) According to the therapist, recognizing the difference between compromise and control is essential to preventing frankensteining from damaging a relationship. Compromise allows both partners to make adjustments while retaining their individuality. By contrast, repeatedly pressuring someone to change their appearance, personality, or interests to satisfy another person’s preferences can undermine their agency.  Drobot Dean/Adobe Stock (not the actual photo) Sloane emphasized that accepting differences is crucial to maintaining a healthy connection. “The best way to avoid frankensteining your partner is to allow them to maintain their autonomy,” she stated.  “Allow them to be different than you, or different than your ideal.”  Studio Romantic/Adobe Stock (not the actual photo) Some X users questioned whether the behavior needed another dating-related label, and others pointed out how familiar the concept sounded. “Are we just making up terms now?” one person asked. “In my day we called this ‘keeping a chameleon,” another added. Others turned the discussion into a gender debate, suggesting that women had been practicing the behavior for centuries.   “You mean what every woman that ever was in a relationship has done,” one person commented, while another quipped, “I can change him after we are married!” Meanwhile, a separate user appeared tired of the seemingly endless stream of dating terminology, writing, “There’s a new one every week. I’m just gonna be over here lonermaxxing.” The discussion also reminded one user of a classic Hollywood musical. “Have you not seen My Fair Lady?” they asked, referencing the 1964 movie.  Paramount Movies In My Fair Lady, a professor attempts to transform a working-class woman into someone who can pass as a member of high society. The story follows Eliza Doolittle, a flower seller in London whose strong Cockney accent sets her apart from the upper classes.  Paramount Movies Henry Higgins, an expert in phonetics, believes that a person’s speech determines how society perceives their social standing.  Following a bet with his friend, Colonel Pickering, he sets out to transform Eliza’s speech and manners.  Paramount Movies Eliza agrees to the lessons because she hopes to improve her circumstances and find work in a respectable flower shop. She eventually succeeds in passing as a member of the high class. For Higgins, however, the experiment comes at a cost.  He becomes so absorbed in his project that he often treats Eliza as a subject to be transformed rather than an individual with feelings and ambitions of her own.  Paramount Movies Eventually, Eliza confronts him over his behavior, asserting her independence and right to make her own choices. The comparison between the film and frankensteining did not convince everyone, however, with one netizen arguing that the two situations were significantly different. “Eliza was not becoming someone else just to romantically please a man,” they argued.
