by Jason Lemkin | Artificial Intelligence (AI), Blog Posts Palantir just reported Q3 2026, and it is growing faster at about $9.3 billion in run-rate than it was at $4 billion. Revenue grew 96% year-over-year and 20% quarter-over-quarter to $2.313 billion, and quarterly revenue surpassed $2 billion for the first time ever. The stock went down anyway. Palantir traded at $172.99 after the print, down from $178.30 just before earnings. The reason is in the bookings numbers, covered in #3 below.  For 20 years, Palantir was a government company that also sold to enterprises. That flipped this quarter. U.S. commercial revenue grew 148% year-over-year and 29% quarter-over-quarter to $984 million, while U.S. government revenue grew 96% year-over-year and 18% quarter-over-quarter to $953 million. U.S. commercial was $764 million in Q2, so it added about $220 million of quarterly revenue in 90 days. A year ago, the entire U.S. commercial segment did $397 million in a quarter. One quarter’s increase was more than half of what the whole segment did a year ago. Government is not slowing down to let it happen. Government growing 96% is now the slower half of the business. Karp’s line on it: “our sequential growth in U.S. commercial of 29% would be an astonishing annual growth rate of any public software company in America.” Most public B2B companies would take 29% a year. The founder decision: Palantir took years of criticism for pushing into commercial when government was the proven money. AIP bootcamps and the commercial sales buildout were expensive for a long time. The second market is now bigger than the first. If you have a second segment compounding faster than your core, move your best people onto it before the numbers make it obvious.  Palantir still has a very small customer count for its revenue. U.S. commercial customers rose 29% YoY to 686 while average trailing 12-month revenue per U.S. commercial customer grew 88% YoY, and company-wide net dollar retention rose 800 basis points QoQ to 165%. $984 million in a quarter across 686 customers is about $1.43 million per customer per quarter, or roughly $5.7 million annualized. Customers grew 29%. Revenue grew 148%. Nearly all of the growth is existing customers buying more. NRR is also rising at scale: 134% a year ago, 157% last quarter, 165% now. At most companies NRR declines as they get bigger. Two expansion examples from the call: That second one went from $3 million to $29 million in about 90 days. The founder decision: Palantir lands with a paid pilot that has to show value fast, then expands aggressively once it does. It does not chase logo count. At 110% NRR, new logos are your main growth lever. At 165%, each good customer drives its own growth.  This is why the stock fell. Palantir closed TCV of $2.918 billion, up 6% year-over-year, including $1.463 billion of U.S. commercial TCV, up 11% year-over-year. U.S. commercial RDV was $6.517 billion, up 79% year-over-year and 4% quarter-over-quarter. Total RPO was $4.9 billion, up 88% year-over-year but flat sequentially. In Q2, Palantir closed $2.132 billion in U.S. commercial TCV, up 153% year over year and 81% sequentially. So U.S. commercial TCV went from $2.13 billion to $1.46 billion in one quarter, while revenue grew 148%. Palantir attributes the gap to contract length. CFO Dave Glazer flagged that the new eight-figure contracts are shorter in duration than in prior periods, which helps explain the gap between 96% revenue growth and 6% TCV growth. Management expects deal durations and sizes to expand as customers begin harvesting value from their deployments. Two numbers support that read: 165% NRR, and billings of $2.39 billion, up 114% year on year. The risk is that shorter contracts give customers more points to leave. The founder decision: Palantir traded contract length for speed of close. That accelerates revenue and makes backlog look weaker. If you make the same trade, expect TCV and RPO to look bad for a few quarters, and expect investors to judge you on whether renewals and expansions actually come in. For Palantir, that test is Q4 and Q1.  Adjusted income from operations was $1.427 billion, a 62% adjusted operating margin compared with 51% a year earlier. Add 96% growth and the Rule of 40 score is 158. The benchmark is 40. The GAAP numbers hold up too. GAAP income from operations was $1.085 billion, a 47% margin, and GAAP net income was $1.128 billion, a 49% margin. Stock-based compensation was $319 million in Q3, about 14% of revenue, well below most high-growth B2B companies. Expenses are growing at about half the rate of revenue. Non-GAAP adjusted expense rose 53% year over year to $887 million. Revenue grew 96%. That is a deliberate choice, because management said internal capacity falls short of demand. The founder decision: When demand outruns capacity, most CEOs hire as fast as they can. Palantir held expense growth to about half of revenue growth and relies on AIP and the ontology to carry more of each deployment. If your AI product needs a proportional team of forward-deployed engineers for every new customer, these margins are out of reach.  International commercial revenue was up 21% YoY but just 1% QoQ to $184 million, and international government revenue was up 31% YoY to $192 million. U.S. revenue was $1.937 billion of $2.313 billion, or 84% of the business. U.S. commercial grew 29% sequentially. International commercial grew 1%. Palantir has said for years that Europe adopts more slowly, and it is not forcing it. Resources are going where buyers are signing now. The founder decision: When one market grows 29% a quarter and another grows 1%, don’t split resources evenly to look global. Put them into the market that’s growing. Palantir is capacity-constrained in the U.S., so international stays a lower priority until that changes.  The operating business is exceptional: 96% growth, 165% NRR, 49% GAAP net margin, and $10.4 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and U.S. Treasury securities. The weak spot is bookings, with TCV up 6% and U.S. commercial RDV up 4% sequentially. At a $428.6 billion market cap, about 46x run-rate, investors want evidence that the shorter contracts renew at larger sizes. The pilot conversions to $15 million and $29 million suggest they will, and Q4 and Q1 TCV will confirm it or not. A nonpartisan ethics watchdog group has asked for an investigation into whether a top Department of Health and Human Services official violated ethics laws after a recent ProPublica investigation revealed actions experts called “alarming” and an “obvious conflict of interest.”  Alicia Jackson, who heads the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, publicly endorsed a change to federal health policy on hormone replacement therapies while owning stock in a company that provides access to menopause treatments.  In a letter to the department’s inspector general, the Campaign Legal Center also questioned whether Jackson properly identified up to $400 million in underlying assets held by her husband’s investment firm. The center’s review identified an additional potential conflict — investments in a second firm that provides hormone treatments for menopause.  Jackson, who heads the HHS agency that invests taxpayer money in medical technology and research, was recently placed on administrative leave, though health officials have not publicly explained why. In its letter, the Campaign Legal Center cited the ProPublica investigation that found Jackson spoke at an HHS press conference last November and was quoted in a department news release announcing the decision to remove “black box warnings” from hormone replacement therapy products.  At the time, Jackson owned at least $115,000 in stock and an unknown amount of stock options in Evernow, a company she founded that connects women to hormone replacement treatments, according to her financial disclosures.  It’s unclear what role, if any, Jackson played in the decision to drop the requirement to display a black box warning, the most serious type of federal safety warning. The Food and Drug Administration regulates drugs. And an FDA panel of experts had recommended ending the requirement months before Jackson became her agency’s director in October 2025. Still, ethics experts noted that federal law prohibits government employees from participating “personally and substantially” in matters that could influence their personal finances — even making statements at a press conference or in a news release.   The Campaign Legal Center asked the inspector general to examine whether Jackson broke federal ethics laws by failing to recuse herself. Neither Jackson nor the HHS will say whether she obtained a conflict-of-interest waiver before participating in the policy announcement.  “Americans have a right to know that government decisions are not being made to benefit a federal employee’s financial interests,” the organization wrote. The center also asked the inspector general to determine if Jackson failed to fully and accurately disclose her and her spouse’s financial interests in private investment funds. ProPublica’s investigation found that Jackson reported she and her husband owned more than 60 venture capital and private equity funds that she said do not disclose their holdings to investors. These include at least 13 funds managed by 137 Ventures, a venture capital firm co-founded by her husband, Alex Jacobson. The company invests in a wide range of industries, including healthcare, digital health and medical device companies. Ethics experts said the funds could pose a serious conflict of interest if the underlying businesses received grants or contracts from her agency.  The Campaign Legal Center’s review of Jackson’s disclosures identified one of those funds — 137 Ventures IV LP — as an investor in Thirty Madison Inc., a virtual healthcare company. Thirty Madison owns a subsidiary that provides hormone replacement treatments for women experiencing menopause symptoms. Jackson’s disclosures do not show her divesting from the fund before the black box warning announcement, the center said. Under federal law, financial disclosure forms filed by federal officials like Jackson must then be certified by ethics staff as complying with the law. But Jackson’s two financial disclosures — filed last October and two months ago — remain uncertified.  HHS’ inspector general’s office would not confirm or deny whether it is investigating Jackson. The inspector general, T. March Bell, was one of nearly 100 appointees confirmed by the Senate in a December 2025 party-line vote. President Donald Trump fired the previous inspector general just days into the president’s second term. ProPublica also requested responses from HHS, Jackson, Jacobson and 137 Ventures, but none commented. In a statement to ProPublica last month, an HHS spokesperson said that while Jackson was on leave the agency would “assess the facts before determining any change in her status. HHS requires all officials to comply with federal ethics laws, regulations, and policies.”  Jackson was appointed by Trump as her agency’s second director and sworn in on Oct. 20, 2025. The agency, created three years earlier to spur revolutionary biomedical research and technologies, has a $1.5 billion budget. It has issued numerous contracts and grants, including $160 million for genetic medicines combating rare diseases and $144 million to study existing treatments for age-related illnesses. Jackson’s disclosures are among 2,400 added last month to ProPublica’s Trump Team Financials database, a searchable tool launched in March. The records detail the finances of more than 2,300 officials appointed by Trump. Since last year, we’ve requested disclosure records from 127 federal agencies and the White House. Disclosures from roughly 1,500 appointees remain unreleased.  	I am a Pulitzer Prize-winning reporter at ProPublica. I welcome tips about ethical conflicts or misdeeds inside the federal bureaucracy. Watch CBS News  November 13, 2026 / 4:32 PM EST             / CBS News            Even if you never bought a single share of Nvidia, the embattled chipmaker's steep slide this week could still ding your retirement savings.  Nvidia is a component of the S&P 500 and many other indexes, including the Nasdaq 100 and Dow Jones Industrial Average, all popular with retirement savers through funds offered by millions of employer retirement plans. About 97% of retirement plans now offer index funds, up from 79% in 2006, according to March research from the Investment Company Institute and ISS Market Intelligence. That means even if you haven't directly bought Nvidia stock, your 401(k) is likely exposed to the chipmaker through an index fund, such as the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust or Vanguard's S&P 500 ETF (which trade under the tickers SPY and VOO, respectively).  Overall, Nvidia represents about 6% of the S&P 500 index, making it the second-largest component after Apple, according to Yahoo Finance.  Nvidia's shares started falling on Monday amid revelations that cofounder Jensen Huang had an extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Huang resigned from his role as CEO on Thursday, causing a further drop in the stock.  Since Nov. 6, the company's value has declined by more than $550 billion — a decline of about 13% in one week. While that will certainly hurt investors who directly own Nvidia shares, it may also impact people with indirect investments through funds that hold the chipmaker. Nvidia's woes underline the risks inherent in many big tech companies widely held by U.S. investors, Shiva Rajgopal, a Columbia Business School professor who studies corporate governance, told CBS News. The "Magnificent Seven" tech stocks account for about one-third of the S&P 500. As with Nvidia, several of those companies are closely associated with CEOs whom investors see as central to their success, such as Elon Musk at Tesla, Rajgopal noted. And as Nvidia's selloff showed this week, trouble for a charismatic CEO can quickly spill over into the company's stock. "They are amazing wealth creators for shareholders," Rajgopal said. "But hopefully, shareholders know what they are doing when they buy the stock of these companies, because the exact same structure also has a lot of fragility built into it." The AI industry's influence on Wall Street was evident this week, as turmoil at Nvidia triggered a broader slump in technology stocks. Yet more companies within the S&P 500 rose rather than fell this week, boosting the index by 2.9% for the week through Thursday's close. Excluding Nvidia, the index would have gained an estimated 3.8%. "If you check your account today, tomorrow, you're going to see some sort of fluctuation, especially if you own shares of Nvidia," Sabrina Escobar, a reporter at Barron's, told CBS News. "The decline we saw over the past couple of days will certainly have some implications in your daily or weekly stock movements." For investors, Huang's sudden downfall and Nvidia's wobbly stock highlight the importance of properly diversifying their portfolios, Mercer Advisors chief investment officer Donald Calcagni said in a blog post.  "Events like this — where the outcome hinges on one company's leadership — are a risk we try to minimize through diversification," he wrote. "This is the core principle behind portfolio diversification strategies: spread your risk broadly enough that no single company's troubles can derail your long-term plan." Of course, that's the idea behind holding a broad-based index fund like the S&P 500 — rather than concentrating your money in a handful of individual stocks, you're spreading your bets across hundreds of types of companies. And the fact that the S&P 500 is on track to post a weekly gain despite Nvidia's turmoil points to how that strategy can pay off.  Investors may be tempted to sell when the market, a stock or a fund tumbles, but research has repeatedly shown that trying to determine the right time to buy or sell an investment usually results in losses.  Meanwhile, tech experts noted that Nvidia's chips remain essential to the artificial intelligence sector, a key competitive edge unlikely to change in the near term even with Huang's abrupt departure. In other words, holding Nvidia shares may be a way to bet on the broader AI industry, rather than on its executive roster. "When a single company's stock drops on unexpected news, the best response is usually the simplest one: pause, keep the news in perspective and let your diversified portfolio do what it was designed to do," Calcagni said. And then you have competition from first-time homebuyers, who are desperately trying to enter into the market and are having a very difficult time being able to do so. So it's a very divided housing market right now. Stephanie Sy: And when you talk about that K-shaped housing economy, you see that people that have wealth continue to grow that through their housing equity, and people that are renting continue to sort of lose out on that. So that has ramifications, doesn't it, for the future. Jessica Lautz: It does. We know that homeowners are continuing to build that wealth. They're building generational wealth really through homeownership. And we know the net worth of an owner is now nearly $460,000, while the net worth of a renter is just over $10,000. And so that divide is continuing as mortgage holders pay down that mortgage, as their home continues to gain in value, and then renters are struggling to invest in the stock market, they're struggling to invest in real estate, certainly. And so we can see that divide continuing to grow. Stephanie Sy: Are there any easy answers for what a first-term -- first-time homebuyer can do in this environment, Jessica? Jessica Lautz: Sure. So we can learn from successful homebuyers this year. When first-time homebuyers did purchase, they made a lot of sacrifices, whether that's sacrificing on cutting spending on luxury items, on goods, on taking a second job, but some of them even moved in with family, and that allowed them not to pay rent for a temporary time period, save for a down payment, get their financial house in order, looking outside that ideal area, taking advantage of government loans that are out there, so an FHA loan or a VA loan. Those are the steps that successful homebuyers were able to take. But important to keep in mind that first-time homebuyers today have higher incomes and they're wealthier than we have historically seen. Stephanie Sy: That is Jessica Lautz, economist with the National Association of Realtors, joining us. Jessica, thank you. Jessica Lautz: Thank you so much for having me. It’s the second Tuesday of the month, and that means another Microsoft Patch Tuesday. The new normal is that the numbers are hard to believe. Brian Krebs reports that this month’s release fixes nearly 1,100 vulnerabilities, 63 of them rated critical, and over 500 that let an attacker elevate their privileges. Only one is reported as actively exploited: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. Microsoft has now shipped more than 5,100 security fixes this year, after more than 1,400 last month, compared to an average of around 100 a month last year. Obviously AI tools get the credit for the volume of bugs fixed, but also of course for the volume of bugs found. Everyone else is busy too. Apple pushed out-of-cycle updates for at least nine vulnerabilities across its operating systems, including an iMessage flaw which could let a remote attacker join a group chat and read its messages, and backported the fixes to iOS 18. Chrome 157 fixes CVE-2026-125350, another Chrome zero-day, a week after a Chrome release which fixed more than 200 bugs, Firefox 160 fixes almost 100 CVEs, and Adobe fixed more than 110. Also since last week, zlib 1.4 shipped with more than a dozen security fixes, eight more vulnerabilities were disclosed in the X.Org server and XWayland, and Microsoft’s own Azure Linux update lists more than 470 CVEs fixed across the open source packages it ships. And for a perfect encapsulation of 2026, last month’s Patch Tuesday included a remote code execution bug in Windows Paint (CVE-2026-83844), though its description admits the code runs locally. So now I guess you can pop Calc through Paint? Does this count as a win? Despite the absolute firehose of vulnerabilities, the Krebs article notices that of the roughly 95,000 CVEs assigned this year, only around 200 made it into the CISA list of known expoited vulnerabilities (KEV). If you have to pick and choose which updates are the most critical, start there.  Last week we covered sshole, the bug where OpenSSH on musl libc without PAM accepts any long enough password for accounts that shouldn’t take a password at all. (And we had a serious moment thinking about putting “sshole” in the article title.) It now has a CVE, CVE-2026-123158, and Ars Technica reports that it’s already being exploited. GreyNoise says honeypots it runs in Southeast Asia were hit by a group it tracks as GT10, which installed Python in order to run a backdoor with Chinese-language comments that appears to have been written with AI. WatchTowr reports exploitation tied to botnets and cryptocurrency, and Previdian has seen attempts from thirteen IP addresses in nine countries. CISA added it to its KEV catalog on November 9, with a deadline of just three days for federal agencies to patch. Kevin Beaumont points out that, in practice, the affected population looks like Alpine Linux. Debian, Ubuntu, SUSE, Red Hat, and CentOS aren’t affected, and neither is stock OpenWrt, which uses Dropbear instead of OpenSSH. The researcher who found the bug suggests checking other musl-based systems like OpenWrt with OpenSSH installed, Buildroot, and Yocto, along with “a lot of the docker images you’ve pulled.” The OpenSSH 10.6p2 release notes credit Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield with the report, and include a notable comment about the current state of things: the OpenSSH team has “seen a number of cases where a security bug identified by AI tools is subsequently independently discovered by a different researcher,” so they’ll be making more frequent releases instead of batching fixes. “Type a really long password” as a way past authentication isn’t new, unfortunately. Back in 2014, a five-year-old found he could log into his dad’s Xbox Live account by filling the password verification screen with spaces, and Microsoft added him to its list of credited security researchers. If you run Alpine anywhere with SSH reachable from the Internet, update OpenSSH, or at minimum turn off password logins with “PasswordAuthentication no”. I suppose it’s the flip side of the password “4” for your certificate authority? (More on this below.) GitBook, the documentation platform used by a lot of open source and commercial projects, has published a post mortem on a breach on November 2. An attacker used a flaw in GitBook’s single sign-on flow to create login sessions as GitBook staff, used those sessions to pull the credentials of a misconfigured GitHub App in GitBook’s own organization, used that to get into GitBook’s internal code repositories and eventually a Cloudflare API key, and used that key to get production secrets with full infrastructure access. If you tried to access documentation or manuals for something and it failed mysteriously, you might now know why. GitBook took the entire platform offline for about 16 hours while it rotated every secret, revoked API tokens, and rebuilt its infrastructure, which is a painful but correct call when you don’t know what an attacker can still reach. GitBook believes the attack was aimed at a single customer, but is treating all customer data as exposed. That includes API and integration tokens, session signing secrets, and, most concerning, the ability to act as the GitBook app in any GitHub or GitLab repositories customers had connected to it. GitBook says it can’t determine whether the attacker took any action in those repositories. Each step in that chain is a familiar mistake, but strung together they go from a login bug to the source code repositories of GitBook’s customers. GitBook has already rotated the keys for its GitHub and GitLab sync, but if you use GitBook, create new API tokens and rotate any integration secrets, and if you’ve connected it to your repositories, review recent commits and pull requests made by the GitBook app. Bitdefender has found a way to lock an Android phone into a crash loop just by installing an app. The app requests no permissions, contains no code, and never has to be opened. A core system process reads a malformed file inside the app, crashes, restarts, reads it again, and crashes again. Rebooting doesn’t help, and neither does safe mode; the only fix is a factory reset, unless USB debugging was already enabled and you can race the crashes to delete the file over ADB. An Android app (APK) is really a ZIP file, and ZIP files store the same information, like file sizes and compression methods, in several places without requiring that they agree. Android reads each app many times, with separate pieces of code, to check its signature, install it, load its resources, and run it. When those readers disagree about what a file contains, you get bugs; past examples include the “Master Key” bug (CVE-2013-4787), where Android checked the signature of one file and installed a different one with the same name, and Janus (CVE-2017-13156), where a single file could be both a validly signed APK and executable code at the same time. In this case, Android’s ZIP library only checks the declared uncompressed size against the real file for entries marked as uncompressed, while the code that loads app resources treats anything not marked as compressed as uncompressed. An entry with an unusual compression method and a bogus size slips between the two, Android maps memory past the end of the file, and the process crashes when it tries to read it. Bitdefender found the bug when a banking malware sample, mangled by a packer, crashed its analysis systems, and reproduced the crash loop on a Pixel 10 running Android 17 with the August 2026 security patch; it affects Android 10 and newer. Google closed the report as not a security issue, and says it has passed it on to a feature team. A phone that can be bricked by a zero-permission app sounds like a security issue to me, and Bitdefender points out that Google rated a similar factory-reset bug as a security fix back in 2016. Be careful what you sideload. eMudhra has published its full post-incident report, and the Indian Express has a summary of how its certificate authority ended up with private keys as small as “4”. The keys were generated correctly in a hardware security module, but eMudhra needed to move them to new facilities in the US and EU, and wrote its own Python script to wrap and unwrap them for transport. During a rehearsal in April 2025, the script read the unwrapped key back incorrectly, truncating it, and created a new key from the result. Nobody checked the key strength or compared the certified public key to the original, the bad copy had an almost identical label, and the weak certificates passed two audit cycles. eMudhra also revealed it revoked eight more RSA keys on November 7, after previously saying they were unaffected, because it can’t show they were handled properly. BleepingComputer notes that the problem could have been caught more than a year earlier: in June 2025, eMudhra noticed certificate revocation lists signed with keys that didn’t match its CA certificates. The fallout makes a good case for taking revocation more seriously. Ubuntu 26.10 has started rolling out upki, a Rust project which brings browser-style certificate revocation checking to the rest of the operating system, starting with curl, with OpenSSL support planned for 27.04. And in a lighter take, a thread on Mastodon demonstrates “vanity” RSA keys with readable messages embedded in the public key, including “A certificate authority almost got away with the number 4”. In more serious follow-ups, France has formally accused Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of the supermarket refrigeration attacks last month. Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot called it “the first large-scale cyber-attack aimed at sabotage on our national territory,” summoned the Iranian ambassador, and promised sanctions, and the Paris prosecutor has opened an investigation into the head of Shahid Kaveh, an IRGC cyber unit previously linked to attacks on industrial controllers at US water utilities, and two of his deputies. Iran’s foreign ministry has rejected the accusation. It’s still not known whether the attacks elsewhere in Europe that we covered last week are related. Researchers have also found multiple exploitable vulnerabilities in the control software of the freezers, beyond the risk of default passwords, but all the articles referencing them appear to be paywalled at the moment. Finally, Ubuntu now lists fixed kernels for the Linux MPTCP remote code execution bug from last week on 22.04, 24.04, 26.04, and 26.10. Fixes for the older 16.04, 18.04, and 20.04 releases are still in progress. Red Hat has raised its rating to Critical and has been shipping fixed kernels for RHEL 8, 9, and 10 since November 1, with OpenShift updates following this week. Both Red Hat and Ubuntu now stress that the bug isn’t specific to MPTCP. MPTCP only comes into it because that’s what Anthropic’s exploit used, so turning MPTCP off isn’t a fix, and Red Hat says OpenShift nodes in their default configuration, with MPTCP disabled, are still affected. The good news, for now, is that nobody else seems to have a working exploit. Anthropic still hasn’t released its exploit, and as of October 30 TuxCare hadn’t reproduced it, and no independent public reproduction had turned up. The closest thing public is a proof-only PoC on GitHub which wins the race and detects the kernel leaking freed memory into a SYN-ACK, but stops well short of code execution. The Stack and BleepingComputer both report no confirmed exploitation in the wild, and the bug still isn’t in CISA’s KEV catalog. The scanning Hutchins saw last week suggests someone is preparing for the day a working exploit shows up. Browser fingerprinting identifies a browser without cookies, by combining lots of individually boring details: installed fonts, screen size, graphics hardware, how the audio system rounds numbers, and so on. Back in August, we saw AliExpress using audio fingerprinting to identify visitors. Mozilla has now published research, accepted at the ACM CCS conference, measuring which details actually make Firefox users unique, using data from almost 25 million users collected through privacy-preserving relays. The research is behind a set of fairly small changes, shipped over the past year starting with Firefox 143, which add up. Firefox hides the size and position of the taskbar or dock from screen size measurements, reports the number of CPU cores as either 4 or 8 instead of the real count, and fixes inconsistencies in image rendering, Web Audio, and math on Android that made some users stand out. According to the study’s companion site, the percentage of users who could be uniquely identified by the most effective of three commercial fingerprinting scripts dropped from 75% to 46%. Some protections are only on by default in Private Browsing and Strict tracking protection for now. The site also has a test you can run to see how unique your own browser looks. Let’s Encrypt has received more than €1 million from Germany’s Sovereign Tech Agency to build a Merkle Tree Certificate authority, its largest single investment in post-quantum readiness so far. Post-quantum signature algorithms are much larger than the ones used today, and replacing every signature in a TLS handshake with a post-quantum one would push the handshake well past 10 kilobytes, slowing all connections and breaking others. Merkle Tree Certificates keep things small by covering a whole batch of certificates with a single signature. The funding runs through the end of 2027, covering standards work and a production launch. Vanderbilt University told everyone on campus to shut down university devices and disconnect from university WiFi on Monday while it responds to an active cybersecurity incident, and to report anything suspicious from a separate device. Vanderbilt Health, which is a separate organization, says its systems haven’t been affected. On Tuesday, a ransomware group calling itself BYOD claimed the attack, and says it stole Social Security numbers and records for more than a million students and employees. Vanderbilt hasn’t commented on the claim. If it feels like these announcements are getting more common, Sophos agrees. In a post on incident response demand, it argues that AI is less about new kinds of attacks and more about attackers running the same playbook faster and at larger scale, while defenders can’t patch at the same speed. Sophos says two thirds of the intrusions it investigated started with compromised credentials or other identity attacks, and attackers reached Active Directory in an average of under three and a half hours. Everyone, it says, is hiring incident responders. Security researchers flamed (pun intended) the security in the Danfoss freezer control systems. we consider piecemeal patching or enabling of strict session control to be a misallocation of scarce security and personnel resources since they have minimal security ROI against such a fundamentally flawed codebase missing basic exploit mitigations and yielding multiple pre-auth RCEs with an hour’s casual glance. https://www.midnightblue.nl/blog/multiple-rce-danfoss-aksm800a US-wide GroundStop in effect Do they really have any security with a hard coded username and password that changes every day to the current date. A $5.8 million Bitcoin options loss pushed Nakamoto’s quarterly operating revenue below zero, while the company extended repayment of $60 million in Kraken debt to 2027. Update (Nov. 13 at 19:04 UTC): This article has been updated to include details of Nakamoto’s amended loan agreement with Kraken. Shares in Nasdaq-listed Bitcoin treasury company Nakamoto fell 6.5% in premarket trading on Friday after the company reported that losses on Bitcoin options pushed third-quarter operating revenue below zero. Nakamoto also extended the repayment deadline for $60 million in Bitcoin-backed debt owed to Kraken by one year. Nakamoto’s shares traded at $5.40 at 12:02 pm UTC on Friday, according to Yahoo Finance. At that price, the stock was down about 62% year to date. Nakamoto reported its third-quarter results after the market closed on Thursday. The company generated $3.9 million in revenue from its businesses. A $5.8 million net loss on Bitcoin options brought total operating revenue to negative $1.9 million, according to its quarterly filing.  Analysts had expected about $17.4 million in revenue, according to estimates compiled by Yahoo Finance. Nakamoto reported $85.5 million in net income and a $15.8 million adjusted operating loss for the quarter. A $110.4 million gain from revaluing its digital assets, chiefly Bitcoin (BTC), drove the profit. The adjusted operating loss excludes that gain. Nakamoto held 4,283 BTC worth $357.9 million as of Sept. 30, down from 4,467 BTC at the end of June. Nakamoto also disclosed that it had extended the repayment deadline for $60 million in Tether USDt (USDT) owed to crypto exchange Kraken by one year, from Dec. 4, 2026, to Dec. 4, 2027, according to an SEC filing. The amendment leaves the company’s total outstanding debt to Kraken unchanged at 165 million USDT, with the remaining 105 million USDT due June 30, 2027. No principal repayments are scheduled for 2026. The revised agreement also allows the positive net value of certain Bitcoin derivative positions held with Kraken to count toward collateral requirements, potentially helping Nakamoto offset declines in the value of its pledged Bitcoin before it must provide additional collateral or repay part of the loan. Nakamoto had pledged 3,030 BTC as collateral at the end of September, representing about 71% of its total holdings, according to its quarterly report. POPULAR SEARCHES                         BROWSE BY            Two years ago, first baseman Jake Bauers nearly retired. On Friday, he agreed to a four-year, $58 million contract with the Red Sox, according to multiple reports. It’s the richest contract of his turbulent career, and the capstone to the best season of his life. And he can paint the town red knowing he gets to keep his health insurance.     Bauers seriously considered retiring from Major League Baseball after the 2024 season. The Brewers had just removed Bauers from the 40-man roster and he elected free agency. There wasn’t much interest in Bauers around the league. Up until that point, he was a career .208/.302/.361 hitter with a negative WAR. At 29 years old, Bauers was a journeyman. He'd shuffled across seven organizations, was traded four times, and was designated for assignment once.  So Bauers called his agent, told him he was done playing, and planned to become a stay-at-home dad. Life had other plans.  In that same offseason, Bauers’ wife, Lauren, was pregnant with their second child. Needing health insurance for their growing family, Bauers decided to sign a minor-league deal with the Brewers. After an encouraging 2025 season in Milwaukee, Bauers fully broke out in a dream season for the 2026 championship Brewers. He led the team with 26 home runs, slashed .266/.389/.484, posted a 140 OPS+ and came up clutch several times throughout the postseason, eventually winning NLCS MVP for his star performance en route to lifting the World Series trophy. Now, he’s an integral part of Boston’s championship dreams. Let’s dive into what’s next for the Red Sox, the Brewers, and the rest of the free-agent market. If there was one thing the Red Sox needed to improve this offseason, it was slug. Boston ranked 26th in home runs and 20th in slugging percentage last season. After trading slugger Rafael Devers to the Giants, the Red Sox’ 2026 lineup was far too reliant on first baseman Willson Contreras to provide power, and now Bauers will help boost those offensive numbers. Speaking of Contreras, where will he play? It seems most likely that the Red Sox will split designated hitter and first base duties between Bauers and Contreras, with the former’s left-handed bat complementing the latter’s right-handed power.  Even with that solution, there is still a surplus at DH on the roster. Masataka Yoshida filled that role for the Red Sox last year, taking at-bats as a DH in 67 of the 87 games he logged. He played just seven games in left field. Boston is also set in the outfield, with Jarren Duran, Wilyer Abreu, and Ceddanne Rafaela patrolling the diamond.  The Red Sox have floated Duran’s name in recent trade deadlines, and it’s possible they’ll look to move him again this winter. But, if Boston is trying to move Yoshida this offseason to clear up space, it’s likely to be difficult. The 33-year-old is entering the final year of his five-year deal, and he’s owed nearly $20 million in 2027. Yoshida, a lefty-swinging bat, is not exactly sought after on the market. Could Jarren Duran be on the outs in Boston? (Photo by Courtney Kramer/MLB Photos via Getty Images)  Craig Breslow, Boston’s president of baseball operations, still has plenty of work ahead of him this offseason. Signing Bauers is just the first major move of their winter. And give credit to Breslow & Co. for getting the deal done before the expected lockout after Dec. 1. Bauers gives the Red Sox the clarity they needed to bulk up their offense. The Brewers offered Bauers a one-year, $23.15 million qualifying offer after his breakout season in Milwaukee. As recently as this week, during the GM Meetings in Las Vegas, Brewers brass had no idea which way the situation with their stellar first baseman would unfold. "He meant a lot to our group, and he’s a great story," Brewers president of baseball operations Matt Arnold told FOX Sports this week. "The family’s unbelievable. It’s really neat. I just want whatever’s best for Jake. He’s a really, really good person." Jake Bauers celebrating the World Series victory. (Photo by Aaron Gash/MLB Photos via Getty Images)  Now that Bauers rejected the qualifying offer, Milwaukee will receive a compensation pick between the end of the first round and the start of Competitive Balance Round A in the 2027 Draft. Still, that compensation hardly lessens the sting of losing Bauers, who became a fan-favorite and a key clubhouse voice with his leadership.  Milwaukee’s biggest need this offseason is replenishing the power that Bauers took with him to Boston. Last season, left fielder Jackson Chourio finished second on the team in home runs (25) behind Bauers, with Brice Turang (21) and William Contreras (18) behind him. The Brewers don’t need power to win the division and lead the majors in wins. Last season, they accomplished both feats while recording the second-lowest home runs (154) in the big leagues. But clutch home runs are what helped them defeat the Dodgers in the NLCS. Milwaukee led all playoff teams with 13 homers this October. Andrew Vaughn is a likely option at first base now. (Photo by G Fiume/Getty Images)  The Brewers are expected to fill the hole at first base with internal options. The leading candidate is Andrew Vaughn, who could take over at the corner infield spot next year, while top prospect Andrew Fischer, who could be the long-term answer, completes his development in the minors. Another future first-base option could be prospect Blake Burke, who finished last season at Triple-A but isn’t quite ready just yet. Vaughn, 28, does look ready to take over as the club’s everyday first baseman. He hit .306/.390/.444 (130 OPS+) in 104 games for the Brewers last season.  In the end, Bauers’ decision to leave Milwaukee shouldn’t change the Brewers’ offseason plans all that much. They knew they probably couldn’t afford to keep Bauers, who chose long-term stability over a one-year deal, and they don’t fault him for it. Arnold said this week, "We’re not that far removed from winning, but also we have to spend the time to assess that." They’ll look to continue supplementing their roster needs in hopes of repeating as world champions in 2027. MLB executives remain compelled to try and get deals done before the sport's Collective Bargaining Agreement expires on Dec. 1. Within the industry, there is talk of a free-agency frenzy expected in the next two weeks to close out the month. Bauers is a huge bat off the board early, and contenders who are aiming to beef up at first base will have to pivot to the next best option.  First baseman Ty France, 32, is now the best first baseman available after Bauers signed with the Red Sox.  France was one of the best signings of the year for the Padres, who inked him to a one-year minor-league deal for 2026. France significantly outperformed his contract by hitting .295/.363/.502 (139 OPS+) with 21 home runs, 72 RBI and 37 walks across 133 games for San Diego while also excelling defensively at first base. France, of course, is looking for a multi-year deal after his strong season, and he shouldn’t have a problem finding one. Many around the sport continue to expect top free-agent starter Tarik Skubal to sign before the expected lockout, with the New York Mets remaining the favorites — in terms of financial might and starting pitching needs — to sign him. Mets president of baseball operations David Stearns indicated this week at the GM Meetings that the club is also looking to add at first base. This video can not be played How could the Nvidia CEOâs affair threaten US national security? How close is Donald Trump to Jensen Huang? The answer is very. The Nvidia boss was one of the few business leaders with direct access to the US president. He had met Trump repeatedly, travelled with him to Britain and, in May, joined him on Air Force One for his trip to China. Jensen Huang wasn't just another tech billionaire seeking the president's ear. He had become an important voice in one of the biggest arguments inside the administration: how much of America's most advanced technology should be allowed to reach China. Nvidia makes the chips that power the AI revolution. Washington has restricted exports of its most advanced processors to China since 2022, believing they could help Beijing develop its military and technological capabilities. But enforcing those restrictions is difficult. Chips can be bought legally by customers in countries such as Singapore and Malaysia and then diverted to China. Chinese companies can also rent access to computing power through data centres outside the country. Jensen Huang has long argued that the restrictions are counterproductive. They shut Nvidia out of a huge market and encourage Chinese companies to develop their own alternatives. Trump appeared sympathetic to this view, allowing Nvidia to resume sales of certain chips to China last year in return for a share of the revenue, although its most advanced Blackwell chips remain off limits. But that relationship now looks rather more complicated.  The allegations surrounding Jensen Huang's reported affair with Alice Huang, of no relation but a former executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed, have raised the possibility that a foreign intelligence operation was targeting not just a powerful businessman, but someone with unusually close access to the American president.  US intelligence reportedly suspects Alice Huang of having links to Chinese intelligence. Beijing has rejected the allegations. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. But the affair has opened up a much bigger question: what did the administration in Washington know, and what did it do about it? That question leads directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. His department was responsible for controlling exports of sensitive American technology. It was also being pressed to act on concerns about Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China.  On Thursday, Megaspeed chief executive, Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan, said the company "takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously" and is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government". He said the company had co-operated with US Commerce Department inspections. A highly classified memo was shared with Lutnick about the concerns surrounding Alice Huang and Megaspeed. He resisted taking action against the company, a decision that is now under scrutiny.  Other senior officials wanted a tougher response.  Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was among those who reportedly questioned why Megaspeed had not been placed on the Commerce Department's blacklist. On Friday, Bessent pointed the finger at Commerce for not blacklisting the company, telling CNBC that several government agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months". "But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added. There have also been questions about why an investigation into the Singapore-based company was stopped after Nvidia intervened. The New York Times reported that Nvidia's general counsel contacted Commerce Department investigators probing suspected chip smuggling by Megaspeed invoking a senior Trump appointee. The department allegedly then froze its investigation and handed the case to the Justice Department. This apparently highlighted a significant disagreement about the direction of Trump's China policy. Huang wanted access to the Chinese market. Other officials were supposedly worried about the national security consequences. Lutnick was caught in the middle. Now the political pressure is building. Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned to testify before Congress about affair with alleged Chinese spy Bessent blames Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to block Megaspeed Members of Congress from both parties want answers. Democrats have launched an investigation into how the Commerce Department vetted Chinese companies approved to buy AI chips. Republicans are also questioning the administration's approach. And Jensen Huang's departure has not eased the pressure. Republican representative John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, said it was in the national interest for Nvidia and other American AI firms to succeed, but that companies "should never jeopardise our nation's security" by giving Chinese firms access to their most advanced chips. Senator Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said Huang's resignation did not absolve him of responsibility, and urged Lutnick to explain why export control loopholes remain open. Meanwhile Jensen Huang's team told Republican lawmakers on Wednesday that he plans to cooperate with their request to testify behind closed doors. The White House has not responded to the BBC's request for comment. It has, however, told the New York Post that Trump has complete confidence in Lutnick, describing him as "the most transformative commerce secretary in modern history". That is a fairly emphatic show of support, particularly amid reports that officials are weighing whether Lutnick should be forced out. There are some obvious questions. If Lutnick had indeed been warned about the risks, why did his department fail to act? And if other senior officials were indeed pressing for action, why did it take so long? The BBC has contacted the Commerce Department for comment. But there is an even bigger question for Trump. The president cultivated a close relationship with Huang. He was directly involved in decisions about chip sales to China. And, according to reporting in the New York Times, he was briefed on the intelligence concerns. This is becoming difficult to dismiss as the misjudgement of one businessman or one government department. Jensen Huang's personal life may have triggered the crisis, but the questions now reach into the White House itself. How much influence did he have? What did the president know? And who was ultimately responsible for protecting America's most sensitive technology? Who is Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress - and who could take over permanently? By   	Jordan Moreau   	For the first time since 2018’s “Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald,” Johnny Depp is back on the big screen in a major Hollywood movie with Paramount’s “Ebenezer.” His new, darkly comedic take on “A Christmas Carol” has made $1.5 million in previews at the box office.  	“Ebenezer,” directed by Ti West, is expected to open with $20 million domestically and another $20 million overseas. Paramount spent $38 million to produce the spin on the classic Charles Dickens tale, plus another $50 million to market it, and it’ll need the adoration of Depp’s diehard fans to power it through the holiday season. He stayed busy with the 2020 drama “Minamata,” the 2023 period piece “Jeanne du Barry,” and he directed the 2024 biopic “Modì, Three Days on the Wing of Madness.” “Ebenezer” marks his first major Hollywood film in eight years since “Fantastic Beasts” (Warner Bros. replaced him with Mads Mikkelsen in the third film, “The Secrets of Dumbledore”). Up next, he’ll star in Lionsgate’s revenge thriller “Day Drinker” with Madelyn Cline and Penelope Cruz, set to hit theaters in March.  	The “Ebenezer” cast also includes Rupert Grint as Scrooge’s employee Bob Cratchit, Ian McKellen, Daisy Ridley, Sam Claflin, Andrew Riseborough as the Ghost of Christmas Past, Tramell Tillman as Christmas Present and Robert Strange as Christmas Yet to Come. BMWBLOG » Models » BMW X4  BMW X4 The NA7 BMW iX4 is the second Neue Klasse model built in Debrecen, and the iX4 50 xDrive is rated at up to 828 km WLTP.    Horatiu Boeriu    November 13, 2026 The BMW iX4 is now in series production at BMW’s plant in Debrecen, Hungary, four months ahead of its March 2027 market launch. It’s the second Neue Klasse model built there after the iX3, and the longer-range iX4 50 xDrive is rated at up to 828 km (514 miles) on the WLTP cycle, which is more than the iX3 manages. Internally coded NA7, the iX4 takes the X4’s recipe of a sloping roofline over SUV proportions and moves it onto Neue Klasse hardware.  Two versions launch in March, and both are already coming off the line. The iX4 50 xDrive pairs its 828-km WLTP rating with a 400-kW peak charging rate, enough to add up to 387 km (240 miles) in 10 minutes. The iX4 40 xDrive is rated at up to 638 km (396 miles) WLTP. A range-topping iX4 M60 xDrive follows shortly and will also be built in Debrecen. Against the iX3 50 xDrive, the coupé comes out ahead on both counts. The iX3 is rated at up to 805 km (500 miles) WLTP and adds 372 km (231 miles) in 10 minutes at the same 400-kW peak. BMW doesn’t explain the gap, but a lower roofline that pushes through less air is the obvious suspect. Both launch models use BMW’s sixth-generation eDrive, with cylindrical battery cells and an 800-volt electrical system. Their electric motors come from BMW’s plant in Steyr, Austria, which already supplies the motors for the Debrecen-built iX3.  The iX4 lands in a busy factory: Debrecen’s iX3 ramp-up was the fastest ever at a new BMW Group plant, with the 50,000th car built in July, less than a year after production began. A few weeks later, BMW added a third shift, and the plant has run 24 hours a day since September. More than 100,000 European customers ordered the iX3 in the year after its world premiere, and it was named 2026 World Car of the Year. Hans-Peter Kemser, president and CEO of BMW Group Plant Debrecen, called the start of iX4 production “an important new chapter in the history of the Debrecen plant.” He added that the factory now takes on a larger role in building BMW’s electric models, and the workforce is still growing, with training running alongside the expansion.  Debrecen is a complete vehicle plant, with its own press shop, body shop, paint shop and final assembly, and it builds electric cars only. It also assembles the high-voltage batteries for its cars on site, so the iX4’s pack doesn’t have to travel before it meets the body. BMW planned the whole factory digitally under its iFACTORY production concept, and the plant officially opened in September 2025 as BMW’s first new car factory in Europe in more than two decades. BMW is investing more than €2 billion in the 400-hectare site, which is planned for about 150,000 cars a year. Debrecen burns no fossil fuels and runs entirely on renewable electricity. Solar panels on site cover about a quarter of its annual power needs, and surplus solar energy goes into a thermal storage system with 1,800 cubic meters of volume and 130 MWh of capacity. What BMW hasn’t said is how those 150,000 annual slots will split between the iX3 and the iX4, a mix that shifts again in March 2027, when production of the iX4 M60 xDrive is due to begin. TOKYO -  Japan's recent stock market recovery has prompted warnings against excessive optimism, with investors urged to remain disciplined and avoid chasing short-term gains before there is clearer evidence that the market has established a sustainable upward trend.   The caution comes after a period of sharp market fluctuations that tested investor confidence and raised questions about whether share prices accurately reflect the underlying financial performance of Japanese companies. While a rebound can provide welcome relief following a prolonged decline, it can also encourage investors to take excessive risks, particularly when rising prices create a sense that the worst of the downturn has passed. The danger is that short-term gains may be mistaken for the beginning of a lasting recovery, leaving investors vulnerable to renewed selling if market sentiment deteriorates. This was a central message of the November 13 edition of Bull and Bear, a weekly Japanese financial market program that examined whether stocks had finally emerged from their recent slump. Using a lighthearted exchange between its bull and bear characters, the program compared the market's recovery to climbing out of a deep abyss, while emphasizing that investors should remain firmly grounded rather than become carried away by early signs of improvement. The bear character warned that investors could easily lose their footing just as conditions appeared to be improving, while the bull character stressed that difficult periods eventually pass, invoking the familiar expressions that no rain lasts forever and that the darkest hour comes before dawn. However, the bull also cautioned against becoming distracted by attractive opportunities that might not be as promising as they initially appeared. The underlying message was that recovering markets require patience and careful judgment, particularly when investors are tempted to pursue rapidly rising shares without examining their financial fundamentals. The discussion also drew attention to the relationship between stock prices and corporate earnings, suggesting that the two do not always move together. With interim financial results for the fiscal year ending March 2027 largely completed by November 13, investors have an opportunity to reassess companies based on their actual business performance rather than short-term price movements. Strong earnings can provide a foundation for higher share prices, but they do not guarantee immediate gains. Conversely, a company's stock may decline even when its financial results remain healthy, reflecting broader market concerns, changing expectations or shifts in investor sentiment. This divergence makes it especially important to distinguish between companies benefiting from temporary speculative interest and those demonstrating sustainable earnings growth. The program emphasized that corporate performance remains a crucial consideration, with the bull character repeatedly insisting that company earnings were strong despite recent turbulence in share prices. Investors were encouraged to identify businesses whose interim financial results stood out, rather than simply following stocks that had risen most sharply during the recovery. The program also invited viewers to nominate an "Earnings MVP," recognizing companies that had delivered particularly impressive results during the first half of the fiscal year. The broader lesson was that a market rebound should not be confused with the disappearance of investment risk. Even when sentiment improves, investors face the possibility of further volatility, particularly if expectations rise faster than corporate profits. For investors assessing the outlook for Japanese equities, the challenge is therefore not simply determining whether the market has reached its lowest point, but identifying which companies have the financial strength to support their valuations over the longer term. The November 13 discussion concluded with a reminder that renewed confidence should be accompanied by restraint, as the temptation to chase a recovery can be greatest precisely when investors begin to believe that the danger has passed. China’s sharpest geopolitical weapon is an export ban on rare earths.              Thomas Kolbe  |             November 13, 2026           China’s sharpest geopolitical weapon is an export ban on rare earths. Raw-material dependence makes the EU a plaything of other countries’ interests. Free trade offers a realistic way out of the trap -- an antidote to Brussels centralism. Energy independence and abundant raw-material deposits are unquestionably among the most powerful geopolitical assets available to a country, a region, or a union of states. It is therefore unsurprising that, over the course of history, Europeans traveled far and wide to secure what they lacked: raw materials and precious metals. Europe is an energy- and raw-material-poor continent and currently imports around 60 percent of its energy needs from other regions. And no matter how confidently the Union’s representatives strut across the international stage -- Ursula von der Leyen, Friedrich Merz, and their colleagues lost negotiating leverage at the very moment China launched its technological overtaking maneuver. High energy costs, already unaffordable electricity prices, and looming gas shortages do not fall from the sky. They are the undeniable consequence of failed energy policy. Brussels miscalculated: from Germany’s nuclear phase-out to its delusional climate policy -- an attempt to deprive competitors of the advantage of using fossil fuels -- the entire strategy has failed. It is likely to rank among the greatest strategic errors of recent European history. That Brussels nevertheless clings to its climate-policy stance is a phenomenon of power politics -- too many people profit handsomely from this redistribution mechanism. Yet the solution to raw-material and energy scarcity is obvious: free markets and free trade with equal partners. Yet free-trade agreements with resource-rich regions such as South America simply refuse to be translated into practice. Brussels blocks itself with its climate protectionism, to which only a few are still willing to submit. The state should keep its hands off the market and confine itself to concluding trade agreements with resource-rich regions. This would, of course, also mean non-discriminatory access to the European single market -- without hidden protectionism through the European climate catalog. Unfortunately, however, confidence in the market economy and its healing powers has eroded. European cultural Marxism has triumphed through the media and a wholly subjugated education system, settling like lead over society and the economy. The state is supposed to solve the very problems it creates. A curious logic, but nonetheless typical of modern central planners. In these circles, the market economy is regarded as an outdated concept, one that has, strangely enough, also been imbued with a nationalist tinge. Yet it is precisely the market economy that delivers what central planners botch. A few years ago, it was said that the West would eventually run out of lithium, cobalt, and nickel. The energy transition and electromobility, it was claimed, would cause entire industries to fail because of the insufficient supply of these raw-material groups. That the energy transition is failing for other reasons -- massive subsidization and central planning -- is another matter. Today, the balance sheet looks considerably more positive. Despite massive state investment, market forces have managed to resolve much of the problem. BloombergNEF’s Transition Metals Outlook 2026 concludes that nine out of ten of the raw materials examined are likely to have sufficient supply capacity through 2050. Copper remains the exception, where a substantial supply gap is emerging. The AI boom is materializing in rising raw-material demand, unless it is curtailed by the Democrats just elected in the United States. The answer to high energy and raw-material prices is obvious: the price mechanism triggers investment. In recent years, price increases in scarce raw materials and important minerals such as cobalt, nickel, and tin triggered massive investment in mining activity. The financing of new projects, exploration, and the development of new mines has progressed well since then. Production volumes are rising. The old stock-market adage applies: the best cure for high prices is high prices. High returns and margins attract fresh capital -- the market mechanism kicks in. As if to prove this thesis, the price of cobalt, a raw material fundamental to the modern economy, fell by around 57 percent from its peak in May 2022 to approximately $33,500 per tonne by 5 November 2026. The same applies to nickel, which fell from almost $26,000 per tonne in 2022 to just over $16,000 most recently. Market data are incorruptible; the argument cannot be dismissed: even the International Energy Agency confirms that this development is attributable to massive investment in new production capacity and an expansion of supply. What else, one might add. Despite rising demand -- as the example of the cobalt market shows -- supply grew by around 25 percent over the past two years, while demand increased by about 10 percent. Technological substitution, efficiency programs, and new mining projects brought about the easing. We see that a functioning market mechanism can even turn feared scarcity into a surplus. In the field of rare earths, the United States is likewise attempting to reduce its dependence on China step by step. The agreement concluded in September 2026 between Washington, Copenhagen, and Nuuk also covers cooperation on critical minerals and economic development. Here, there is undoubtedly a need for action: China currently controls around 90 percent of global refining capacity for rare earths. Understandably, the United States is seeking to break this dominance step by step through its own projects and new partnerships. For Europeans, developments in the raw-material market mean that there is indeed a realistic way out of the scarcity problem. The key out of the energy-policy trap lies in participation in international trade. One would have to integrate into global value chains without imposing conditions that fragment the free market from the outset, as current climate policy does. This idea applies to metals just as it does to energy. Energy is, at its core, nothing other than the lifeblood of every industrial society -- indeed, of every society. Yet those who consistently treat trading partners and political competitors with hostility and rebuff them with maximalist demands should not be surprised when electricity prices for industry in Europe are more than twice as high as in the United States and almost 50 percent above the level in China. And Europe will have a hard time, in the long run, reintegrating Russia -- one of the world’s most important suppliers of raw materials -- into its own economy. Emergency Backstory Newsletters 中文新闻 BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA TOK PISIN By Angus Verley ABC Rural Topic:Sheep Farming Lachlan and Olivia James, and their children Florence and Scarlett, were at the sale in Naracoorte on Thursday to watch their sheep set a national record.  (Supplied: James family) Sheep prices have hit another national record. First-cross ewes at a sale in Naracoorte on Thursday sold for an unprecedented $650-a-head. Those in the industry expect prices will remain high for some time, given the historically low national sheep flock. Sheep price records continue to tumble at saleyards across the country, in a golden age for sheep producers. A line of 1.5-year-old ewes set a new record at the prestigious selling centre at Naracoorte in South Australia yesterday. They sold for $650-a-head, overtaking the previous record of $641 set at Corowa in New South Wales only last month. Sheep values have risen significantly this year, reflecting an excellent season in many areas, as well as strong demand and a critical flock shortage. Drought conditions in key livestock areas in recent years led to a big sell-off of sheep, exacerbating the long-term trend of declining flock numbers in Australia. The record-breaking ewes at Naracoorte belonged to the James family, who farm up the road at Mundulla West. Trevor James said he felt a great sense of accomplishment, but was keeping it in perspective. "It's a thrill, but you don't take long to reflect on why you get there," he said. "We enjoy the support of buyers, and repeat buyers who keep buying our sheep, and that's a humbling experience. "This is our 50th year selling first-cross ewes, and no-one ever thought we'd be at $650, or even in the 500s." The James family's record-breaking sheep were also named 'best presented' at the Naracoorte sale.  (Supplied: James family) It was only three years ago livestock values fell so sharply that some sheep were almost worthless, and Mr James said that was fresh in his memory. "We need the return, because the last few years have been difficult, for one in price — the 2023 spring fell away quickly, and a couple of tough seasons in terms of feed costs, and now costs in general," he said. He said he was not sure what the future would hold, but expected continuing strong demand while the sheep flock remained low. "The shortage of sheep is now playing out and I would imagine it will take some while to rebuild numbers," he said. "We're hoping it's not a bubble, because we're hoping to get a little bit more out of it." There was a huge amount of interest in the James family's record-breaking sheep.  (Supplied: James family) Almost all sheep prices have been hitting new highs in recent months. The national first-cross record has been broken numerous times, and at a state level, the Victorian record was also broken yesterday, with ewes at the Edenhope sale selling for $625-a-head. Only a week before, the national first-cross lamb record was broken, with a pen of lambs at the Bendigo sale selling for $595. In the Merino industry, a new ewe record of $515-a-head was set at the Hay sheep sale in September. These records all refer to breeding animals, but they also reflect extraordinary and unprecedented demand at the saleyards for sheep and lambs for slaughter — lambs have sold for up to $500, and sheep have topped $400. Livestock specialist with stock agency AWN, Wayne Driscoll, said his clients had done the hard yards through tough years, sticking with sheep, and deserved to be rewarded. "It's a wonderful time — it's great reward for persistence," he said. "We're so pleased for the vendors who have stayed in it, because there was a lot of heartache a couple of years ago, they went through a lot and it certainly took people out of the industry, so let's not forget that." Nigel Starick says he never dreamed sheep prices would reach the levels they have.  (Supplied: Elders Bendigo) Elders Bendigo livestock manager Nigel Starick said he never expected to see prices so high. 'It's fantastic to see people get rewarded for sticking with something that hasn't always gone their way, but the ones in it now are getting well rewarded," he said. "It's as good as I've ever seen it in 25 years in this job — never in my life did I think I'd see those prices. It's just phenomenal. "When you actually get up and auction those sheep and command that sort of value for producers, it's a good place to be." Asymmetric Intelligence by asymco-admin How to spot a Black Swan “Evercore ISI downgraded Nvidia from outperform to in-line and slashed its price target from $465 to $186.”  I don’t follow Nvidia but this quote caught my eye. A 60% drop in the price target of the second-largest company by market cap (largest if you look a few weeks ago) made me look twice. The drop was not because the company issued a warning or that new data about their next quarterly earnings had dropped. The drop was due to something nobody anticipated, discussed, discounted or modeled.  The drop was because Nvidia’s structural weakness was finally evident. I don’t mean the shenanigans of the CEO. I mean the structural weakness of concentration. Nvidia represents concentration at every level. To put it another way, Nvidia is an engineering department. It prospers as long as there is a budget but if that budget disappears it disappears.  But, more ominously, if that budget increases by 15,000% then it also disappears. Management no longer works because it loses its constraints.   I’m all for engineering departments. I’ve worked in one for years and it’s very energizing. But they are not businesses. Engineering departments are focused on measurable improvements in performance. The concept of a business, especially one designed for longevity, is the emphasis on the customer. Performance is desirable but is not the objective.  For a business, satisfaction of the customer base and its expansion is its purpose.  Causality therefore rests on “social” constructs. Satisfaction, loyalty, jobs to be done. At the core is the purchase decision. Such decisions are not calculations but are subject to a calculus. A calculus of politics, circumstances, dependencies, stressors and, shockingly, emotions. See “The Essence of Decision” for more. Engineering departments are blind to decision theory. They are allocated resources on the basis of performance only.  But this is not news. What struck me about Nvidia’s journey is that an engineering department was elevated to a “great business” without a closer look at its culture.  The evidence is in the abundance of analyst reports. Over 1200 were issued in the last 4 years by upward of 70 analysts. They have been overwhelmingly positive about the “business” without questioning whether it is even structured as such.  Subscribe to Asymco One for full access to our research. Consider the anecdotes about Nivida being a “flat organization”. It has one boss and 60 direct reports. That boss has a cult of personality. In reality this meant that there was no organization at all.  Then there are the anecdotes about a single point of control with no succession plan. In fact no predecessor either as the founder was the only manager ever. One individual does not make a resilient organization. That individual was clear about the idea that succession meant the company needed to be re-built, not merely restructured. L’État, c’est moi! Nvidia was Jensen Huang and Jensen Huang was Nvidia. Couple that with the fact that the customer list is basically 5 customers for one singular product that went from zero to hero and one can see that there is something wrong. It’s a great deal of sales but within a very short period of time. This success story says nothing about diversification and competitive advantage. These are “Management 101” issues. So are ethics. At least they were when I went to business school in the 1990s. But analysts were not going to go against the narrative. Note the graphs below: There were no dissenting voices on Nvidia for the last 18 months (perhaps one? sell rating). Apple, shown on the right, with a rock solid billion-and-a-half-or-more customer base of rock solid satisfaction, had nearly half of the analysts recommend to sit on the sidelines or get out! The analysts were fixated on the slope of the sales curve. The culture must be right if the results are great and vice versa. They got the causality wrong. This is why business analysis is not financial analysis. Nor is it technology analysis nor is it market analysis.  Fundamentally it is cultural analysis. You must know finance, accounting, technology and markets. But they are all multiplied by culture. A culture of prudent management, a culture of customer satisfaction and a culture of resilience and longevity. If these render as zero, the resulting product is also zero. Jensen Huang's resignation is hitting Nvidia's stock hard, but the implications could spill into the wider AI trade, investors say.  Huang has been central to Nvidia and the AI ecosystem, brokering deals and leading innovation at the company for over three decades. But after news broke that Huang had two extramarital affairs, including one with an suspected Chinese spy, the now ex-CEO stepped down on Thursday morning.  Reuters later reported that Huang had a relationship with a second employee at the company.  Huang's exit has shaken the tech world, and the outlook for Nvidia and the AI sector have dimmed among analysts and investors. Wall Street firms soured on the stock amid the scandals, issuing a wave of downgrades that center on Huang's pivotal role and the vacuum his absence creates.  Investors are now watching nervously as the stock slides and the company that's been a lynchpin of the AI economy drifts into a new era.  Here's how investors and strategists are thinking about Huang's departure. Arnott said Nvidia's sell-off is a cautionary tale for the broader AI trade, with valuations still high across many of its pockets. One piece of bad news can sink a stock priced for perfection. "They're all priced as if that'll never happen," Arnott told Business Insider on Thursday. As for Nvidia's stock itself, Arnott said that while it looks like a bargain right now, there's still meaningful risk on the table for the company's future profit. Perhaps the company falls out of grace with the US government, he said, or perhaps revenues are lower in the absence of Huang's dealmaking.
