There's a real possibility that this has an impact on future business," he said. "That's why it got clobbered. It got clobbered because Jensen Huang mattered. He was absolutely central to their success." McMillan said the Jensen Huang saga could be yet another catalyst for higher regulation for AI firms, especially as a Democrat majority comes into power in Congress after AI oversight proved to be a sticking point for voters. Specifically, the Commerce Department could institute tighter export rules, stricter "know your customer" checks, and potentially implement geotracking into certain advanced GPU chips. That's generally bad for the AI trade because regulation slows business and increases costs, which "Wall Street hasn't fully priced in yet," he said. Makino isn't as bearish as some finance pros, even as tech stocks continue to trend downward on negative speculation about the AI trade.  That said, he says that short-term volatility is likely to persist. "I don't see the worst-case outcome scenario some people envision," he said. "Obviously the worst part is the long-term and the product roadmap going into 2029 and beyond. I think if that does falter a bit, there may be some market share gains by competitors. There may be some lower spend cases in 2028/2029 and beyond, but whether it's structurally downward or a spend shift towards other comps is hard to tell. " Hackett said the risk stemming from Huang's departure largely looks confined to Nvidia for the moment, with investors piling into other tech names amid Nvidia's sell-off. But he sees a risk that investors could begin to punish other AI giants with poorer balance sheets and growth that relied more heavily on speculation, he said, pointing to other volatile chipmakers and neocloud firms. "Everything we've seen more recently, it is a little bit more winners vs. losers, a little bit more discernment about growth projects," he told BI. "The riskier you are in this space, I think the more permanent this damage is." "I think that the game of musical chairs is what I've been worried about, where it's like, everybody feels like they have to overspend because the music's going to stop at some point and you want to be in the lead when that happens." Like many finance pros, Hathorn is waiting for Nvidia's earnings before issuing a formal prediction on where the AI trade may go from here, though she's not overly concerned about its longer-term growth prospects. "It will be a case of seeing what comes in the next few days. We have earnings next Tuesday and that will shed some light on the recent profitability of the company. It's hard to know what the Huang situation will result in until we get more information about what was possibly shared or not," Hathorn said in an email. "AI as a whole continues to be driven by future expectations of monetization, not much should change there." Jump to

By Dominic Patten  Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics  Microsoft feels really bad about the Outlook outage and 365 services crash that brought many business communications and personal email around the globe to a screeching halt this week.  	“We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused you and your business,” the Redford, WA-based software company said late Friday morning as email and other Microsoft 365 programs started working again, some more sporadically than others.  	Just before noon PT, another update from the company scaled back expectations of when everyone would be able to use their usually much-used products. “As infrastructure stabilizes, we’re still draining queued messages and rebalancing traffic, so customers may see improved sign-in/access while delivery and processing continue to catch up,” Microsoft said. “We do not have an ETA for full recovery yet. Service access can recover before mail flow fully normalizes.”  	           			Watch on Deadline		       	The November 12 blackout of sorts shuttered business and squeezed courts, hospitals, law enforcement and schools on what some cheekily termed an adult snow day. With repairs continuing, Microsoft earlier Friday provided a bit more insight into what went so wrong and how the conspiracy theories were incorrect. Adrian Padeanu    November 13, 2026 BMW rolled out the proverbial red carpet for the facelifted 7 Series to the Bulgarian market, and as you can tell, the Dingoling-made luxobarge didn’t arrive alone. The national media presentation brought together five examples of the posh sedan, each configured differently to showcase the extensive range of customization options available to buyers. The cars pictured include both traditional combustion-engine models and fully electric i7 derivatives, illustrating BMW’s continued commitment to its Power of Choice strategy. Rather than forcing customers into a single type of propulsion, Munich’s flagship continues to cater to different preferences, whether they involve gasoline, diesel, plug-in hybrid, or fully electric power. With the iX5 Hydrogen, a fifth powertrain will arrive later this decade. Circling back to the range-topping sedan, it’s also a particularly good opportunity to see how differently the same G70 can look depending on the specification. From exterior paint finishes and alloy wheels to interior materials and equipment, BMW has substantially expanded the possibilities for making its largest sedan stand out.  As we previously reported, the facelifted 7 Series takes personalization to another level. BMW offers more than 500 exterior colors and combinations, including two-tone finishes and approximately 130 Individual paint choices. The most elaborate option is the new Dual-Finish paintwork, which combines matte and gloss finishes on the same body. It takes around 75 hours to complete, with extensive manual work involved in preparing and painting the car. It’s an expensive way to make a statement, but that’s hardly a concern for someone shopping in this segment. BMW has also expanded the alloy wheel selection, with designs measuring up to 22 inches available. Combined with the various exterior packages and trim choices, there’s plenty of room to give the 7 Series a more understated or decidedly extravagant appearance. The customization possibilities don’t stop once you open the door. BMW estimates there are approximately 700 combinations of equipment and interior materials, making the cabin almost as configurable as the exterior. Customers can choose from leather, artificial leather, cloth, wood, metal, and crystal glass elements. BMW has also introduced Alcantara trim strips as an alternative to carbon fiber and traditional wood finishes. Individual leather and cashmere wool upholstery remains available, extending to details such as the central armrest and rear neck cushions. Those who still can’t find the right combination can turn to BMW Individual Manufaktur. The division can accommodate particularly demanding requests, including exclusive special editions and even one-off builds. In other words, there’s a route to an exceptionally personalized 7 Series beyond what the regular configurator offers.  There’s even more on the way. The 7 Series will level up in 2027 when BMW ALPINA introduces its own interpretation of the G70, reportedly known internally as the G72. Expected to revive the B7 nameplate, the range-topping sedan will take luxury, performance, and exclusivity a step further, positioning itself above the regular BMW lineup and below Rolls-Royce. A twin-turbocharged 4.4-liter V8 will headline the range, potentially joined by a six-cylinder derivative and an all-electric version. Expect more distinctive styling, an even more sumptuous cabin, bespoke materials, along with the signature 20-spoke wheels and heritage colors. BMW is effectively creating a new luxury layer above its flagship sedan, giving customers another reason to spend considerably more on a 7 Series. See more of our coverage in your search results. by Chris Allen Canva Speed matters at work, but rushing careful tasks can create much bigger delays. A new supervisor demanded faster inventory checks and dismissed every warning about accuracy. Instead of arguing again, this employee followed her instructions exactly and let the numbers speak. See what happened when her obsession with speed met some very expensive reality. I work at a big retail chain, where the stockroom is the wild west and chaos is the norm. We recently got a new supervisor, Sarah, who seems to think she’s running the Navy SEALs or something. She’s obsessed with speed—constantly on us about how we need to get things done faster. Doesn’t matter if it’s done right, as long as it’s done fast. Sarah had a bad idea. So one day, during peak restock time when we’re drowning in boxes, Sarah storms in with her clipboard and her best “I’m in charge” face. She corners me while I’m halfway through a massive inventory check and says, “You’re taking way too long with these. Just get through them quickly. We don’t have time to check every single item!” I try to explain that rushing inventory checks is a bad idea. But she cuts me off with a condescending smile. “If you can’t speed this up, maybe this job isn’t the right fit for you,” she says, all smug like she just dropped a bombshell. 😒 He decides to be faster. Alright, Sarah. You want speed? Let’s see how fast things can spiral out of control. So, I take her words to heart and decide to follow her instructions exactly. The next day, I’m scheduled for another inventory check. Instead of my usual process where I count everything carefully, I decide to play Sarah’s game. Surely this is fast enough for Sarah! I glance at the shelves and make up numbers that seem about right. I don’t even bother opening boxes to check if what’s inside matches the labels. I fly through the whole process, marking items off like I’m speed-running a video game. What usually takes me 2 hours, I finish in just 20 minutes. Sarah was happy, but Mike wasn’t. Sarah sees me finish up, and I can see her eyes light up. She walks over, grinning ear to ear. “See, that wasn’t so hard, was it? If you keep this up, you might even get a little bonus this month,” she says, patting herself on the back for her brilliant leadership skills. 🙄 Fast forward a week, and the store manager, Mike, calls an emergency meeting. The inventory reports have come back, and they’re a total disaster. According to the report, we’re missing thousands of dollars worth of products. It looks like we either lost half the stock or we’re running some underground black market. OP was not about to let Sarah get out of this mess acting all innocent. Mike’s mad, customers are complaining about out-of-stock items, and the regional manager is breathing down his neck. Mike turns to Sarah and asks her to explain how this could’ve happened. Sarah, trying to save face, immediately points at the team and says, “They must’ve messed up the counts. They weren’t thorough enough.” She’s throwing us under the bus without a second thought. This is where I decide to strike. I raise my hand and say, “Actually, I did exactly what Sarah told us to do. She said to skip checking the items and just get it done as quickly as possible. I was just following orders.” Sarah had no way to defend herself. You could hear a pin drop. Mike slowly turns to Sarah, his expression going from confused to furious. “Is this true?” he asks, narrowing his eyes at her. Sarah’s stammering now, trying to backtrack. “Well, I—uh, I didn’t mean to skip it entirely. I just meant to speed it up…” But it’s too late. The damage is done. Now they have to fix it. Mike’s already fuming. “So you decided to cut corners on the one thing that affects our bottom line? You do realize we have to do a full recount now because of this mess, right?” And that’s exactly what happens. The next day, Sarah and a few unlucky team members spend 12 hours redoing the entire inventory check from scratch. The rest of us get to enjoy watching them sweat it out while we handle our regular duties. It’s glorious. OP loved taunting Sarah about her mistake. As they’re counting, I make sure to walk by every so often and ask, “Need any help speeding things up? I could skip a few checks for you if that helps!” The look on Sarah’s face every time is pure rage mixed with embarrassment. She can’t say anything because she knows I’m just doing what she asked for. By the end of it, we’ve found thousands of dollars in discrepancies. Turns out, rushing through inventory checks leaves a lot of room for errors—who knew? 🙄 Sign up to get our BEST stories of the week straight to your inbox. Sarah backed off. The regional manager isn’t happy and Sarah ends up getting a formal warning. She stops harping on us about speed after that and even tries to be extra nice whenever I’m around. Guess she realized that maybe, just maybe, some tasks shouldn’t be rushed. It gets even better! The best part? A couple of weeks later, I get a small bonus for “outstanding attention to detail” in helping fix the inventory mess. Oh, the irony. Sarah couldn’t even look me in the eye when I got the bonus slip. And every time she walks by me now, I just give her a friendly smile and say, “Don’t worry, boss, I’m working as fast as you want!” That was definitely malicious and definitely compliance. Going fast with inventory and not being accurate was clearly a huge mistake. Let’s see how Reddit reacted to this story. This is the goal. Three Trezor Safe 5 wallets bought from the reseller CryptoBilis contain an implant, an extra circuit board that can copy their recovery phrases, hardware wallet maker Trezor said yesterday. The implant reads the phrase from the wallet's screen and sends it over the mobile network to a server controlled by the attackers. The company examined one of the wallets in its lab, identified the other two from photos their owners sent, and has had no reports of lost funds. A firmware update released earlier this week, version 2.13.1, stops the implants found so far from capturing anything on wallets that run it, the company said, but “the update can’t protect a wallet backup that was captured before it.” The company has not changed its advice to anyone who bought a Trezor from CryptoBilis since March, including from the reseller's stores on Tokopedia and Shopee: Version 2.13.1 was released for the Safe 7, Safe 5, Safe 3 and Model T, according to the company's firmware changelog. The company will not publish technical details that could help attackers or put customers at risk, it said in an investigation update. Its engineers extracted and analyzed the implant's firmware from the first wallet it reported. The implant sits between the Safe 5's main board and its screen and changes nothing on the wallet itself, including its firmware and Secure Element, the company found. The implant copies the recovery phrase when the wallet shows it during backup creation, and when someone types it in to restore an existing wallet to the device. It also copies a passphrase if one appears on the screen. It encrypts the data before sending it, and if it cannot connect, it keeps the data and tries again until it succeeds. The company first warned of a suspected implant on October 30, two days after a buyer reported it and before its lab had seen the wallet. CryptoBilis served as an official reseller for the company's wallets in Southeast Asia until October 9, when the company removed it. That was the day Ledger, another hardware wallet maker, began investigating losses of funds among the reseller's customers. Ledger later confirmed an unauthorized implant in a wallet the reseller sold. Attackers had fitted genuine Ledger devices with hidden components designed to capture the recovery phrase during setup, then drained wallets in a single coordinated operation, Ledger said in an incident statement. Trezor says the implants in its wallets work the same way as those found in Ledger devices, adapted to the Safe 5's display. It has not said who fitted the implants or where in the supply chain that happened. The three wallets were bought between August 20 and September 23. So far the company has found implants only in Safe 5 wallets sold by the reseller, and none in wallets from its other resellers or in its other models. After the October reports, it asked people who bought a Trezor from the reseller to get in touch, and 48 have done so. It is checking their wallets in its lab or from photos of the insides, and has not said how many it has checked so far. The company says none of the three owners has lost funds. Trezor wallets are self-custodial, so it cannot see anyone's balance. The company says it has cut its reseller network by about 80%, dropping trustworthy partners that posed no immediate threat but did not fit its stricter new rules. It first announced the reduction on October 13 in a post on X, more than two weeks before the first report of an implant in one of its own wallets. In a partner letter that day, it told the dropped resellers that they would get no new stock, could sell what they had until January 1, 2027, and would then be removed from its list of authorized sellers. It is still investigating. It will post an update if it confirms an implant outside the reseller's wallets or the Safe 5, receives a report of lost funds linked to the implants, or releases new protections. European companies have already been part of a sovereign push to switch their cloud providers to more local, homegrown alternatives, but new research shows the same could be happening for cybersecurity. New sales figures in a Context report (via The Register) claims sales from EU-based vendors rose by 35% in the two years ending Q3 2026. While it may not sound like a massive growth, overall sales rose by just 10%, showing just how much effort is being put into switching to sovereign cybersecurity options. On the flip side, US vendors saw just an 8% growth during the same period. Although it's clear European companies are trying to invest more in local alternatives, US vendors still dominate 62% of the EMEA cybersecurity market, which means there's a long way to go before European companies top the charts. Among the areas where EU-based vendors see the most interest are security awareness training, vulnerability management and SIEM. However, US companies are still doing a lot of the heavy lifting across identity and access management and cloud security – a possible tie to the fact that many companies are still using US clouds. "Digital sovereignty is becoming a buying decision," Research VP Joe Turner summarized. "As customers and resellers get clearer about what it means in practice, they're asking who holds the encryption keys, who can access sensitive logs and where that data is stored." But more broadly, there are also concerns about sovereignty claims. An October 2026 Omdia report found as many as 28% of providers don't actually disclose proof of sovereignty. "No one is regulating who can call themselves a sovereign AI provider," Telco B2B Research Director Camille Mandler warned. A global Microsoft outage has disrupted work and public services for millions worldwide, hitting email, workplace tools, and customer communications as the breakdown stretches into a second day. Problems began on Thursday and continued into Friday, spreading from the Americas into Asia and Europe. Microsoft has reported improvements, but repeated attempts to restore services have failed to fully resolve the disruption. Users have reported inaccessible Outlook inboxes, delayed emails, and problems with calendars and meeting invitations. Outage tracker Downdetector received complaints from roughly 75 countries and territories, with US Outlook reports peaking at around 140,000 on Thursday. Microsoft's outage reports on November 12 reached 74 countries and territories in about an hour on Downdetector.  Microsoft says its Exchange Online incident began at 16:17 UTC. Reports to Downdetector about Outlook began climbing at about 17:25 UTC, 12:25 in New York. By 18:25, reports about five Microsoft services combined reached 19,650 a minute, against <15 a minute on an average Thursday.   Outlook reports alone peaked at more than 2,000 times their normal level.  Reports did not stay in the Americas. They jumped tenfold in the UK at 17:43, in India at 23:21 local time and in New Zealand at 06:55 local time. Between 17:00 and 18:55 UTC, nearly 3 in 10 reports came from outside the US. We count a country here once its reports reach ten times normal and at least 20 in five minutes.  Reports about Microsoft 365, Copilot, Teams and OneDrive each rose more than a hundredfold, and Azure about a hundredfold. Xbox, GitHub and LinkedIn, also Microsoft's, rose far less.  Microsoft said a portion of its infrastructure was experiencing elevated load across multiple regions. At 19:38 UTC, reports were still running at more than 11,000 a minute. The failure centers on Exchange Online, Microsoft’s cloud-based email and calendar system. Problems there have also extended to Teams, Copilot, SharePoint, and other workplace products. While most Teams calls, meetings, and chats remain available, scheduling and other features dependent on Exchange have been failing. OpenAI and Anthropic have also reported disruption to their Microsoft integrations, affecting tools that retrieve information from connected accounts. The consequences have extended well beyond office workers unable to check their inboxes. British police forces reported problems receiving online crime reports, while government communications and operations were affected in Japan, Singapore, the Philippines, and Hong Kong. Australia’s intelligence agency and federal police were also among the organizations caught in the outage, Reuters reported. Healthcare providers in Britain, meanwhile, have warned of delays to patient enquiries as email and administrative systems failed, although emergency care and scheduled appointments have continued. Indian airlines reported disruptions to customer email support, while a US electric-truck manufacturer postponed its earnings call. In New Zealand, a university reported that its travel provider could no longer accept online bookings. It also warned that scammers had started exploiting the outage with fake IT-support messages. Several businesses and financial firms in Australia, Japan, and New Zealand have even been forced to switch back fax machines, phones, and messengers to keep operating and confirm trades. The company noted that traffic had not increased, and that its systems had simply lost the capacity to cope with normal demand. Restarting the failed servers did not fully solve the problem, as some stopped responding again as users reconnected. Engineers began undoing a recent network change and bringing systems back online gradually to avoid overloading them. Microsoft is investigating whether that change triggered the disruption. It says it has found no evidence of a cyberattack and has pledged to publish a full explanation once services are restored. Microsoft shares fell roughly 2.5% in Friday’s premarket trading, reflecting a loss of nearly $100 billion in market value as the outage continued. The financial damage has extended beyond shareholders, with Ashwin Pal, a privacy and security expert at advisory firm RSM Australia, estimating that direct and indirect costs in Australia alone would run into billions of dollars. He warned that smaller businesses would be particularly exposed, with costs continuing to accumulate after services returned as staff worked through the backlog. The breakdown could have consequences beyond communications, disrupting decisions, revenue, and the delivery of services, Saurabh Verma of consultancy Frost & Sullivan warned. For Microsoft, the longer-term risk is customer confidence, Josh Gilbert, a market analyst at eToro said. He noted that while investors could probably look past this outage because customers cannot easily abandon Microsoft’s products, repeated failures could make businesses reluctant to depend more heavily on the company or spend more on its Copilot AI tools. Microsoft has not provided a firm deadline for full restoration. Its Friday updates reported improving access to mailboxes and email delivery in some regions, but warned that intermittent problems could remain as recovery continued in stages. The company is also working through a backlog of delayed messages. It has extended the delivery window for emails to 48 hours, giving them more time to reach recipients before being returned as undeliverable. A first-in-class blood thinner has been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration to prevent repeat strokes in people who have recently experienced a serious event or what healthcare professionals call "mini" episodes. The drug, asundexian (brand name Sunharbo) developed by Bayer has become the first treatment approved in the US designed to prevent blood clots by blocking a specific protein that hasn't been targeted by medications currently on the market. Sunharbo stops the clotting protein Factor XIa (FXIa), as opposed to existing medications that take aim at a different protein known as Factor Xa. The approval was granted following positive results from a global Phase 3 study. FXIa is believed to contribute to the development of "pathological thrombus growth and vessel blockage" – aka clotting. "Asundexian, an oral, once-daily Factor XIa inhibitor, reduces the risk of secondary stroke, in combination with antiplatelet therapy and is the first approved drug in a new class of Factor XIa inhibitors worldwide," Bayer notes in its official news release. The chances of stroke patients experiencing a secondary episode within five years is estimated to be one in five, which is a significant percentage of people considering how life-threatening such events can be. "For those who survive a stroke, the risk of another potentially devastating event is highest in the days and weeks after the initial event, and that risk persists over time,” says Ashkan Shoamanesh, M.D., Senior Scientist at Population Health Research Institute, a Joint Institute of Hamilton Health Sciences and McMaster University, Ontario. “I believe asundexian introduces an important new addition to post-stroke care that can be used to help patients reduce the risk of a secondary stroke.” It's estimated nearly 800,000 Americans suffer a stroke each year and it remains one of the biggest killers globally. Secondary strokes can be more dangerous and debilitating than the initial episode, making clot prevention medicine pivotal in reducing this risk. In the autumn of 1885, Robert Louis Stevenson was living in Bournemouth, England, in a house he called Skerryvore, sick, broke, and often confined to bed. One night he cried out in his sleep, and his wife, Fanny, woke him up.  He wasnât grateful.  âI was dreaming a fine bogey tale,â he told her, and by daybreak he was writing it down. Three days later he had a first draft of what would become Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde, and soon after that the draft was gone, burned in the fireplace. Mental Floss has noted that thereâs more than one version of how that happened: the two eyewitnesses who wrote about it left three, because one of them told it two ways. The account that made headlines came out in October 2000, when a letter Fanny had written to Stevensonâs friend, the poet W.E. Henley, surfaced ahead of an auction at Phillips in London. As The Guardian reported, Fanny dismissed the draft as âa quire full of utter nonsense,â and wrote: âHe said it was his greatest work. I shall burn it after I show it to you.â Phillips expected the letter to sell for around Â£1,500, and the head of the auction houseâs book department, Liz Merry, offered a theory about Fannyâs motive: she may have found âDr Jekyll and the duality of man rather distasteful,â and Merry added that Fanny seemed uneasy that he was writing for a âshilling shockerâ market. That was Merryâs guess, not Fannyâs words, and Fanny had reasons beyond taste to worry. In an earlier letter quoted by The Guardian, she complained that her husband was âpossessed of a storyâ and that she feared âit will only be energy wasted â as all his late work has been.â The couple were deep in debt. Long before that letter turned up, in a preface written for a 1905 edition of Stevensonâs works, Fanny had told the story without casting herself as the arsonist. In her version, the first draft, âcontaining thirty thousand words,â was finished in three days, âonly to be entirely destroyed and immediately re-written from another point of view.â She didnât say who destroyed it, only what had been wrong with it: it had missed the allegory, âprobably from haste, and the compelling influence of the dream.â Fannyâs son from her first marriage, Lloyd Osbourne, was in the house at Skerryvore that autumn, and in 1924 he published the most dramatic account of all. He remembered Stevenson reading the draft aloud to him and his mother, and his mother criticizing it: Stevenson had âmissed the allegoryâ and made it âmerely a story.â Stevenson was furious, and Lloyd left the room rather than listen to them argue. When he returned, Stevenson came downstairs and conceded the point. âI have absolutely missed the allegory, which, after all, is the whole point of it,â he said, and then he threw the manuscript into the fire himself while Fanny made an âineffectual start to prevent him.â âIt was all wrong,â Stevenson explained when they protested. ââ¦The only way was to put temptation beyond my reach.â According to Lloyd, he wrote the new version in another three days. The three accounts donât agree on who struck the match, and they donât even agree on the numbers: Fanny put the total at sixty thousand words in six days, Lloyd at sixty-four thousand. Every version ends with the first draft gone. The second one was a smash.  Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde came out in 1886, and Fanny later wrote that it was pirated across America and that clergymen used it as a text for their sermons. Whatever was in the version that burned, the only people who ever described it were the ones arguing about the fire. Â© 2026 Minute Group - All Rights Reserved

Arthur Hayes said he was “flattered” by Coinbase’s defense of US stock perpetual futures, a decade after BitMEX launched perpetual swaps. Arthur Hayes, co-founder of BitMEX, said he was “flattered” by Coinbase’s support for the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) in a US legal dispute over stock perpetual futures. “When we launched the perpetual swap at BitMEX in 2016, Washington’s reaction was less than warm,” Hayes told Cointelegraph. “Ten years later, Coinbase is in federal court defending the right to offer them on US stocks. I’m flattered. Imitation is the sincerest form of regulation.” Coinbase and five other companies submitted a brief on Monday opposing the alliance’s request to block trading in perpetual futures tied to individual stocks. The court accepted the brief on Tuesday. The Capital Markets Alliance Association (CMAA), which brought the lawsuit, says the contracts should be treated as security-based swaps, which face tighter restrictions on retail trading. Hayes was CEO of BitMEX when the crypto derivatives exchange launched its Bitcoin perpetual swap, which let traders take leveraged positions on Bitcoin without a fixed expiration date. The product helped make perpetual swaps a staple of crypto trading. The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) reportedly submitted a proposed court brief on Monday, opposing the alliance’s request to temporarily halt trading in the contracts. The agency said it was reviewing the exchanges’ rules for listing the contracts. The brief left open whether the SEC would set those rules aside and whether the contracts qualify as security futures or security-based swaps. Related: EU DeFi proposals could push users to riskier platforms, says Coinbase exec In a Tuesday court filing, CMAA said that the CFTC had approved the contracts without adequately explaining its decision or addressing unresolved regulatory questions. The group also cited about $375 million in reported 24-hour notional trading volume for Kalshi’s stock perpetuals shortly after launch, claiming the products were already diverting business from traditional stock markets. Stock perpetuals let traders speculate on individual share prices without owning the underlying stocks. Unlike traditional futures, the contracts have no fixed expiration date. On Nov. 3, US District Judge Valerie Caproni denied the group’s request for a temporary restraining order because it had yet to show likely irreparable harm. She found the alliance was likely to succeed on its claim that the CFTC exceeded its authority. Wojciech Kaszycki, strategy adviser to BTCS SA, said the lack of a fixed expiration or delivery date could complicate the case for treating perpetual contracts as futures. Kaszycki told Cointelegraph that the case “sale for future delivery.”  However, he warned that a ruling against the CFTC could push trading activity toward offshore and decentralized platforms. “The product doesn’t die; it just changes address,” he said. De redactie van NRC selecteert de beste artikelen uit The Economist voor een breder perspectief op internationale politiek en economie. Lees meer over de samenwerking.  A journey through the annals of corporate crises.  			Dit artikel komt uit The Economist  In the gossip columns it is the story of a steamy affair between an American billionaire who wears a leather jacket and a younger woman who allegedly works for Chinese intelligence. On Wall Street it illustrates a three-fold concentration risk: the danger of a stock market which depends on one technology, which depends on one firm, which depends on one man. In Washington they talk of a rotten Commerce Department, the closeness of President Donald Trump to tech bosses, and divisions in the Republican Party over China. „Two clichés make us laugh. A hundred clichés move us,” wrote Umberto Eco of the film „Casablanca”. And so it is with the Jensen Huang affair: not one scandal, but many. De redactie van NRC selecteert de beste artikelen uit The Economist voor een breder perspectief op internationale politiek en economie. The annals of corporate crisis contain nothing like it. Chief executives frequently face trouble in the boardroom over something that has happened in the bedroom. Every few years some more serious crisis fundamentally changes how the world views an important firm. These things do not happen simultaneously. John Browne was the oil industry’s „sun king”. In 2007 the BP boss resigned after telling a „white lie” in court about a relationship: a mark on the man, but not so much his firm. Conversely, there was not one individual to blame for, and nothing titillating about, BP’s oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico three years later. Rupert Murdoch’s media empire has been shaped by his five marriages and four divorces. But Wendi Deng, his wife at the time, never hacked phones for the News of the World. After the crisis comes the crisis response. This means a press release which attempts to maximise contrition and minimise legal risk. Mr Huang sent an all-staff email which mixed the panicked clichés of the disloyal husband („cannot undo what I have done”) with those of the disgraced leader („privilege of my life”). In all communications, the word „independent” must be used as frequently and liberally as possible: Nvidia’s „independent directors” tasked „independent counsel” to do an „independent investigation”. Sides are quickly chosen. Mr Trump jumped to Mr Huang’s defence. „He’s got to stay in that seat, at all costs” said one presenter of „All-In”, a bro-ish tech podcast, going all-in to defend Mr Huang and protect the stock market. Bad news often begets more bad news. Reports then emerged that Mr Huang may also have slept with a subordinate and on November 12th Nvidia announced that Mr Huang had resigned from the firm. He went quicker than most. Volkswagen’s boss resigned within a week after its emissions-rigging scandal in 2015. The boss of Wells Fargo lasted a month after the bank was fined for opening thousands of fake accounts in 2016. Boeing’s boss stuck around for a year after a 737 MAX crashed in 2018. The worst crises linger. Boeing’s next boss was felled by the same issue. The very worst become lengthy trials. In the early 2000s Roland Dumas, a French government minister, was tried (and eventually acquitted) over his girlfriend’s lobbying for a state-owned oil firm. Some end up immortalised in salacious books. The same girlfriend recounted the affair in a tell-all entitled „The Whore of the Republic”. Mr Huang’s Chinese affair could go down as the most expensive shag in history. Nvidia is worth perhaps $500bn less than it was at the end of last week, which ranks this among the most costly corporate crises of all time. (The sum is greater still when you consider that the rest of the market is up.) The ultimate financial cost depends on two hard questions. How much was the influence wielded by Mr Huang in the White House actually worth? And can Colette Kress, the chief financial officer who Nvidia’s board said will run the company until a permanent successor is found, maintain the carefully balanced financial deals that Mr Huang assembled? Both matter not only for the chipmaker’s shareholders, but all of Silicon Valley. Mr Huang was the industry’s most vocal lobbyist and its keenest financial backer. The worst scandals are obvious in hindsight. Researchers drew attention to Volkswagen’s dodgy emissions figures a year before it was sued by the American government over „dieselgate”. A report by a short-seller on Mr Huang’s dealings with his mistress, Alice Huang, was published in May. That she might be a Chinese agent would have been obvious to Mr Huang had he inquired about her background: before going into business, Ms Huang worked at a Chinese state-run broadcaster known by its unimprovable acronym, „CCTV”. Mr Huang’s lack of inquisitiveness is bested only by that of Neil Bush, son of one American president and brother of another. When travelling in Asia during the 1990s, women would show up uninvited to his hotel room and have sex with him. „It was very unusual,” Mr Bush said later during his divorce proceedings. A great scandal is like a sponge, soaking up everything around it. The Huang affair is likely to become the focus of corruption inquiries by Democrats in Washington. How might it have been prevented? Investment restrictions have been adopted in recent years to prevent the Chinese from acquiring secrets by buying companies. But there are no good rules to stop them sleeping with executives. Never has the stock market depended on so few people so unaccustomed to being playboys. The best precedent for the Huang affair has nothing to do with Silicon Valley, and it exploded all the way back in 1963, the year Mr Huang was born. John Profumo, an up-for-it British government minister with a national-security brief, had an affair with a young showgirl who was also said to be involved with Yevgeny Ivanov, a Soviet naval attaché. It mattered little that an official (indeed an „independent”) inquiry determined that no state secrets had been compromised by their relationship. Harold Macmillan, the prime minister, resigned soon after. Profumo withdrew from public life and spent the remainder of his days helping the poor of London’s East End. How will Mr Huang spend his?  © 2026 The Economist Newspaper Limited. All rights reserved.  			Bij Google kan je nu zelf aangeven welke nieuwsbronnen jij vaker wil zien in je zoekresultaten. Bitcoin traded around the average from March to October 2023 and again from June to mid-August this year. Decisive moves back above it on the weekly chart have preceded sharper rallies. In his latest analysis, Keith Alan, cofounder of crypto trading platform Material Indicators, flagged the 200-week SMA as having confluence with a resistance/support flip level on Bitcoin’s relative strength index (RSI).  Weekly RSI has returned to 41.5, a level that it established as support in late July after it spent several weeks attempting a breakout. “Losing 41.5 on Weekly RSI opens the door to test the cycle low at $57.7k,” Alan wrote Friday on X, noting the bullish implications that successfully defending the support zone would have. "This enables a more efficient allocation of development resources and enhances overall production speed." Crimson Desert and DokeV developer Pearl Abyss is planning to further integrate generative AI into its workflow. The South Korean studio said as much in its latest quarterly Earnings Letter, explaining that it had previously "validated game systems only after implementing them manually." Now, Pearl Abyss is using AI "to rapidly validate diverse design concepts prior to actual implementation," and argues the move "enables a more efficient allocation of development resources and enhances overall production speed." "However, AI serves strictly as a tool to support concept validation and pipeline productivity, while the core gameplay experience and actual content creation remain fully driven by our development team," the developer said. When Crimson Desert first launched, players spotted a crop of suspicious in-game images that looked like they were prompted into existence. Pearl Abyss soon explained that some "2D visual props" were generated with AI tools, but were always intended to be replaced with human-made art, before quickly patching them out of the hit open-world game. It seems Pearl Abyss is now even more keen on the controversial tech, however: "We are integrating AI technologies to enhance development productivity and overall quality. AI is being utilized across various stages of development - including the automation of repetitive tasks, content creation support, and test optimization - and we are expanding its implementation throughout our entire development pipeline. We view AI not as a substitute for human developers, but as a tool to elevate development efficiency and quality. We will continue to expand our application of AI to deliver higher-fidelity games to the market more expeditiously." Elsewhere in the letter, the studio said its previously announced creature-collector DokeV is "targeting a launch in the second half of 2028" and we should hear more about it within the year. DokeV was initially targeting a 2023 launch a few years ago. Meanwhile, Crimson Desert is being prepped for a Nintendo Switch 2 launch "in the first half of next year." The use of generative AI in game development has been a hot topic for years, though it's only become more prevalent in recent months as 'AI slop' floods Steam and big companies like Epic Games proudly adopt the tech. A recent report even estimated that around 40 percent of active developers use AI tools in their work. Vice President JD Vance is seriously considering shelving his dreams of a 2028 presidential campaign, as GOP hopefuls are rushing to distance themselves from President Donald Trump.  Vance was once considered the GOP frontrunner for 2028, but people close to him told CNN Friday that the Ohio Republican has become less than convinced of his own candidacy, following sweeping Republican losses in the midterm elections last week.  “The question isn’t if JD can do it. It’s: If the Iran war is still happening, can any Republican do it?” one Vance ally told CNN. “If they don’t end the war in Iran, no Republican has a shot at 2028.” Republicans are already turning on Vance’s nascent presidential run. As Election Day results rolled in last week, Vance received a text from one of his confidants advising him to consider sitting out of the next presidential race. Another Vance ally noted that a lot could change in two years: “Just look at how far Trump has fallen since his win.”  Meanwhile, Rich Baris, a pollster closely connected to the MAGA movement, had a more dreadful analysis: “MAGA is dead.” “The problem the vice president is going to have is that he has to motivate [MAGA voters] and make them believe again, because the Republican brand has completely lost credibility with them,” he said.  Vance’s soul-searching comes as he and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have rushed to distance themselves from the Trump administration. After Trump suffered a stunning rebuke in the midterm elections, Rubio and Vance have begun leaking to publications “like crazy,” according to Majority Report podcast host Emma Vigeland on X. TL;DR: The American Securities Association is asking a federal court to consider retail-investor harm in the challenge to single-stock perpetuals. Its November 10 submission, publicised on November 12, supports interim relief. The CFTC has defended the products as a regulated domestic alternative to offshore trading. The legal battle over US single-stock perpetuals is gaining another angle: what happens to ordinary investors while the court decides whether the products were properly authorised? The American Securities Association put that question at the centre of a submission supporting the Capital Markets Alliance’s challenge to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. ASA announced its intervention on November 12. The accompanying court-stamped documents show that its motion and proposed friend-of-the-court brief were filed on November 10, an important distinction between the announcement date and the legal event. In its filed motion and brief, ASA says it represents a perspective different from the exchange and trading firms arguing about competitive injury. It focuses on retail investors and the wider equity market. The association contends that leverage, forced liquidation and trading during thinner sessions could expose customers to substantial losses and transmit stress into underlying shares. Those are arguments advanced by an interested participant, not findings that the predicted harm has occurred. ASA is asking for a halt while the dispute proceeds. Its submission itself neither grants that relief nor settles the legal classification of perpetual contracts. The regulator’s position is set out in Chairman Michael Selig’s November 3 statement. The CFTC says the pathway involves designated contract markets that are also notice-registered with the SEC for security-futures products. Selig argues that bringing perpetual contracts into regulated US markets gives participants a domestic route to instruments used for risk management and price discovery. He also describes cooperation between the CFTC and SEC as central to the framework. That position and ASA’s objections address different sides of the same policy trade-off. Supporters emphasise regulated availability; opponents dispute whether the chosen legal category preserves the protections the law requires. Describing the debate simply as regulation versus no regulation misses that disagreement. NewsBTC previously covered the crypto and trading firms supporting the CFTC. ASA’s intervention adds an opposing retail-investor argument to that wider dispute. In the November 3 temporary-restraining-order decision, Judge Valerie Caproni denied emergency relief because the plaintiff had not demonstrated the required imminent, irreparable harm. The judge nevertheless considered the plaintiff likely to succeed on its statutory-authority argument at that stage. The result was therefore narrower than a final endorsement of the approvals. ASA’s emphasis on retail harm is relevant to the interim-relief question, but the court must determine what weight that submission deserves. An example appears in the SEC’s September notice of Nadex contract specifications: the proposed perpetual products have no fixed expiry, are cash-settled and do not convey ownership of the underlying security. That document describes a particular venue’s filing rather than every contract involved in the lawsuit. NewsBTC’s coverage of Kalshi’s separate security-futures listing standards also shows why individual filings need to be read carefully. Similar product names do not make all terms or regulatory questions identical. The next decisive development is judicial treatment of the requested relief. Another party’s argument can sharpen the dispute, but only the court’s orders establish what the litigation changes for the affected products. Any restrictions would depend on the terms and effective timing of a court order, which an advocacy announcement cannot establish. written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae. Derrick Goold of the St. Louis Post-Dispatch reports that the Cards have received interested in catchers Jimmy Crooks and Pedro Pagés, shortstop Masyn Winn and first baseman Alec Burleson, though Goold notes that the club quickly turned away the interest in both Winn and Burleson. It’s not surprising that the phone would ring. The Cardinals have been in seller mode for a while. Last offseason, they traded away Sonny Gray, Nolan Arenado, Willson Contreras and Brendan Donovan to clear payroll and make room for younger players. At this year’s deadline, they traded away Dustin May, JoJo Romero and Lars Nootbaar. Those pitchers were all impending free agents while each position player was under club control through at least 2027. With all that selling, it’s understandable that clubs with needs would keep the lines open. The Cards seem to be planning for 2027 to be another evaluation year, so players nearing free agency would be logical trade candidates. Burleson is under club control through 2028. The Cards could emerge as legitimate contenders in that time frame but it’s unclear how aggressively they plan to tackle things in that window. He just hit 26 home runs this year and slashed .279/.343/.473, so now would be a good time to sell high. MLBTR placed Burleson in the #10 spot on our list of the Top 40 Trade Candidates entering the winter.  MLBTR contributor Matt Swartz projects Burleson for an $8.3MM salary next year and he would be due another raise for 2028. The Cards don’t have to trade him now but his value will likely only go down from here as his window of club control shrinks and his salary increases. There’s also the chance of him suffering a notable injury or having a dip in performance. As mentioned, he is coming off a good season, so his stock is up.  However, if the Cards are turning down interest, then perhaps they are planning to hold him to see if the 2027 club emerges as a contender. If he stays healthy and productive but the team falls out of the race, they could give more serious consideration to a trade at next year’s deadline or in the subsequent offseason. Then again, a stronger offer later in the offseason could perhaps compel them to change their minds. Winn’s situation is slightly different. He is still under club control for another three years, so it’s much more likely the Cards are contending in his window. However, they could have considered it anyway. JJ Wetherholt came up as a shortstop prospect. He mostly played second base this year in deference to Winn and had a good season. They then could have found a second base replacement, either from within the system or on the open market. Roughly half of the climate finance that flows to Africa comes in the form of debt, with multilateral and bilateral development-finance institutions often lending at commercial rates to economies already struggling to carry the added costs. To maximize fiscal space, the instruments used to deliver climate finance need to change. JOHANNESBURG—Discussions about climate finance follow a familiar script: a financing gap is declared, pledges are announced, and the size of the commitments is the main concern. But the form that financing takes matters as much as the amount of money pledged, particularly in Africa. A global AI ecosystem controlled by the US and China would make other countries dangerously dependent on foreign technologies. A jointly funded, independent AI company could give middle powers access to open-weight models without placing their economies and national security at the mercy of either superpower. According to the Climate Policy Initiative’s most recent data, climate-finance flows to Sub-Saharan Africa reached $55 billion in 2024, more than double the 2019 level. This represents important progress. But the continent still faces several challenges. For starters, the CPI’s report “Landscape of Climate Finance in Africa 2024” showed high levels of concentration, with ten countries receiving 50% of Africa’s climate-finance flows, while the continent’s ten most climate-vulnerable countries received only 10%. The difference is even starker for private climate finance, 76% of which goes to ten countries, further narrowing access to capital. Meanwhile, multilateral climate funds under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, which are meant to deliver concessional support, account for only 2% of Africa’s climate finance. Perhaps more importantly, the report found that as much as 51% of climate finance to Africa comes in the form of debt, evenly split between concessional and market-rate borrowing. By contrast, debt accounts for only 18% of climate finance in East Asia and the Pacific, and 20% in Latin America and the Caribbean. It is also worth noting that 82% of Africa’s debt-based climate finance priced at market rates comes from official sources, mainly multilateral and bilateral development-finance institutions. The contradiction is glaring. Institutions that are supposed to support sustainable economic growth, create jobs, and improve social outcomes by financing businesses and projects deemed too risky or unattractive for private investment are lending at commercial rates to economies already struggling to carry the added costs. To be sure, this is partly a response to Africa’s immense climate-finance needs, which are estimated at just under $2 trillion until 2030, of which only 23% is currently being met. But instead of continuing to rely on debt-based lending, development-finance institutions must change the instruments through which climate finance is delivered. In 2026, 54 of the world’s most climate-vulnerable countries, many of them in Africa, will spend $304.8 billion on servicing debt, compared to $12.3 billion on climate action. That is a ratio of nearly 25 to one. While most of this debt was not borrowed specifically for climate action, servicing it still leaves policymakers with limited fiscal space for investing in such measures, with debt repayment absorbing 65% of their combined national revenue. The implications for national climate plans, known as nationally determined contributions (NDCs), are profound. The climate-vulnerable countries assessed in ActionAid’s report have budgeted for only one-quarter of their combined unconditional NDC costs, with Tanzania allocating 0.9% of its unconditional NDCs costs and Malawi allocating 10.3%. Zambia has devoted just 0.32% of its budget to climate policies, highlighting the constraints debt-burdened governments face in using public finance to fund their NDCs. Addressing these countries’ fiscal constraints requires reporting climate finance in a way that reflects its actual worth. A loan that must be repaid with interest is currently counted the same as a grant of equivalent size, which ends up overstating how much support is reaching Africa. Reporting a loan’s concessional portion rather than its full value would provide a clearer picture. The OECD’s Development Assistance Committee uses this method to measure official development assistance. Moreover, the recipient country’s debt position should be taken into consideration when determining the concessionality of loans, so that countries at moderate or high risk of debt distress receive grants rather than being saddled with an even heavier burden. There is also a strong case for lending in local currencies, so that borrowers are not also carrying exchange-rate risk, and mobilizing Africa’s domestic capital. Even though international sources provide 87% of Africa’s tracked climate finance, the continent has roughly $2.4 trillion in domestically managed bank, insurance, and pension assets. Recent domestic issuances have shown what is possible with the right regulatory frameworks and financial instruments. In February 2024, Tanzania’s Tanga UWASA issued East Africa’s first subnational water infrastructure green bond, worth Tsh53.12 billion (approximately $20 million). The bond was oversubscribed by 103%, with 65% of the total raised from domestic investors. In Zambia, Copperbelt Energy Corporation Renewables raised $150 million to finance solar capacity by issuing the country’s first green bond over two tranches, both of which were oversubscribed and priced without a sovereign guarantee. While these issuances are just a drop in the bucket compared to Africa’s total climate-financing needs, they demonstrate the potential of mobilizing the continent’s significant amounts of institutional capital. True, domestic issuances are subject to market pricing, but they remove currency risk, keep debt-service payments within domestic economies, and build a base of local institutional demand that could reduce long-term reliance on foreign lenders. None of this is a substitute for scaling up grants and concessional finance from official creditors. Rather, it gives African countries a new tool to help fund the climate transition on their own terms, as opposed to relying on money delivered through instruments that risk exacerbating the crisis. Gemini’s third-quarter trading rebound masked a deepening retail slump. Crypto exchange Gemini has just reported its lowest quarterly retail trading volume in three years, despite an increase in overall crypto trading volume. Total spot trading volume rose 18% from the second quarter to $4.5 billion, according to Gemini’s Q3 earnings report. Institutional volume climbed 26% to $3.9 billion, while retail volume fell 14% to $600 million, its lowest level since the third quarter of 2023.  Gemini said the quarterly increase in spot trading volume was “supported by increased institutional Zcash activity and expanded affiliated market-making,” but did not give a specific reason for the decline in retail trading.  Despite the retail slump, Gemini’s exchange revenue increased 7% from the previous quarter to $13.4 million as institutional revenue more than doubled. Retail traders remained its largest source of exchange revenue, contributing nearly three-quarters of the total. A number of crypto exchanges also reported softer crypto trading activity in the most recent quarter.  Coinbase reported softer retail and institutional activity, with consumer spot trading volume falling 9% from the previous quarter to $23.4 billion. Coinbase chief financial officer Alesia Haas said “continued growth in prediction markets helped offset softer crypto trading activity.” At Robinhood, crypto revenue fell 55% year-on-year to $120 million, offset by a sixfold increase in event-contract revenue to $173 million.  Related: Strategy stock sheds 5% amid MSCI index removal, Bitcoin sell-off Gemini also got some help from its own prediction exchange, Gemini Predictions, with revenue from that business unit increasing 52% quarter-on-quarter to $796,000, though it wasn’t significant enough to offset declines elsewhere.  Gemini reported stronger prediction-market activity heading into the fourth quarter, with average daily traders in October running about 50% above the third-quarter average.  Nearly a third of new prediction traders were new to Gemini, more than double the proportion in Q3. The company is also seeking to distribute its event contracts through other platforms. An August nonbinding agreement with Apex Fintech Solutions would make Gemini Titan the exclusive venue for crypto event contracts distributed through Apex’s futures brokerage to its brokerage customers, subject to definitive agreements. Explore ↓ Network ↓  By  Nicole Stawiarski    Updated 1 day ago, November 12, 2026   Gratitude is often talked about as a mindset, but it also shows up in everyday habits, emotional patterns, and the way people relate to what they already have. Some individuals naturally tend to appreciate stability, relationships, achievements, and even small comforts more deeply than others. In personality writing, birth months are often used as a playful lens to explore these differences and reflect on how people process abundance, loss, and contentment. These patterns can offer a fun way to think about gratitude and how it shapes our daily lives. As you read, notice how each birth month expresses appreciation in its own unique way. Those born in May are equally grateful for their material and non-material possessions. They only buy things they absolutely love, worrying less about price than personal value. This means they’re never stuck standing in front of their closet with nothing to wear, because every garment is a cherished and curated piece. They are proud of the personality they have accumulated through these belongings and all of the decisions they represent. The same applies to all of their relationships and other accomplishments. May natives are just as picky as the people they surround themselves with and know that things like love, trust, and respect are priceless. The investment here is time, a resource so limited they know the people who spend it on them, and in fact, investing not minutes but a part of their life. October just knows how to take it all in. They know what they have and what they don’t, and they can take stock from that reality and still know how to find contentment. Where one thing is lacking, they know how to shrink the gap with the rest of life’s blessings. In the times where being single makes them feel lonely, they choose to lean heavily into friends and family. When work is a source of stress, they show gratitude for their physical and mental wellbeing by exercising and reading. It’s like substituting ingredients in a flexible recipe. There is always something in abundance to make up the difference. It may deviate from expectations, but everyone gets fed and the result is equally delicious.  Related Articles People born in November are always so afraid of losing what they have, that they’re always working to keep or make the most of it. November-born individuals are always trying to cherish every moment with their parents and idealizes their childhood. Their gratitude is sometimes tinged with grief. They are so, so thankful for the experiences they’ve had, that they also feel sadness that those times have passed. The challenge they face is to not let those thoughts get in the way of their ability to enjoy the present. Life evolves at such a rapid pace, it’s sometimes easier to see how good something was when we’re looking at it through a rearview mirror. The same way we gush about a movie once the credits start rolling. January appreciates every single penny they have in the bank because they know how much effort it took to earn each one. They look at the credit card points they’ve earned and remember all the paid off debt they represent. They remember the early days, when they were just starting out and they had no idea how they would be able to afford rent, or a car, or any other of life’s many expenses. But those born in January are self-made, and proudly so. They value above all else what they can provide for themselves. Food in a pantry, clothes in a closet, books on a shelf. It may just be a collection of possessions, but to them it’s about the stability it represents. Being able to come home to a place of their own and know they are safe and cared for. A month after a Houthi missile attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport killed 13 people, Saudi Arabia's hotel pipeline is at a record 401 projects and 109,320 rooms, up 15% and 16% respectively from a year ago, according to Lodging Econometrics. Developers and operators told Skift they know of no projects canceled because of the attacks, though IHG CEO Elie Maalouf said some would probably be delayed. The damage is showing up elsewhere: 86% of scheduled Riyadh departures were canceled between October 8 and late October, according to Cirium data; the Saudi Grand Prix, the Future Investment Initiative, and the Red Sea International Film Festival were scrapped, postponed, or moved; and the U.S. Embassy now requires government employees to get special authorization to use any Saudi airport. This year's openings are concentrated on the Red Sea coast — Four Seasons, Rosewood, Six Senses, Equinox, Nammos, and Raffles — the properties most dependent on the international guests the attacks are deterring. Investors are leaning on a domestic base that accounted for 93.3 million tourists in 2025, or 76.1% of the total, plus religious travel for Hajj and Umrah. Growth had already stalled before October, with 61.2 million tourists in the first half of 2026, up about 1% year over year, against a Vision 2030 target of 150 million a year.
